topics.title: Arrays & Prefix Invariants
topics.shortDescription: Master contiguous memory indexing, running prefix/suffix state, in-place compaction, and boundary-safe traversal invariants.
topics.whyItMatters: Arrays underpin nearly every interview and systems problem; clear loop invariants prevent off-by-one bugs and turn O(n^2) scans into single-pass O(n) pipelines.

topics.title: Hash Maps, Sets & Canonical Keys
topics.shortDescription: Trade O(n) space for O(1) expected lookups using complement maps, frequency tables, structural signatures, and prefix-sum index maps.
topics.whyItMatters: When nested loops waste time re-scanning history, a well-chosen hash key captures exactly the past state you need in constant expected time.

topics.title: Binary Search & Monotonic Boundaries
topics.shortDescription: Eliminate half the search space every step using strict half-open or closed interval invariants over sorted arrays and monotonic predicates.
topics.whyItMatters: Binary search is notorious for infinite loops and off-by-one errors; treating it as finding the first index where a boolean predicate flips makes it rock-solid.

topics.title: Two Pointers & Partition Invariants
topics.shortDescription: Eliminate O(n^2) pair scans by coordinating converging,同-direction, or multi-way partition pointers with monotonic elimination proofs.
topics.whyItMatters: Two pointers turn nested brute-force searches into linear O(n) passes with O(1) auxiliary memory whenever sorted order or bottleneck bounds rule out entire rows/columns of pairs.

topics.title: Sliding Window & Subarray Monotonicity
topics.shortDescription: Maintain dynamic contiguous subarrays `[left..right]` using incremental window state, frequency counters, and monotonic expand/shrink invariants.
topics.whyItMatters: Every element enters via `right` at most once and exits via `left` at most once, proving O(n) amortized time for substring and subarray optimization.

topics.title: Linked Lists & Pointer Rewiring
topics.shortDescription: Manipulate node references safely without losing suffix chains using sentinel dummy heads, three-pointer reversal, and Floyd fast/slow runners.
topics.whyItMatters: Pointer bugs happen when you overwrite `.next` before saving the suffix; explicit link-state diagrams make node surgery predictable and crash-free.

topics.title: Stacks, Queues & Monotonic Frontiers
topics.shortDescription: Enforce LIFO/FIFO ordering and maintain monotonic stacks and deques to resolve next-greater, histogram-span, and sliding-extremum queries in O(n) amortized time.
topics.whyItMatters: A monotonic stack or deque discards dominated history as soon as a stronger element arrives, turning O(n^2) lookback/lookahead scans into 2n push/pop operations.

topics.title: Binary Trees, BSTs & Recursive Invariants
topics.shortDescription: Distinguish top-down inherited parameter constraints from bottom-up post-order subtree summaries and level-frozen BFS queue snapshots.
topics.whyItMatters: Most tree bugs come from mixing local parent-child checks with global ancestor bounds or mutating shared state across sibling branches.

topics.title: Heaps, Priority Queues & Streaming Extrema
topics.shortDescription: Maintain dynamic top-k subsets, k-way sorted stream frontiers, and balanced two-heap medians in O(log k) or O(log n) per update.
topics.whyItMatters: Sorting the entire dataset costs O(n log n) and requires all data upfront; a bounded heap of size k answers online streaming top-k queries in O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
keyPatterns: Size-K Min-Heap Bouncer for Top-K Largest

topics.title: Graphs, Traversals & Topological Sort
topics.shortDescription: Model networks as adjacency lists or implicit grids, enforce cycle-safe visited invariants, and solve multi-source BFS, topological sort, and shortest-path problems.
topics.whyItMatters: Graphs generalize trees by allowing cycles and multiple paths; mastering enqueue-time visited marking and Kahn indegree queues unlocks connected components, dependency scheduling, and network routing.

topics.title: Recursion & Backtracking Search Trees
topics.shortDescription: Construct combinatorial subsets, permutations, and constraint solutions by choosing, exploring, and cleanly undoing state mutations along a decision tree.
topics.whyItMatters: When no greedy or polynomial invariant exists, systematic state-space search with early sibling-duplicate and constraint pruning is the only exact way to enumerate valid configurations.
keyPatterns: Reversible Grid & O(1) Constraint Set Pruning

topics.title: Dynamic Programming & State Transitions
topics.shortDescription: Transform exponential recursive search with overlapping subproblems into polynomial time by defining minimal state parameters, base cases, and topological recurrence transitions.
topics.whyItMatters: Dynamic programming is the capstone synthesis of recursion and state tables—turning intractable sequence, knapsack, and grid optimization problems into fast, verifiable recurrences.

lessons.title: Single-Pass Loop Invariants & Running Extrema
lessons.measurableObjective: State and maintain a prefix loop invariant that tracks running minimums and best deltas in a single O(n) scan without lookahead errors.
lessons.explanation: A loop invariant is a statement about your variables that holds true before and after every iteration. When scanning an array from left to right, the cleanest invariant defines each state variable strictly in terms of the prefix `nums[0..i]`. For example, when finding the maximum gain `nums[j] - nums[i]` with `j > i`, we maintain `minSoFar = min(nums[0..i-1])` before considering `nums[i]` as a selling point, then update `minSoFar` afterward. This ordering guarantees we never pair an element with a future value or with itself when non-empty intervals are required.

stepByStep: Initialize minPrice = 7 (from index 0), bestGain = 0.
i = 1 (price 1): candidateGain = 1 - 7 = -6; bestGain stays 0; minPrice updates to 1.
i = 2 (price 5): candidateGain = 5 - 1 = 4; bestGain updates to 4; minPrice stays 1.
i = 3 (price 3): candidateGain = 3 - 1 = 2; bestGain stays 4; minPrice stays 1.
i = 4 (price 6): candidateGain = 6 - 1 = 5; bestGain updates to 5; minPrice stays 1.
i = 5 (price 4): candidateGain = 4 - 1 = 3; return bestGain = 5.
workedExample.outputDescription: 5 (buy at 1 on index 1, sell at 6 on index 4)
workedExample.invariantSummary: At the start of iteration i, minPrice equals the minimum of prices[0..i-1] and bestGain equals the maximum gain achievable using any pair (a, b) with 0 <= a < b < i.

pitfalls: Initializing bestGain to -Infinity when zero gain (no transaction) is allowed on strictly decreasing arrays.
Updating minPrice before computing candidateGain when zero-length transactions are forbidden by the problem.

edgeCase.scenario: Strictly decreasing array such as [9, 7, 4, 1]
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Code that picks the global minimum and global maximum independently will pair index 3 (val 1) with index 0 (val 9) backwards in time.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always evaluate the current index against prefix state accumulated strictly from earlier indices.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a single-pass scan where index j must be strictly greater than index i, why do we evaluate the candidate answer at index j BEFORE updating our running prefix minimum with nums[j]?

options.label: To guarantee the prefix minimum only reflects indices 0..j-1, preventing j from pairing with itself.
options.feedback: Correct! Evaluating before updating preserves the strict inequality i < j.

options.label: Because JavaScript engines optimize comparisons before assignments inside for-loops.
options.feedback: Not quite. The ordering is a logical invariant requirement, not a JIT micro-optimization.

options.label: To avoid allocating an extra variable on the stack during iteration.
options.feedback: Both orderings use the same O(1) variables; the difference is correctness when i < j is required.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Evaluating the candidate using state from 0..j-1 enforces i < j automatically.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Where in your own code do you tend to mix up inclusive prefix state (0..i) with exclusive prefix state (0..i-1)?
lessons.provenance: Original NextStep lesson on prefix invariants and single-pass extrema.

lessons.title: Complement Maps & Lookup-Before-Insert Ordering
lessons.measurableObjective: Replace O(n^2) pair searches with a single-pass complement Map while preventing an element from matching itself.
lessons.explanation: When searching for two distinct indices `i < j` such that `nums[i] + nums[j] === target`, each element `nums[j]` needs a specific partner `need = target - nums[j]`. By checking whether `seen.has(need)` BEFORE inserting `nums[j]` into the map, we guarantee that the map only contains elements from `0..j-1`. This single ordering rule eliminates self-matching when `nums[j] * 2 === target` and handles duplicate values cleanly without pre-populating a multi-map.

stepByStep: i = 0 (val 3): need = 3; Map is empty -> insert (3 -> 0).
i = 1 (val 2): need = 4; 4 not in Map -> insert (2 -> 1).
i = 2 (val 4): need = 2; 2 is in Map at index 1 -> return [1, 2] immediately.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At the moment we check `indexByVal.has(need)` in iteration i, the map stores the latest index of every value in `nums[0..i-1]`.

pitfalls: Populating the entire Map in a first pass and then matching `target - nums[i]` without checking `map.get(need) !== i`, causing `[3, 2, 4]` with target 6 to return `[0, 0]`.
Using `if (indexByVal.get(need))` in JavaScript, which evaluates to `false` when the stored index is `0`!

edgeCase.scenario: Partner resides at index 0, e.g., nums = [3, 3], target = 6
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: A truthiness check `if (map[need])` treats index `0` as falsy and misses the valid match at the first position.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always use `map.has(need)` or check `!== undefined` explicitly.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does `if (indexByVal.get(need))` cause a classic bug in JavaScript index maps?

options.label: Because index 0 is a valid array position, and 0 is falsy in JavaScript boolean contexts.
options.feedback: Spot on! Whenever index 0 holds the needed value, `if (0)` evaluates to false and skips the match.

options.label: Because Map.prototype.get throws a TypeError if the key is missing.
options.feedback: Map.prototype.get returns `undefined` for missing keys, never an exception.

options.label: Because negative numbers cannot be used as keys in a JavaScript Map.
options.feedback: JavaScript Maps support any number (including negative numbers and 0) as keys.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Index 0 is falsy in JS; always use `map.has(key)` or `map.get(key) !== undefined`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Have you ever written a two-pass hash table where a one-pass lookup-before-insert would have avoided self-collision bugs?
lessons.provenance: Original NextStep lesson on complement lookup invariants and JS Map truthiness pitfalls.

lessons.title: Half-Open Intervals & First-True Lower Bound Invariants
lessons.measurableObjective: Implement lower-bound binary search without infinite loops by maintaining a half-open candidate range [lo, hi) over a monotonic boolean predicate.
lessons.explanation: Instead of memorizing three different binary search templates (`lo <= hi`, `lo < hi`, `lo + 1 < hi`), view binary search as finding the first index where a monotonic predicate `isTrue(idx)` turns from `false` to `true` (for example, `nums[idx] >= target`). Set `lo = 0` and `hi = nums.length` (one past the end, in case no element satisfies the predicate). At every step, `mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)`. If `nums[mid] >= target`, `mid` might be the first true index, so keep it: `hi = mid`. Otherwise `mid` and everything left of it are false, so exclude `mid`: `lo = mid + 1`. Because `mid < hi` always holds when `lo < hi`, both branches strictly shrink `hi - lo`.

stepByStep: Start lo = 0, hi = 6.
mid = 3 (nums[3] = 4 >= 4): predicate is true -> hi = 3 (keep index 3 in play).
lo = 0, hi = 3 -> mid = 1 (nums[1] = 4 >= 4): predicate is true -> hi = 1.
lo = 0, hi = 1 -> mid = 0 (nums[0] = 2 < 4): predicate is false -> lo = 0 + 1 = 1.
lo === hi === 1 -> loop terminates; return 1 (the very first index of 4).
workedExample.invariantSummary: At every step, all indices < lo have nums[i] < target, and all indices >= hi (within bounds) have nums[i] >= target.

pitfalls: Setting `hi = nums.length - 1` with `while (lo < hi)`, which cannot return `nums.length` when the target is larger than every element in `nums`.
Writing `lo = mid` when `mid` is rounded down (`Math.floor`), which causes an infinite loop whenever `hi === lo + 1`.

edgeCase.scenario: Target is strictly greater than all elements, e.g., nums = [1, 3, 5], target = 9
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Clamping `hi = nums.length - 1` forces `lo` to stop at index 2 instead of insertion index 3.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Initialize `hi = nums.length`; if `lo === nums.length` at termination, all elements are `< target`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a `while (lo < hi)` loop where `mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)`, why does setting `lo = mid` in the false branch cause an infinite loop?

options.label: When hi === lo + 1, floor division sets mid === lo, so `lo = mid` leaves `[lo, hi]` completely unchanged.
options.feedback: Correct! On a 2-element interval `[lo, lo + 1]`, floor midpoint equals `lo`, so `lo = mid` makes zero progress.

options.label: Because `hi - lo` overflows 32-bit integers when `lo = mid`.
options.feedback: The issue is progress termination on a size-1 gap, not integer overflow.

options.label: Because `lo = mid` skips the middle element when the array has odd length.
options.feedback: `lo = mid` keeps `mid`; the bug is that it fails to shrink the interval when `hi - lo === 1`.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Floor division biases `mid` toward `lo`, so the `lo` update must be `mid + 1` (or `mid` must use `Math.ceil` with `hi = mid - 1`).

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How can you express "last index <= target" in terms of `lowerBound(nums, target + 1) - 1`?
lessons.provenance: Binary search lower-bound invariant adapted from Open Data Structures (CC BY 4.0) with original NextStep boundary proof.

lessons.title: Converging Pointers & Sorted Pair Elimination Proofs
lessons.measurableObjective: Prove why incrementing `left` when `nums[left] + nums[right] < target` (and decrementing `right` when `> target`) never misses a valid pair in a sorted array.
lessons.explanation: In a sorted array `nums[0..n-1]`, placing `left = 0` and `right = n - 1` starts at the top-right corner of the conceptual `n × n` pair matrix. If `nums[left] + nums[right] < target`, then because `nums[right]` is the largest remaining element in `[left..right]`, pairing `nums[left]` with ANY smaller index `k < right` will also be `< target`. Thus `left` is provably useless and `left += 1` eliminates an entire row of pairs in O(1) time. Symmetrically, `nums[left] + nums[right] > target` proves `right` is too large for every remaining index `>= left`, so `right -= 1` eliminates an entire column.

stepByStep: Start left = 0 (1), right = 4 (9). sum = 1 + 9 = 10 === target -> return [0, 4].
Suppose target = 9 instead: left = 0 (1), right = 4 (9) -> sum = 10 > 9 -> right decrements to 3 (6).
left = 0 (1), right = 3 (6) -> sum = 7 < 9 -> left increments to 1 (3).
left = 1 (3), right = 3 (6) -> sum = 9 === target -> return [1, 3].
workedExample.invariantSummary: Before each iteration, no valid pair (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] + nums[j] === target has i < left or j > right.

pitfalls: Using `while (left <= right)` when a single element cannot be paired with itself.
Applying converging two-sum pointers to an unsorted array without sorting or preserving original indices.

edgeCase.scenario: Negative numbers and duplicate values such as `[-4, -1, -1, 2, 5]`, `target = -2`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Assuming sums are always positive or stopping early when `nums[right] > target` fails when negative numbers can pull the sum down.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Never prune `right` just because `nums[right] > target`; only compare the full pair sum `nums[left] + nums[right]` against `target`.

knowledgeCheck.question: When `nums` is sorted ascending and `nums[left] + nums[right] > target`, why is it safe to decrement `right` without checking `(left + 1, right)`?

options.label: Because `nums[left]` is the smallest element in `[left..right]`, so any `k > left` satisfies `nums[k] + nums[right] >= nums[left] + nums[right] > target`.
options.feedback: Correct! Every remaining partner for `right` is at least as large as `nums[left]`, so `right` cannot be part of any valid pair.

options.label: Because `nums[right]` is always positive.
options.feedback: The proof holds even if all numbers are negative; it relies on sorted monotonicity, not sign.

options.label: Because binary search already checked `left + 1`.
options.feedback: Two pointers does not run binary search; monotonicity alone rules out `(k, right)` for all `k >= left`.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Sorted order guarantees `nums[left]` is the minimum available partner for `nums[right]`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How does thinking of `left` and `right` as eliminating a full row or column of pairs clarify why the algorithm takes at most `n` steps?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from Tech Interview Handbook two-pointer patterns and NextStep invariant proofs.

lessons.title: Fixed-Length Rolling Windows & O(1) Boundary Deltas
lessons.measurableObjective: Maintain exact aggregate state across every contiguous window of fixed length `k` by adding the entering element `nums[i]` and subtracting the exiting element `nums[i - k]`.
lessons.explanation: When a problem asks for the maximum sum, average, or vowel count across all contiguous subarrays of fixed size `k`, recomputing the window from scratch takes `O(n * k)`. Notice that consecutive windows `[i - k..i - 1]` and `[i - k + 1..i]` share `k - 1` elements! Once the initial window `nums[0..k - 1]` is accumulated, each step `i` from `k` to `n - 1` updates the state in O(1) via `windowSum += nums[i] - nums[i - k]`.

lines: for (let i = k; i < nums.length; i += 1) {

stepByStep: Seed first window [0..3] ([1, 12, -5, -6]): windowSum = 2, maxSum = 2.
i = 4 (enter 50, exit nums[0] = 1): windowSum = 2 + 50 - 1 = 51; maxSum updates to 51.
i = 5 (enter 3, exit nums[1] = 12): windowSum = 51 + 3 - 12 = 42; maxSum stays 51.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At the end of iteration i (for i >= k - 1), windowSum equals the exact sum of the k elements in nums[i - k + 1 .. i].

pitfalls: Initializing `maxSum = 0` instead of `windowSum`, which fails when all window sums are negative.
Subtracting `nums[i - k + 1]` instead of `nums[i - k]`, which evicts an element that should still remain inside the window.

edgeCase.scenario: Single-window array where `k === nums.length` and all values are negative (`[-5]`, `k = 1`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If `maxSum` starts at `0`, the second loop never runs and `0 / 1 = 0` is returned instead of `-5`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always initialize `maxSum = windowSum` immediately after seeding the first `k` elements.

knowledgeCheck.question: When `right = i` enters a fixed-size window of length `k` (0-indexed), which index is exiting the window?

options.label: `i - k`, because the new window spans `[i - k + 1 .. i]` which contains exactly `k` elements.
options.feedback: Correct! `i - (i - k + 1) + 1 = k` elements remain in the window after `i - k` exits.

options.label: `i - k + 1`, the leftmost index of the new window.
options.feedback: `i - k + 1` is the first index KEPT in the new window; `i - k` is the index that just fell off the left edge.

options.label: `i - 1`, the immediately preceding index.
options.feedback: That would only keep a window of size 1!

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A window ending at `i` of length `k` covers `[i - k + 1 .. i]`, so `i - k` just exited.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is dividing `maxSum / k` once at the end preferable to dividing `windowSum / k` on every iteration?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from Tech Interview Handbook sliding window patterns.

lessons.title: Sentinel Dummy Heads & Safe Pointer Rewiring
lessons.measurableObjective: Eliminate head-deletion and empty-list special cases using a stack-allocated sentinel `dummy` node (`dummy.next = head`).
lessons.explanation: Every linked-list insertion or deletion requires modifying the `.next` pointer of the **predecessor** node. The original `head` node has no predecessor, forcing messy `if (head === target)` branches that break when the first node itself is deleted or replaced. Creating `const dummy = { val: 0, next: head }` gives `head` a real predecessor (`dummy`)! You advance a `prev` or `tail` pointer starting at `dummy`, perform uniform `prev.next = ...` rewiring, and return `dummy.next` at the end.

stepByStep: dummy -> null, tail = dummy.
Compare 1 <= 2: tail.next = l1(1); l1 advances to 4; tail advances to 1.
Compare 4 > 2: tail.next = l2(2); l2 advances to 3; tail advances to 2.
Compare 4 > 3: tail.next = l2(3); l2 advances to null; tail advances to 3.
Loop ends; tail.next = l1(4); return dummy.next (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4).
workedExample.invariantSummary: dummy.next points to the head of the merged prefix, and tail points to its last node.

pitfalls: Returning `head` instead of `dummy.next` when the original `head` was removed or moved.
Forgetting `tail = tail.next` inside the loop, which overwrites `dummy.next` on every iteration.

edgeCase.scenario: Removing the 1st node of a 1-element list (`Remove Nth Node From End`, `n = 1` on `[10]`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Without a dummy node, `fast` reaches `null` immediately and `slow.next = slow.next.next` dereferences `null`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Start both `slow` and `fast` at `dummy`; to remove the `n`-th from end, advance `fast` by `n + 1` steps so `slow` stops at the predecessor (`dummy`).

knowledgeCheck.question: When removing the `n`-th node from the end of a list of length `L` in one pass, why should `slow` and `fast` start at `dummy` instead of `head`?

options.label: So that when `n === L` (deleting the original `head`), `slow` stops at `dummy` and `slow.next = slow.next.next` cleanly updates `dummy.next`.
options.feedback: Correct! Starting at `dummy` gives the original `head` a predecessor node.

options.label: Because `head.next` is read-only in JavaScript.
options.feedback: Node properties are mutable; `dummy` is used to unify predecessor logic when `head` itself is deleted.

options.label: To reduce the time complexity from O(n^2) to O(n).
options.feedback: Both take O(n) time; `dummy` eliminates null-predecessor crashes when deleting the first node.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Deleting a node requires its predecessor; `dummy` is the predecessor of `head`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which linked-list edge cases disappear immediately as soon as you introduce `const dummy = { val: 0, next: head }`?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from Open Data Structures (CC-BY) linked list sentinel techniques.

lessons.title: LIFO Delimiter Matching & Auxiliary State Stacks
lessons.measurableObjective: Validate nested delimiters and maintain O(1) running stack minimums by pairing each pushed element with its historical prefix state.
lessons.explanation: A Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) stack naturally models nested scopes: the most recently opened delimiter must be the very first one closed. Two failure modes must be checked: (1) encountering a closing bracket when the stack is empty or its top does not match, and (2) finishing the string with unclosed brackets still on the stack (`stack.length > 0`). Similarly, in `MinStack`, storing `[val, Math.min(val, currentMin)]` on each push snapshots the prefix minimum at that stack depth so `pop()` restores the previous minimum in O(1) time.

stepByStep: Read "(", "[", "{": all are openers -> stack = ["(", "[", "{"].
Read "}": matches stack.pop() ("{") -> stack = ["(", "["].
Read "]": matches stack.pop() ("[") -> stack = ["("].
Read ")": matches stack.pop() ("(") -> stack = [].
End of string: stack.length === 0 -> return true.
workedExample.outputDescription: true (all nested scopes closed in exact reverse order)
workedExample.invariantSummary: After processing prefix s[0..i], stack contains the currently open delimiters from outermost (bottom) to innermost (top).

pitfalls: Returning `true` at the end of the loop without checking `stack.length === 0`, which falsely accepts `"((("`.
Using a single counter `openCount` for multiple bracket types, which falsely accepts interleaved `"([)]"`.

edgeCase.scenario: String starting with a closing bracket `")("` or odd-length string `"([]"`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Calling `stack.pop()` without checking emptiness or comparing against `undefined` carefully can misbehave if the map lookup is inverted.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always map closing brackets to their expected opening bracket and check `stack.length === 0 || stack.pop() !== match[ch]`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does a simple integer counter `balance += 1` / `balance -= 1` work for single-type parentheses `"()"` but fail when `"[]"` and `"{}"` are also present?

options.label: Because counts ignore relative ordering and cannot detect interleaved cross-nesting like `"([)]"` where counts are balanced but the innermost opener is `"["` while `")"` arrives first.
options.feedback: Correct! Multiple delimiter types require remembering the exact sequence of open scopes on a LIFO stack.

options.label: Because integer counters overflow on strings longer than 32 characters.
options.feedback: JavaScript safe integers reach `2^53 - 1`; the issue is cross-type ordering, not numeric overflow.

options.label: Because square brackets have higher operator precedence than parentheses.
options.feedback: All bracket types have equal nesting rules; the innermost open bracket must always close first.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: LIFO ordering enforces that the most recently opened bracket type is closed first.

lessons.title: Bottom-Up Post-Order Aggregation (Height, Balance & Diameter)
lessons.measurableObjective: Compute tree height, height-balance, and longest path diameter in a single O(n) post-order DFS pass without redundant subtree re-traversals.
lessons.explanation: Naive tree code often computes `height(node.left)` and `height(node.right)` inside a top-down check `isBalanced(node)`, causing `O(n^2)` time on skewed trees because subtrees are re-measured at every ancestor. Instead, a **bottom-up post-order DFS** visits `left` and `right` children first, combines their returned summaries in O(1), and returns the parent’s summary upward. For example: (1) in `Balanced Binary Tree`, returning `-1` as a sentinel height whenever a subtree is unbalanced propagates failure to the root in O(n); (2) in `Diameter of Binary Tree`, the longest path whose highest point (LCA) is `node` has length `leftHeight + rightHeight`, which we maximize while returning `1 + Math.max(leftHeight, rightHeight)` to `node`’s parent!

workedExample.inputDescription: Tree with root 1, left child 2 (children 4, 5), right child 3
stepByStep: Leaves 4, 5, 3: leftH = 0, rightH = 0 -> maxDiameter = 0, each returns height 1.
Node 2: leftH (from 4) = 1, rightH (from 5) = 1 -> leftH + rightH = 2 updates maxDiameter = 2; returns 1 + max(1, 1) = 2.
Root 1: leftH (from 2) = 2, rightH (from 3) = 1 -> leftH + rightH = 3 updates maxDiameter = 3; returns 3.
Final maxDiameter = 3 edges (path 4 - 2 - 1 - 3 or 5 - 2 - 1 - 3).
workedExample.invariantSummary: After height(u) finishes, it returns the exact node-height of subtree u, and maxDiameter >= leftH(v) + rightH(v) for all descendants v of u.

pitfalls: Returning `leftH + rightH` to the parent instead of `1 + Math.max(leftH, rightH)`—a path continuing upward to a parent can only use ONE child branch, not both!
Assuming the longest path must pass through the global `root` (it can lie entirely inside a deep left or right subtree).

edgeCase.scenario: Single-node tree `[1]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Confusing node count (`1`) with edge count (`0`) on a single-node tree returns `1` instead of `0`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: With base case `height(null) = 0`, a leaf has `leftH = 0, rightH = 0`, so `leftH + rightH = 0` edges and it returns height `1`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In `diameterOfBinaryTree`, why does `height(node)` update `maxDiameter` with `leftH + rightH`, but return `1 + Math.max(leftH, rightH)` to its caller?

options.label: A path bending at `node` uses both `left` and `right` (`leftH + rightH`), while a path ascending to `node`’s parent cannot fork and uses only the deeper branch (`1 + max(leftH, rightH)`).
options.feedback: Spot on! A simple path in a tree can have only one highest turning point (LCA).

options.label: Because `leftH` and `rightH` are always equal.
options.feedback: Subtree heights can differ arbitrarily.

options.label: To avoid integer overflow.
options.feedback: The distinction is structural: a simple path cannot visit all 3 of (left child, right child, parent).

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A path turning at `node` spans `leftH + rightH`, while a path ascending to `node`’s parent extends the single longest downward branch.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Where else in tree problems do we distinguish "best answer turning at `node`" from "best single branch extending upward to `node`’s parent"?

lessons.title: Implicit Array Binary Heaps & Sift Up/Down Invariants
lessons.measurableObjective: Map a complete binary tree into a 0-indexed array (`parent = floor((i-1)/2)`, `left = 2i+1`, `right = 2i+2`) and restore the min-heap invariant on push and pop.
lessons.explanation: A binary heap is a **complete binary tree** (every level filled left-to-right) that satisfies the **heap-order invariant**: in a min-heap, `heap[parent(i)] <= heap[i]` for every `i > 0`, which guarantees the global minimum sits at `heap[0]`. Because the tree has no gaps, it requires zero node objects or pointers! In a 0-indexed array, index `i` has `parent = Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`, `left = 2 * i + 1`, and `right = 2 * i + 2`. Pushing appends to the end and `siftUp`s while `< parent`; popping swaps `heap[0]` with `heap.pop()` and `siftDown`s by swapping with the **smaller** of its two children.

workedExample.inputDescription: Min-heap array [2, 5, 4, 9, 6]; push value 1 at index 5
stepByStep: Append 1 at i = 5: heap = [2, 5, 4, 9, 6, 1].
i = 0 terminates loop; new minimum 1 sits at root index 0.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Every node except possibly index i satisfies heap[parent] <= heap[node]; swapping i with parent(i) moves the violation strictly closer to root 0.

pitfalls: During `siftDown` in a min-heap, swapping with the left child whenever `left < current` without checking if the right child is even smaller (which puts the larger child above the smaller child!).
Mixing 1-indexed formulas (`2i`, `2i+1`) with 0-indexed arrays (`2i+1`, `2i+2`).

edgeCase.scenario: Popping the only element from a 1-element heap `[7]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If you overwrite `heap[0] = heap.pop()` without checking `heap.length === 1`, you push `7` back into `heap[0]` and never empty the heap!
edgeCase.howToHandle: If `heap.length === 1`, simply `return heap.pop()`; only replace `heap[0]` and `siftDown` when elements remain.

knowledgeCheck.question: During `siftDown` in a min-heap, when node `i` is larger than both `left` and `right` children, why MUST you swap `i` with `Math.min(heap[left], heap[right])` rather than always swapping with `left`?

options.label: Because whichever child moves up to index `i` becomes the new parent of the other child, so it must be `<=` the other child to preserve the min-heap invariant.
options.feedback: Correct! Promoting the larger child would immediately violate `parent <= child` against its sibling.

options.label: Because the left subtree is always taller than the right subtree.
options.feedback: Child subtree height does not determine heap-order validity; the smaller value must become the parent.

options.label: Because binary heaps are Binary Search Trees.
options.feedback: Heaps are NOT BSTs: left and right children have no `<` or `>` ordering relative to each other.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The promoted child becomes the parent of its former sibling, so the smaller child must be promoted.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a binary heap NOT a Binary Search Tree, and what operations is each structure optimized for?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from Open Data Structures (CC-BY) binary heap array representation.

lessons.title: Graph Representations & Visited Set Discipline
lessons.measurableObjective: Convert edge lists or 2D grids into traversable adjacency models and enforce cycle-safe visited invariants in O(V + E) time.
lessons.explanation: Unlike trees, graphs can contain cycles and multiple paths between the same pair of vertices. Whether a graph is stored as an adjacency list `adj[u]` or implicitly as 4-directional grid neighbors, every traversal must track a `visited` set (or sink grid cells in-place) so each vertex is expanded at most once in `O(V + E)` time.

lines: if (r < 0 || r >= grid.length || c < 0 || c >= grid[0].length || grid[r][c] !== "1") return;
sink(r + 1, c); sink(r - 1, c); sink(r, c + 1); sink(r, c - 1);

stepByStep: Scan r = 0, c = 0 ("1"): increment count = 1 and launch sink(0, 0).
sink marks (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), and (1, 2) as "0" because they are 4-directionally connected.
Outer nested loop sees only "0"s on remaining cells and returns count = 1.
workedExample.outputDescription: 1 connected island component in O(R * C) time
workedExample.invariantSummary: Every land cell in a discovered island is marked visited ("0") before the outer scan advances to its coordinates.

pitfalls: Forgetting to add both `(u -> v)` and `(v -> u)` when building an adjacency list for an undirected graph.
Checking `grid[r][c]` before verifying that `r` and `c` are within `[0, rows)` and `[0, cols)`.

edgeCase.scenario: Cyclic graph in Clone Graph (`1 <-> 2`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If you insert `map.set(node, clone)` AFTER recursing on `node.neighbors`, the cycle `1 -> 2 -> 1` recurses infinitely!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always register `map.set(node, clone)` BEFORE iterating over `node.neighbors`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why must you mark a node visited (or store its clone in the hash map) BEFORE recursing on its neighbors in a graph with cycles?

options.label: Because a descendant neighbor on the active call stack may have an edge pointing back to the current node, which would cause infinite recursion if the node is not yet marked visited.
options.feedback: Correct! Pre-marking breaks cycles immediately when a back-edge is encountered.

options.label: To sort the neighbors in ascending order.
options.feedback: Marking visited does not change neighbor ordering.

options.label: Because leaf nodes have no incoming edges.
options.feedback: In an undirected graph, every edge is bidirectional.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Pre-marking on entry ensures any back-edge to an ancestor on the call stack sees it as already visited.

lessons.provenance: Adapted from OpenDSA graph representation and traversal invariants.

lessons.title: Decision Trees & The Choose-Explore-Unchoose Invariant
lessons.measurableObjective: Model combinatorial generation as depth-first traversal of a decision tree while keeping a single shared `path` buffer clean.
lessons.explanation: Backtracking explores an implicit decision tree using a single mutable candidate array `path`. Before descending into a child call, you mutate `path.push(choice)`; immediately after the recursive call returns, you execute `path.pop()` so sibling branches see the exact state that existed upon entry. Whenever `path` represents a completed configuration, you MUST push a shallow copy `[...path]` into `results`.

lines: for (let i = start; i < nums.length; i += 1) {

stepByStep: dfs(0): records []. i = 0 pushes 1 -> dfs(1) records [1].
Inside dfs(1): i = 1 pushes 2 -> dfs(2) records [1, 2]. Pop 2 restores path = [1]; dfs(1) finishes and pop 1 restores path = [].
Back in dfs(0): i = 1 pushes 2 -> dfs(2) records [2]. Pop 2 restores path = []. Returns [[], [1], [1, 2], [2]].
workedExample.invariantSummary: Upon exit from dfs(start), the shared path array is byte-for-byte identical to its state upon entry.

pitfalls: Calling `res.push(path)` without cloning `[...path]`, which fills `res` with references to the same array that ends up empty `[]`!
Forgetting `path.pop()` after the recursive call returns.

edgeCase.scenario: Single-element input `nums = [5]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If the base case only records subsets when `path.length > 0`, the empty subset `[]` is missed.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Recording `res.push([...path])` unconditionally at the top of `dfs(start)` captures both `[]` at the root and every non-empty prefix node.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens if you write `res.push(path)` instead of `res.push([...path])` inside a backtracking search?

options.label: Every entry in `res` points to the same mutable `path` array, which is popped back to `[]` by the time the root call finishes.
options.feedback: Correct! Cloning `[...path]` snapshots the current elements before future `.pop()` calls mutate `path`.

options.label: The code runs in O(1) time.
options.feedback: It still explores all branches, but overwrites the saved results.

options.label: Only the longest subset is kept.
options.feedback: Because every push is matched by a pop, `path` is empty `[]` at termination.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Arrays are reference types in JavaScript; `[...path]` creates an independent snapshot.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is the maximum recursion call stack depth of `subsets(nums)` only `O(n)` even though the total number of subsets generated is `2^n`?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from OpenDSA backtracking and recursive state-tree templates.

lessons.title: Overlapping Subproblems: Memoization to 1D Rolling Tabulation
lessons.measurableObjective: Collapse exponential recursive trees with overlapping subproblems into O(n) bottom-up state transitions and O(1) rolling scalars.
lessons.explanation: When a recursive recurrence like `ways(i) = ways(i - 1) + ways(i - 2)` (Climbing Stairs) or `rob(i) = Math.max(rob(i - 1), nums[i] + rob(i - 2))` (House Robber) recomputes the same index `i` across exponentially many branches, caching each state in `dp[i]` solves every subproblem once in `O(n)` time. Better yet, when `dp[i]` depends only on `dp[i - 1]` and `dp[i - 2]`, two rolling variables `prev2` and `prev1` reduce auxiliary space to `O(1)`.

stepByStep: Init: prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0.
x = 2: curr = max(0, 0 + 2) = 2 -> prev2 = 0, prev1 = 2.
x = 7: curr = max(2, 0 + 7) = 7 -> prev2 = 2, prev1 = 7.
workedExample.invariantSummary: After processing prefix nums[0..i], prev1 equals the maximum non-adjacent sum in nums[0..i] and prev2 equals the maximum in nums[0..i-1].

pitfalls: Using an alternating even/odd index sum, which misses optimal patterns that skip two houses in a row like `[2, 1, 1, 2]` (optimal `2 + 2 = 4`).
In House Robber II (circular street), forgetting the single-element base case `nums.length === 1` when slicing `nums.slice(0, n - 1)` and `nums.slice(1)`.

edgeCase.scenario: nums = [2, 1, 1, 2] where optimal choice skips two consecutive middle houses (indices 1 and 2)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Summing only even indices (`2 + 1 = 3`) or odd indices (`1 + 2 = 3`) misses `nums[0] + nums[3] = 4`!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Because `prev1` carries forward the best of `0..i-1` (`dp[1] = max(2, 1) = 2`), at `i = 3` (`x = 2`), `prev2 + x` computes `dp[1] + 2 = 4`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In House Robber II, where houses `0` and `n - 1` are adjacent in a circle, how do we reduce the circular constraint to two linear House Robber passes?

options.label: Since houses `0` and `n - 1` cannot both be robbed, every valid robbery either excludes house `n - 1` (`nums[0..n-2]`) or excludes house `0` (`nums[1..n-1]`), so we take the max of those two linear ranges.
options.feedback: Correct! Splitting a circular constraint into two linear subproblems is a classic DP reduction.

options.label: Run linear DP on `nums` and subtract `Math.min(nums[0], nums[n - 1])`.
options.feedback: You only need to subtract if the optimal linear solution actually robbed BOTH `0` and `n - 1`, and even then a different middle choice might be better.

options.label: Concatenate `nums` with itself and divide the answer by 2.
options.feedback: Doubling the array still allows robbing across the seam.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Any valid subset of a cycle omits at least one endpoint of the seam `(0, n - 1)`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: When debugging a new DP recurrence, why is starting with top-down recursion + memoization often easier to reason about before converting to bottom-up rolling variables?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from CLRS Dynamic Programming optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

lessons.title: Prefix Sums & Left/Right Accumulation Without Division
lessons.measurableObjective: Construct prefix sums and two-pass prefix/suffix accumulations so range queries and leave-one-out products run in O(1) per index without division-by-zero traps.
lessons.explanation: A prefix table precomputes cumulative state so you never re-sum the same subarray twice. Using a 1-indexed padded array `P` of length `n + 1` where `P[k]` stores the sum of `nums[0..k-1]` makes the sum of any closed slice `nums[L..R]` simply `P[R + 1] - P[L]`, eliminating special cases for `L = 0`. When a problem asks for the combination of everything except index `i` (such as Product of Array Except Self), division fails whenever a zero appears. Instead, combine the exclusive prefix product `prod(0..i-1)` with the exclusive suffix product `prod(i+1..n-1)` in two clean passes.

stepByStep: Pass 1 (left-to-right exclusive prefix): out becomes [1, 2, 6, 0].
Pass 2 i = 3 (val 4): suffix = 1 -> out[3] = 0 * 1 = 0; suffix becomes 4.
Pass 2 i = 2 (val 0): suffix = 4 -> out[2] = 6 * 4 = 24; suffix becomes 0.
Pass 2 i = 1 (val 3): suffix = 0 -> out[1] = 2 * 0 = 0; suffix becomes 0.
Pass 2 i = 0 (val 2): suffix = 0 -> out[0] = 1 * 0 = 0; return [0, 0, 24, 0].
workedExample.invariantSummary: After pass 1, out[i] holds the product of nums[0..i-1]. During pass 2 at index i, suffix holds the product of nums[i+1..n-1].

pitfalls: Multiplying `prefix *= nums[i]` BEFORE assigning `out[i] = prefix`, which accidentally includes `nums[i]` in its own exclusion product.
Using total product divided by `nums[i]`, which throws NaN/Infinity when `nums` contains one or more zeros.

edgeCase.scenario: Input contains exactly one zero vs. two or more zeros (e.g., [0, 4, 0])
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: A single zero leaves one non-zero entry at the zero index, whereas two zeros force every output entry to be 0.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Prefix/suffix multiplication handles 0, 1, or multiple zeros naturally without branching.

knowledgeCheck.question: With a padded prefix sum array P of length n + 1 where P[0] = 0 and P[k] = sum(nums[0..k-1]), which expression gives the sum of the inclusive slice nums[L..R]?

options.label: P[R + 1] - P[L]
options.feedback: Correct! P[R + 1] sums indices 0..R and P[L] sums indices 0..L-1, leaving L..R.

options.label: P[R] - P[L - 1]
options.feedback: That is the unpadded formula, which goes out of bounds at L = 0.

options.label: P[R + 1] - P[L + 1]
options.feedback: Subtracting P[L + 1] would wrongly exclude nums[L] from the slice sum.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: P[R + 1] - P[L] cleanly cancels indices 0..L-1 and works even when L = 0.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How does storing the exclusive prefix (`0..i-1`) simplify combining left and right state at index `i`?

lessons.title: Frequency Tables, Anagram Signatures & Canonical Keys
lessons.measurableObjective: Group equivalent items in O(n * k) time by designing collision-free canonical string keys from character or structural frequencies.
lessons.explanation: When two items are considered equivalent (like anagrams or shifted strings), sorting each item takes `O(k log k)` per item, or you can build a fixed-alphabet frequency signature in `O(k)`. Crucially, when serializing a frequency array `[1, 0, 11, ...]` into a hash key, you MUST include a delimiter (such as `counts.join("#")`). Without a delimiter, `[1, 11]` and `[11, 1]` both serialize to `"111"` and collide!

stepByStep: "bdddddddddd" has 1 "b" (index 1) and 10 "d"s (index 3).
"bbbbbbbbbbc" has 10 "b"s (index 1) and 1 "c" (index 2).
Without delimiter (`join("")`), both produce "...010100..." and falsely group together!
With `join("#")`, they produce `0#1#0#10#...` vs `0#10#1#0#...`, keeping them distinct.
workedExample.outputDescription: Two separate canonical keys with zero collision
workedExample.invariantSummary: Two strings map to the same "#" delimited 26-slot count vector if and only if they contain the exact same multiset of lowercase letters.

pitfalls: Joining multi-digit frequency counts with an empty string `counts.join("")`, causing multi-digit boundary collisions.
Mutating a frequency counter without deleting keys whose count drops to 0 when comparing `map.size`.

edgeCase.scenario: Strings with repeated character counts >= 10, such as 10 of one letter vs 1 of two adjacent letters
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Undelimited concatenation cannot distinguish `"1" + "0"` from `"10"`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always join numeric tuple keys with a non-digit separator like `"#"` or `","`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does `counts.join("")` fail as a canonical key for 26-letter frequency arrays on long strings?

options.label: Multi-digit counts (like 10) blur adjacent slot boundaries when concatenated without a separator.
options.feedback: Correct! `0, 1, 0, 10` and `0, 10, 1, 0` both become `"01010..."` without a delimiter.

options.label: JavaScript strings cannot exceed 26 characters when used as Map keys.
options.feedback: JavaScript strings of any reasonable length work as Map keys.

options.label: Because Array.prototype.join sorts the numbers alphabetically before joining.
options.feedback: join() preserves array order; the issue is boundary ambiguity between adjacent numbers.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A separator like "#" ensures injective (one-to-one) serialization from integer tuples to strings.

lessons.title: Rotated Sorted Arrays & Sorted-Half Discrimination
lessons.measurableObjective: Locate minimums and targets in rotated sorted arrays in O(log n) by identifying which half around mid is guaranteed monotonic.
lessons.explanation: When a sorted array without duplicates is rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`), cutting at `mid` always leaves at least one half (`[lo..mid]` or `[mid..hi]`) strictly sorted. To find the minimum element, compare `nums[mid]` against `nums[hi]` (NOT `nums[lo]`): if `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the cliff must lie to the right of `mid` (`lo = mid + 1`); otherwise `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]`, so the right half is sorted and `mid` itself could be the minimum (`hi = mid`). To search for a specific `target`, first check which half is sorted (`nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`), then test whether `target` lies inside that sorted half’s closed bounds.

stepByStep: lo = 0, hi = 6 -> mid = 3 (nums[3] = 7 > nums[6] = 2): minimum is right of mid -> lo = 4.
lo = 4, hi = 6 -> mid = 5 (nums[5] = 1 <= nums[6] = 2): minimum is at or left of mid -> hi = 5.
lo === hi === 4 -> return nums[4] = 0.
workedExample.invariantSummary: The minimum element of the rotated array always resides inside the closed interval [lo..hi].

pitfalls: Comparing `nums[mid]` with `nums[lo]` to find the minimum: when the subarray `[lo..hi]` is already unrotated (e.g., `[1, 2, 3]`), `nums[mid] > nums[lo]` is true even though the minimum is at `lo`, not right of `mid`!
Using `<` instead of `<=` in `if (nums[lo] <= nums[mid])` during rotated target search, which fails when `lo === mid` on a 2-element subarray.

edgeCase.scenario: Array rotated n times (already sorted), e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Comparing `nums[mid]` against `nums[lo]` sees `3 > 1` and wrongly discards the left half containing `1`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always compare `nums[mid]` against `nums[hi]` when searching for the minimum pivot.

knowledgeCheck.question: When finding the minimum of a rotated sorted array, why do we compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]` instead of `nums[lo]`?

options.label: Because `nums[mid] > nums[lo]` happens both in an unrotated array `[1, 2, 3]` (min on left) and a rotated array `[3, 4, 1]` (min on right), whereas `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` unambiguously proves the pivot drop is in `(mid..hi]`.
options.feedback: Correct! `nums[hi]` disambiguates whether the right half wraps around the cliff.

options.label: Because `hi` changes less frequently than `lo` on random inputs.
options.feedback: Both bounds update equally often; the reason is logical disambiguation of unrotated intervals.

options.label: Because `mid` can equal `hi` when `lo < hi`, so we need a tie-breaker.
options.feedback: With floor division and `lo < hi`, `mid` is strictly less than `hi` (and can equal `lo`).

knowledgeCheck.explanation: `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` can ONLY occur if the rotation cliff lies strictly between `mid` and `hi`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is `mid === lo` possible when `hi === lo + 1`, and how does that require `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` when checking if the left half is sorted?

lessons.title: Three-Sum Reduction & Duplicate-Skipping Invariants
lessons.measurableObjective: Reduce 3Sum to `O(n^2)` sorted two-pointer sweeps while skipping duplicate anchors and partner values without missing valid triplets.
lessons.explanation: Sorting `nums` first (`O(n log n)`) lets us fix an anchor index `i` and run converging `left = i + 1, right = n - 1` looking for `nums[left] + nums[right] === -nums[i]`. To emit only unique triplets without a slow hash set of serialized arrays, we enforce two duplicate-skipping rules: (1) if `i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]`, skip anchor `i` because every partner pair from `[i + 1..n - 1]` is a subset of pairs already explored at `i - 1`; (2) AFTER recording a valid triplet `[nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]]`, advance both pointers and skip identical values (`while (left < right && nums[left] === nums[left - 1]) left++`).

stepByStep: Sort ascending: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2].
i = 0 (-4): left = 1 (-1), right = 5 (2); max possible sum with -4 is -4 + 1 + 2 = -1 < 0; pointers converge with no match.
i = 1 (-1): left = 2 (-1), right = 5 (2) -> sum = 0 -> push [-1, -1, 2]; advance to left = 3 (0), right = 4 (1) -> sum = 0 -> push [-1, 0, 1].
i = 2 (-1): nums[2] === nums[1], so skip i = 2 to avoid re-emitting [-1, 0, 1].
i = 3 (0): left = 4 (1), right = 5 (2) -> sum = 3 > 0; loop finishes.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Each distinct anchor value nums[i] is swept once, and within that sweep each distinct nums[left] value that forms a zero sum is emitted once.

pitfalls: Using `nums.sort()` in JavaScript without `(a, b) => a - b`, which sorts numbers lexicographically as strings (`-10` before `-2`!).

options.feedback: Spot on! Processing the first occurrence allows `left = i + 1` to pick up the duplicate as the second member of the triplet.

lessons.title: Variable-Size Windows & Expand/Shrink Monotonicity
lessons.measurableObjective: Trace and prove the O(n) amortized runtime of variable-size windows (`while (invalid) shrink left`) for Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters and Minimum Size Subarray Sum.
lessons.explanation: A variable-size sliding window `[left..right]` advances `right` one step per outer iteration to incorporate `s[right]`, then runs an inner `while` loop that advances `left` until the window invariant is restored (for Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters) or while the target sum is met (for Minimum Size Subarray Sum). Why is a `for` loop containing a `while` loop still `O(n)` and not `O(n^2)`? Because `left` starts at `0`, only increments (`left += 1`), and never resets backward! Across the entire algorithm, `right` increments `n` times and `left` increments at most `n` times, totaling at most `2n` pointer operations.

stepByStep: right = 0 ("a"): lastSeen = {a: 0}, left = 0, len = 1, best = 1.
right = 1 ("b"): lastSeen = {a: 0, b: 1}, left = 0, len = 2, best = 2.
right = 2 ("b"): lastSeen.get("b") = 1 >= left (0) -> left jumps to 1 + 1 = 2; lastSeen.set("b", 2); len = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1.
right = 3 ("a"): lastSeen.get("a") = 0 < left (2) -> ignore stale "a" outside window! left stays 2; len = 3 - 2 + 1 = 2.
workedExample.invariantSummary: After updating left at step right, the substring s[left..right] contains no duplicate characters, and left is the smallest start index with that property for this right.

pitfalls: On `"abba"`, setting `left = lastSeen.get(ch) + 1` without checking `lastSeen.get(ch) >= left` (or using `Math.max`), which moves `left` BACKWARD from 2 to 1 when the second `"a"` is seen!
Using a sliding window for subarray sums when the array contains negative numbers (which breaks sum monotonicity).

edgeCase.scenario: Palindrome with stale duplicate outside current window: `s = "abba"`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: At index 3 (`"a"`), `lastSeen.get("a")` is `0`, which is to the left of `left = 2`. Without `>= left`, `left` regresses to `0 + 1 = 1`, including both `"b"`s and falsely computing length `3`!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always guard with `lastSeen.get(ch) >= left` (or `left = Math.max(left, lastSeen.get(ch) + 1)`).

knowledgeCheck.question: When using a `lastSeen` index map in Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters on `"abba"`, what happens at `right = 3` (`"a"`) if you omit the `lastSeen.get(ch) >= left` check?

options.label: `left` moves backward from `2` to `1`, re-admitting the duplicate `"b"`s at indices 1 and 2 into the window.
options.feedback: Exact diagnosis! `left` must be monotonically non-decreasing.

options.label: The loop enters an infinite cycle.
options.feedback: `right` still advances in the `for` loop, so it terminates—but returns the wrong length `3` instead of `2`.

options.label: Nothing goes wrong because `"a"` was already deleted from `lastSeen`.
options.feedback: With the direct-jump map optimization, old keys are not deleted one by one, so `"a" -> 0` is still in `lastSeen`.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Any index `< left` is already outside the current window `[left..right]` and must never pull `left` backward.

lessons.title: Iterative Three-Pointer Reversal & Sublist Surgery
lessons.measurableObjective: Reverse a singly linked list in-place in O(1) space without losing the unvisited suffix by maintaining `prev`, `curr`, and `nextTemp`.
lessons.explanation: Reversing a singly linked list in-place splits the list into two disjoint chains at all times: `prev` (the head of the already-reversed prefix) and `curr` (the head of the still-forward suffix). Before flipping `curr.next = prev`, you MUST save `const nextTemp = curr.next`, or else the entire remaining suffix is orphaned in memory! The four-line heartbeat (`const nextTemp = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nextTemp;`) preserves every node and terminates when `curr === null`, leaving `prev` at the new head.

stepByStep: Init: prev = null, curr = 10.
Step 1: nextTemp = 20; 10.next = null; prev = 10; curr = 20. (Reversed: 10->null; Remaining: 20->30->null)
Step 2: nextTemp = 30; 20.next = 10; prev = 20; curr = 30. (Reversed: 20->10->null; Remaining: 30->null)
Step 3: nextTemp = null; 30.next = 20; prev = 30; curr = null. Return prev (30 -> 20 -> 10 -> null).
workedExample.invariantSummary: Before each iteration, prev points to the reversed prefix of visited nodes ending in null, and curr points to the unvisited suffix.

pitfalls: Writing `curr.next = prev` before `const nextTemp = curr.next`, which overwrites the forward link and stops after 1 node.
Initializing `prev = head` instead of `prev = null`, which creates a 2-node cycle `head <-> head.next` on the old head!

edgeCase.scenario: Empty list `head = null` or single-node list `10 -> null`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Code that accesses `head.next` before the `while (curr !== null)` guard throws a TypeError on `null`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Start with `prev = null, curr = head` and let `while (curr !== null)` handle `null` (0 iterations, returns `null`) and 1-node lists (1 iteration, returns `head`) automatically.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens if you initialize `let prev = head` instead of `let prev = null` before the reversal loop on `10 -> 20 -> null`?

options.label: Node `10.next` points to `10` (and `20.next` points to `10`), creating an infinite cycle instead of terminating in `null`.
options.feedback: Correct! The original head becomes the new tail and MUST point to `null`.

options.label: It reverses normally except the first node is duplicated.
options.feedback: No nodes are allocated; setting `10.next = 10` creates a reference cycle.

options.label: The loop exits immediately without changing any pointers.
options.feedback: `curr` is not null, so the loop executes and wires `10.next = 10`.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The old head becomes the new tail, so its `.next` must become `prev = null`.

lessons.title: Monotonic Decreasing Stack & Next Greater Element
lessons.measurableObjective: Resolve the next warmer/greater element for every index in O(n) time by maintaining a stack of indices whose values are monotonically non-increasing.
lessons.explanation: Suppose you want to find, for each day `i`, the first future day `j > i` with `temps[j] > temps[i]`. Instead of scanning forward from every `i` (`O(n^2)`), we maintain a **waiting stack of indices** whose temperatures have not yet seen a warmer day. Notice that this waiting stack is automatically **monotonically decreasing** (`temps[stack[0]] >= temps[stack[1]] >= ...`)! When day `i` arrives with `temps[i]`, we pop every waiting index `prevIdx` on top of the stack where `temps[i] > temps[prevIdx]` and record `ans[prevIdx] = i - prevIdx`, then push `i`. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once (`<= 2n` operations).

lines: const stack = []; // stores indices with decreasing temps

stepByStep: i=6 (76): pops 5 (ans[5]=1) and 2 (ans[2]=4); push 6 -> stack=[6].
workedExample.invariantSummary: Before and after each iteration i, the indices on stack are strictly increasing while their corresponding values temps[idx] are monotonically non-increasing.

pitfalls: Pushing temperature values `temps[i]` onto the stack instead of indices `i`, which loses the distance `i - prevIdx` and collides on duplicate temperatures.
Using `if` instead of `while` when popping, which only resolves the single most recent cooler day instead of all cooler waiting days.

edgeCase.scenario: Equal adjacent temperatures `[70, 70, 72]` when strictly warmer (`>`) is required
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If the pop condition uses `>=` instead of `>`, index 0 (`70`) is popped by index 1 (`70`), wrongly reporting a warmer day at distance 1!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Use strict `temps[i] > temps[stack.top]` so equal temperatures wait together on the stack until `72` arrives.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why do we store array INDICES `i` on the monotonic stack rather than the element values `temps[i]`?

options.label: Because index `i` gives us both the value `temps[i]` AND the exact position needed to write `ans[prevIdx] = i - prevIdx` without ambiguity on duplicate values.
options.feedback: Correct! From an index `idx` you can always look up `temps[idx]` in O(1), plus compute index distances.

options.label: Because JavaScript arrays can only store integers.
options.feedback: JavaScript arrays can store any type; indices are chosen because they carry both position and value.

options.label: To make the stack monotonically increasing instead of decreasing.
options.feedback: The monotonicity invariant refers to the values `temps[idx]`, which are still decreasing.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Storing `idx` provides both `idx` (position) and `temps[idx]` (value).

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is the total work of the `while` loop across the entire `for` loop bounded by `n` pops even if a single step pops `n - 1` elements?

lessons.title: Top-Down Ancestor Range Constraints & BST Validity
lessons.measurableObjective: Validate Binary Search Trees by propagating strict ancestor interval bounds `(low, high)` top-down to every recursive call.
lessons.explanation: The classic BST misconception is checking only immediate children: `node.left.val < node.val && node.right.val > node.val`. Why does that fail? Consider root `10` with right child `15`, and `15` has a left child `6`. Locally `6 < 15` looks valid, but `6` is in the **right subtree of `10`** and violates `6 > 10`! Every node in a BST is constrained by an open interval `(low, high)` inherited from its ancestors: going left tightens the upper bound to `(low, node.val)`, and going right tightens the lower bound to `(node.val, high)`.

lines: export function isValidBST(root, low = -Infinity, high = Infinity) {

stepByStep: Call isValidBST(10, -Inf, +Inf): 10 in (-Inf, +Inf) -> ok.
Left call isValidBST(5, -Inf, 10): 5 in (-Inf, 10) -> returns true.
Right call isValidBST(15, 10, +Inf): 15 in (10, +Inf) -> ok.
15.left call isValidBST(6, 10, 15): 6 <= low (10) -> returns false!
workedExample.outputDescription: false (node 6 in right subtree of 10 violates lower bound 10)
workedExample.invariantSummary: Every recursive call isValidBST(u, low, high) receives the tightest ancestor lower bound low and upper bound high that all nodes in subtree u must strictly satisfy.

pitfalls: Checking only `node.left.val < node.val` and `node.right.val > node.val` without passing `(low, high)` bounds.
Using `<` instead of `<=` on the violation check `root.val <= low || root.val >= high`, which falsely accepts duplicate keys `[2, 2, 2]`.

edgeCase.scenario: Node values equal to `-(2^31)` or `2^31 - 1` or duplicate values `[2, 2, 2]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Initializing bounds to `-2147483648` fails when the root itself has value `-2147483648` under strict inequality.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Initialize `low = -Infinity` and `high = Infinity` (or `null` bounds).

knowledgeCheck.question: When recursing from `node` into its left child `node.left` during `isValidBST(node, low, high)`, which bound changes?

options.label: The upper bound `high` becomes `node.val`, while the lower bound `low` remains unchanged: `(low, node.val)`.
options.feedback: Correct! Every node in `node.left` must be strictly smaller than `node.val` while still exceeding any ancestor lower bound `low`.

options.label: The lower bound `low` becomes `node.val`: `(node.val, high)`.
options.feedback: That is the interval for the RIGHT child `node.right`.

options.label: Both bounds reset to `(-Infinity, node.val)`.
options.feedback: Resetting `low` to `-Infinity` would lose the lower bound when `node` itself is inside a right subtree!

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Moving left caps maximum values at `node.val` while preserving the inherited `low` floor.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is an in-order traversal that checks `prevVal < curr.val` equivalent to top-down `(low, high)` interval propagation?

lessons.title: Bounded Min-Heap of Size K (Top-K Largest Bouncer Pattern)
lessons.measurableObjective: Maintain the `k` largest elements of a stream in `O(n log k)` time and `O(k)` memory using a min-heap of size `k`.
lessons.explanation: Why do we use a **Min-Heap** (not a Max-Heap) to track the **K Largest** elements? Think of the heap as a VIP club with capacity `k`. To decide if a new candidate `x` deserves to enter a full club, you compare `x` against the **weakest member currently inside**—which is the minimum of the top `k`! A Min-Heap of size `k` keeps that weakest top-`k` element right at `heap[0]` in `O(1)` time. When `x > heap[0]`, we evict `heap[0]` and insert `x` in `O(log k)`. After scanning all `n` items, `heap[0]` is the exact `k`-th largest element overall!

lines: export function updateTopKMinHeap(minHeap, k, x, pushHeap, popHeap) {

workedExample.inputDescription: Stream = [4, 5, 8, 2], k = 3; then add(3), add(5), add(10)
stepByStep: Initial [4, 5, 8, 2] with k = 3: top 3 in min-heap are [4, 5, 8] with root minHeap[0] = 4 (2 was rejected because 2 <= 4).
add(3): 3 <= minHeap[0] (4) -> ignored! K-th largest remains 4.
add(5): 5 > 4 -> pop 4, push 5 -> minHeap holds [5, 5, 8], root minHeap[0] = 5.
add(10): 10 > 5 -> pop 5, push 10 -> minHeap holds [5, 8, 10], root minHeap[0] = 5.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Once at least k elements have been seen, minHeap contains the k largest elements seen so far, and minHeap[0] is the smallest among those k (the k-th largest overall).

pitfalls: Using a Max-Heap of size `n` when `k` is small (or streaming), which wastes `O(n)` memory and cannot evict the `(k+1)`-th largest element in `O(log k)`.
Using a Min-Heap when the problem asks for the K **Smallest** elements (K Smallest requires a **Max-Heap** of size `k` so the largest of the `k` smallest sits at the root to be evicted!).

edgeCase.scenario: Initial array has `k - 1` elements before the first `add(val)` call (as allowed in LeetCode 703 `KthLargest`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Assuming `minHeap.length === k` during the constructor crashes if the initial array has length `k - 1`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Check `if (minHeap.length < k) push(x)` in `add(x)` so the `k`-th element fills the heap to size `k`.

knowledgeCheck.question: If you want to find the `k` SMALLEST elements (e.g., `K Closest Points to Origin`) in `O(n log k)` time and `O(k)` space, which heap type of capacity `k` should you maintain?

options.label: A Max-Heap of size `k`, so the farthest/largest of the `k` kept candidates sits at `heap[0]` ready to be evicted whenever a smaller candidate arrives.
options.feedback: Spot on! To keep the `k` smallest, your bouncer at `heap[0]` must track the largest among the `k` currently kept.

options.label: A Min-Heap of size `k`, so the smallest element is evicted first.
options.feedback: Evicting the smallest element would throw away the best answers and keep the `k` largest instead!

options.label: A FIFO Queue of size `k`.
options.feedback: Arrival order has nothing to do with distance or magnitude.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Top-K Largest uses a size-K Min-Heap; Top-K Smallest uses a size-K Max-Heap.

lessons.explanation: Breadth-First Search expands vertices in non-decreasing order of edge distance. When multiple sources spread simultaneously (like rotting oranges or reverse ocean reachability from grid borders), pushing all initial sources into the queue at distance 0 lets a single BFS pass assign every reachable cell its minimum distance to the nearest source in `O(V + E)` time.

const nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
if (nr >= 0 && nr < grid.length && nc >= 0 && nc < grid[0].length && grid[nr][nc] === 1) {

lessons.title: Subsets vs. Combinations vs. Permutations
lessons.measurableObjective: Select the exact branching progression—`dfs(i + 1)` single-use, `dfs(i)` unlimited reuse, or `used[i]` boolean mask—for each combinatorial structure.
lessons.explanation: Combinations and subsets care about membership, not order: passing a `start` index enforces canonical non-decreasing index order so `[2, 3]` and `[3, 2]` are never both generated. If each element can be used once, recurse with `dfs(i + 1)`; if an element can be reused unlimited times (Combination Sum), recurse with `dfs(i)`. Permutations care about order: every level loops `i = 0..n-1` and skips indices already marked in a `used` boolean mask.

lines: for (let i = start; i < candidates.length; i += 1) {

stepByStep: dfs(0, 5): pick i = 0 (2) -> dfs(0, 3) -> pick i = 0 (2) -> dfs(0, 1) -> pick 2 gives rem = -1 (pruned!).
Back in dfs(0, 3) with path = [2]: advance loop to i = 1 (3) -> dfs(1, 0) hits rem === 0 -> records [2, 3].
Root advances to i = 1 (3): loop starts at i = 1, so it never looks back at index 0 (2), avoiding duplicate [3, 2].
workedExample.invariantSummary: Indices chosen along path are monotonically non-decreasing (i_1 <= i_2 <= ... <= i_k), guaranteeing canonical combination order.

pitfalls: Looping `for (let i = 0; ...)` in Combination Sum instead of `for (let i = start; ...)`, which generates every permutation of the same combination.
Passing `dfs(i + 1)` when unlimited reuse of `candidates[i]` is allowed.

edgeCase.howToHandle: Check `if (digits.length === 0) return [];` before launching `dfs(0)`.

options.label: Passing `i` allows choosing `candidates[i]` again while forbidding earlier indices `< i`, which prevents generating reordered duplicate combinations.
options.feedback: Correct! Staying at `>= i` allows repeats like `[2, 2, 3]` while blocking reordered `[2, 3, 2]` or `[3, 2, 2]`.

options.label: Passing `i` limits the recursion depth to `candidates.length`.
options.feedback: Recursion depth is bounded by `rem < 0` (at most `target / min(candidates)`), not `i`.

options.label: Passing `i` sorts the input array automatically.
options.feedback: Index progression does not sort an unsorted array.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Passing `i` enforces non-decreasing index order with repetition allowed.

lessons.title: Unbounded vs. 0/1 Knapsack State Transitions
lessons.measurableObjective: Build capacity/sum state tables and control item reuse via forward (unbounded) vs backward (0/1 single-use) capacity iteration.
lessons.explanation: In knapsack and subset-sum problems, the DP table is indexed by achievable amount/sum `a` from `0` to `target`. In **Unbounded Knapsack (Coin Change)**, each coin can be used unlimited times, so `dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - coin])` reads `dp[a - coin]` that may already include the same coin (forward loop). In **0/1 Knapsack (Partition Equal Subset Sum)**, each number can be used at most once: when compressing to a 1D array `dp[0..target]`, we MUST iterate `s` **backward** from `target` down to `num` so `dp[s - num]` still holds the previous row’s value before `num` was used!

stepByStep: Init: dp[0] = 0, dp[1..6] = Infinity.
At a = 6: coin 1 -> 1 + dp[5] = 3; coin 3 -> 1 + dp[3] = 2; coin 4 -> 1 + dp[2] = 3. Minimum is dp[6] = 2 (3 + 3).
workedExample.invariantSummary: After outer iteration a, dp[a] holds the minimum number of coins required to form exact amount a (or Infinity if impossible).

pitfalls: Iterating sum `s` forward `for (let s = num; s <= target; s++)` in 0/1 Subset Sum, which reuses a single array element multiple times!
Returning `Infinity` instead of `-1` when `dp[amount] === Infinity` in Coin Change.

edgeCase.scenario: Partition Equal Subset Sum when the total sum of `nums` is odd (e.g., `[1, 2, 5]`, sum = 8 vs `[1, 2, 4]`, sum = 7)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If `totalSum` is odd, `totalSum / 2` is a `.5` fraction (`3.5`), causing `dp[3.5]` indexing bugs if not rejected upfront!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Immediately check `if (totalSum % 2 !== 0) return false;` before allocating `dp` of size `(totalSum / 2) + 1`.

knowledgeCheck.question: When compressing 0/1 Subset Sum (`Partition Equal Subset Sum`) into a 1D boolean array `dp[0..target]`, why MUST the inner loop run backward (`for (let s = target; s >= num; s--)`)?

options.label: Because a forward loop updates `dp[num] = true` first and then reads that newly updated `dp[num]` at `s = 2 * num` in the same pass, illegally using `num` twice.
options.feedback: Correct! Iterating downward ensures `dp[s - num]` still holds the state from BEFORE the current item `num` was considered.

options.label: Because `dp[target]` must be initialized to `true` before `dp[0]`.
options.feedback: `dp[0]` is initialized to `true` and `dp[1..target]` to `false`.

options.label: To sort `nums` in descending order.
options.feedback: The backward loop works regardless of whether `nums` is sorted.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Backward iteration in 1D knapsack prevents reading current-row updates (`0/1` single use), whereas forward iteration intentionally reads current-row updates (unbounded reuse).

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a greedy largest-coin-first strategy work for US coins `[1, 5, 10, 25]` but fail for `coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6`?
