lessons.title: In-Place Compaction & Read/Write Pointer Partitioning
lessons.measurableObjective: Partition or deduplicate an array in-place in O(1) extra space by maintaining a slow write pointer and fast read pointer.
lessons.explanation: Whenever you need to filter, deduplicate, or compact an array in-place without shifting elements repeatedly in O(n^2) time, split your index into two roles: a fast `read` pointer that inspects every element once, and a slow `write` pointer that marks the next slot of the kept prefix. Because `write <= read` at all times, writing to `nums[write]` never overwrites an uninspected future element.

stepByStep: Start write = 1 (nums[0] = 2 is always kept).
read = 1 (val 2): equals nums[write - 1] (2), skip.
read = 2 (val 5): differs from nums[0] (2) -> write nums[1] = 5, write becomes 2.
read = 3 (val 5): equals nums[write - 1] (5), skip.
read = 4 (val 8): differs from nums[1] (5) -> write nums[2] = 8, write becomes 3; return 3.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Before each read step, nums[0..write-1] contains the deduplicated elements from nums[0..read-1] in sorted order, and write <= read.

pitfalls: Comparing `nums[read]` against `nums[read - 1]` when allowing at most k duplicates, after earlier writes have already mutated `nums[read - 1]`.
Forgetting to guard `nums.length === 0`, returning `write = 1` on an empty array.

edgeCase.scenario: All elements identical, e.g., [4, 4, 4, 4]
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Calling `splice` inside a forward loop skips every second element when indices shift left.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Keep `write = 1` fixed while `read` advances to the end in a single O(n) pass.

knowledgeCheck.question: When generalizing sorted deduplication to allow at most K copies of each value, which element should `nums[read]` be compared against?

options.label: nums[write - K] in the already-compacted valid prefix
options.feedback: Correct! Since the kept prefix is sorted, if nums[read] !== nums[write - K], there are fewer than K copies of nums[read] in the kept prefix.

options.label: nums[read - K] in the raw array
options.feedback: Careful! When writing in-place, nums[read - K] may have already been overwritten by an earlier write.

options.label: nums[0] at the start of the array
options.feedback: Comparing against nums[0] only checks the very first value, not the most recent run.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Comparing against `nums[write - K]` inspects the authoritative compacted prefix.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is `write <= read` the critical safety guarantee that makes in-place forward compaction lossless?
lessons.provenance: Pedagogical pointer invariant design inspired by OpenDSA (MIT) with original JavaScript implementation.

lessons.title: Prefix-Sum Hash Maps for Exact Subarray Targets
lessons.measurableObjective: Count or measure subarrays summing to K in O(n) time even when negative numbers break sliding windows.
lessons.explanation: Sliding windows require monotonicity (non-negative numbers). When an array contains negative values, the window sum can both grow and shrink unpredictably. However, the identity `sum(L..R) = prefixSum[R] - prefixSum[L - 1]` still holds! Therefore, a subarray ending at `R` has sum `K` if and only if an earlier prefix sum equaled `currentPrefix - K`. By seeding a frequency map with `{ 0: 1 }` (representing the empty prefix before index 0), we count all matching earlier splits in O(1) per step.

stepByStep: Seed prefixCounts = { 0: 1 }, runningSum = 0, totalMatches = 0.
num = 1: runningSum = 1, need 0 -> add prefixCounts.get(0)=1 (total=1); map becomes {0:1, 1:1}.
num = -1: runningSum = 0, need -1 -> add 0 (total=1); map becomes {0:2, 1:1}.
num = 1: runningSum = 1, need 0 -> add prefixCounts.get(0)=2 (total=3); map becomes {0:2, 1:2}.
num = 1: runningSum = 2, need 1 -> add prefixCounts.get(1)=2 (total=5).
workedExample.outputDescription: 5 matching subarrays ([1], [1,-1,1], [1] at idx 2, [-1,1,1], [1] at idx 3)
workedExample.invariantSummary: Before updating prefixCounts at index i, prefixCounts.get(x) equals the number of prefix boundaries in 0..i where the prefix sum equaled x.

pitfalls: Forgetting the base seed `new Map([[0, 1]])`, which misses every valid subarray that starts at index 0.
Storing only a boolean Set instead of frequencies, which undercounts when zeros or negatives revisit the same prefix sum multiple times.

edgeCase.scenario: k = 0 with alternating positives and negatives like [1, -1, 1, -1]
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Updating `prefixCounts` BEFORE adding `prefixCounts.get(runningSum - k)` when `k = 0` matches the current prefix with itself (an empty subarray of length 0).
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always query `runningSum - k` first, then increment the count of `runningSum` in the map.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why do we initialize `prefixCounts` with `[0, 1]` before iterating through the array?

options.label: To represent the empty prefix before index 0, so subarrays starting at index 0 with runningSum === k are counted.
options.feedback: Correct! When runningSum === k, neededPrefix is 0, which matches the empty prefix before index 0.

options.label: Because JavaScript Maps require at least one initial entry to infer numeric key types.
options.feedback: JavaScript Maps are dynamically typed and can start empty.

options.label: To prevent division by zero when computing the average subarray length.
options.feedback: No division is performed; `[0, 1]` accounts for the prefix sum of `nums[0..-1]` being 0.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: An empty prefix has sum 0 and occurs once before index 0.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: If a problem asks for the LONGEST subarray with sum K rather than the COUNT of subarrays, should the map store frequency counts or only the earliest index of each prefix sum?
lessons.provenance: Original NextStep lesson combining prefix sums and hash maps.

lessons.title: Binary Search on Monotonic Answer Spaces
lessons.measurableObjective: Solve min-max capacity and rate problems in O(n log(range)) by binary searching over candidate answers with a linear feasibility check.
lessons.explanation: Binary search does not require a sorted input array! Whenever a problem asks for the MINIMUM capacity/speed `X` such that a task can be completed within `H` hours or `D` days, check whether the feasibility function `canFinish(X)` is monotonic: if speed `X` is fast enough, then any speed `> X` is also fast enough (`false, false, ..., true, true`). Once you establish monotonicity, define the tightest safe search bounds `[lo, hi]` in answer space (e.g., `lo = 1` or `max(weights)`, `hi = max(piles)` or `sum(weights)`) and run standard `first-true` binary search.

stepByStep: Search space is speed in [1..11].
speed = 6: hours = ceil(3/6)+ceil(6/6)+ceil(7/6)+ceil(11/6) = 1+1+2+2 = 6 <= 8 (feasible -> hi = 6).
lo = 1, hi = 6 -> speed = 3: hours = 1+2+3+4 = 10 > 8 (too slow -> lo = 4).
lo = 4, hi = 6 -> speed = 5: hours = 1+2+2+3 = 8 <= 8 (feasible -> hi = 5).
lo = 4, hi = 5 -> speed = 4: hours = 1+2+2+3 = 8 <= 8 (feasible -> hi = 4); return 4.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Every speed < lo requires strictly more than maxHours, while speed = hi is guaranteed to finish in <= maxHours.

pitfalls: Setting `lo = 1` in shipment capacity problems where items cannot be split across days, which allows the feasibility check to loop forever or undercount when `capacity < max(weights)`.
Stopping the binary search the moment `hoursUsed === maxHours` instead of continuing to shrink `hi = speed`, since a smaller speed might also hit the exact same ceiling sum!

edgeCase.scenario: Multiple speeds produce the exact same total hours due to ceiling division (e.g., speeds 4 and 5 both take 8 hours)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Returning immediately on `hoursUsed === maxHours` returns 5 instead of the minimum feasible speed 4.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always treat `hoursUsed <= maxHours` as the `true` branch (`hi = speed`) until `lo === hi`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is it a bug to return `speed` immediately when `hoursUsed === maxHours` in a minimum-rate binary search?

options.label: Because `Math.ceil(pile / speed)` is a step function; a smaller speed can yield the exact same `hoursUsed === maxHours`.
options.feedback: Correct! In the worked example, both speed 5 and speed 4 take 8 hours, and we need the minimum speed (4).

options.label: Because `hoursUsed` might have floating-point rounding error.
options.feedback: `Math.ceil` produces exact integers; the issue is step-function plateaus.

options.label: Because we want the maximum speed, not the minimum speed.
options.feedback: The problem asks for the minimum feasible speed.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Ceiling sums plateau across ranges of speeds, so you must keep tightening `hi = speed` to find the left edge of the plateau.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How do you choose `lo` and `hi` for an answer-space binary search when items cannot be split vs. when items can be split across time steps?
lessons.provenance: Monotonic feasibility search pattern informed by Tech Interview Handbook (MIT) with original plateau analysis.

lessons.title: Bottleneck Exclusion & Container / Rainwater Proofs
lessons.measurableObjective: Prove why moving the shorter wall inward in Container With Most Water and Trapping Rain Water never discards a better area or water level.
lessons.explanation: Even when an array is NOT sorted, two pointers work whenever the objective is governed by `min(height[left], height[right])`. In Container With Most Water, `area = (right - left) * Math.min(height[left], height[right])`. Suppose `height[left] <= height[right]`. Every other container that keeps `left` as its left wall and chooses some `k < right` has strictly smaller width `(k - left) < (right - left)` AND height capped at `min(height[left], height[k]) <= height[left]`. Therefore, NO container using `left` and `k < right` can beat `(left, right)`. Moving `left += 1` safely discards all those inferior pairs in O(1) time.

lines: if (w * h > best) best = w * h;

stepByStep: left = 0 (1), right = 8 (7): width = 8, h = min(1, 7) = 1 -> area = 8, best = 8. Since 1 <= 7, left += 1.
left = 1 (8), right = 8 (7): width = 7, h = min(8, 7) = 7 -> area = 49, best = 49. Since 8 > 7, right -= 1.
left = 1 (8), right = 7 (3): width = 6, h = 3 -> area = 18. right -= 1.
left = 1 (8), right = 6 (8): width = 5, h = 8 -> area = 40. left += 1; remaining widths <= 4 cannot beat 49.
workedExample.outputDescription: 49 (between index 1 of height 8 and index 8 of height 7)
workedExample.invariantSummary: At every step, best >= the area of any discarded pair (i, j) where i < left or j > right.

pitfalls: Moving the taller wall inward hoping for an even taller wall, which shrinks width while staying bottlenecked by the shorter wall.
In Trapping Rain Water, forgetting that trapped water at `left` depends on `leftMax - height[left]` only when `leftMax <= rightMax`.

edgeCase.scenario: Equal heights `height[left] === height[right]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Developers often stall wondering which side to move when heights tie.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Moving either side (or both) is valid because any narrower container using ONLY one of the tied walls is still capped by that same height at a smaller width.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Container With Most Water, when `height[left] < height[right]`, why can we increment `left` without checking `(left, right - 1)`?

options.label: Because `(left, right - 1)` has smaller width and its height is still capped by `height[left]`.
options.feedback: Correct! `height[left]` is the bottleneck: narrower width × height `<= height[left]` is strictly smaller than `(right - left) * height[left]`.

options.label: Because `height[right - 1]` is guaranteed to be smaller than `height[right]`.
options.feedback: `height[right - 1]` could be huge, but even if it is `1000`, `min(height[left], 1000)` is still capped at `height[left]`!

options.label: Because heights are sorted in ascending order.
options.feedback: Container heights are unsorted; the proof relies on the `min(h[left], h[right])` bottleneck, not sorting.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Keeping the shorter wall while shrinking width can never increase `min(h1, h2) * width`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How does the bottleneck principle unify Container With Most Water and Two-Pointer Trapping Rain Water?
lessons.provenance: Original NextStep lesson on bottleneck elimination proofs.

lessons.title: Frequency-Constrained Windows & O(1) Validity Tracking
lessons.measurableObjective: Track window validity in O(1) per step using `maxFreq` or `formedCount` instead of re-scanning the entire frequency map on every character.
lessons.explanation: In problems like Minimum Window Substring or Longest Repeating Character Replacement, checking whether the current window `[left..right]` satisfies the frequency requirement by iterating over all keys in the hash map adds an `O(|Σ|)` factor per step. Instead, we maintain a scalar summary variable: in Minimum Window Substring, `formed` counts how many distinct required characters currently meet `windowCounts.get(ch) >= targetCounts.get(ch)` (incrementing `formed` ONLY on the exact transition where `windowCounts.get(ch) === targetCounts.get(ch)`). In Character Replacement, `windowLen - maxFreq <= k` tells us whether the non-majority characters in the window can all be replaced within `k` operations.

stepByStep: right = 0..3 ("AABA"): counts={A:3, B:1}, maxFreq=3. replacements needed = 4 - 3 = 1 <= k -> valid, best = 4.
right = 4 ("AABAB"): counts={A:3, B:2}, maxFreq=3. len=5, 5 - 3 = 2 > k -> shrink left=0 ("A"): window becomes "ABAB" (len 4), best stays 4.
right = 5 ("ABABB"): counts={A:1, B:3}, maxFreq=3. len=5, 5 - 3 = 2 > k -> shrink left=1 ("B"): window "BABB" (len 4).
right = 6 ("BABBA"): shrink left=2 -> return best = 4.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At the end of each step, right - left + 1 equals the maximum valid window length seen so far, because window size only grows when maxFreq increases.

pitfalls: In Minimum Window Substring, incrementing `formed` whenever `windowCount >= targetCount` instead of strictly `===`, which overcounts a single repeated character.
Re-scanning all 26 letters on every step when `maxFreq` or `formed` can be updated in O(1).

edgeCase.scenario: `k = 0` on `"AAABBC"`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Code that assumes at least 1 replacement is always available will bridge across different characters.
edgeCase.howToHandle: The condition `(right - left + 1) - maxFreq > k` naturally requires `windowLen === maxFreq` when `k = 0`, shrinking until the window is 100% homogeneous.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Minimum Window Substring, why do we increment `formed` ONLY when `windowCounts.get(ch) === requiredCounts.get(ch)` (and not `>=`)?

options.label: Because `formed` tracks how many distinct character requirements are satisfied; extra copies of an already-satisfied character must not increment `formed` again.
options.feedback: Spot on! Only the exact threshold crossing `===` changes a character’s requirement from unmet to met.

options.label: Because `windowCounts.get(ch)` can never exceed `requiredCounts.get(ch)`.
options.feedback: A window can easily contain more copies of `ch` than required while searching for other characters.

options.label: To save memory inside the Map.
options.feedback: Map size is the same; `===` is required for counting distinct satisfied characters.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Threshold transition `===` on expand (and `<` right after decrement on shrink) keeps `formed` exact.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why doesn’t `maxFreq` need to be decremented when the window shrinks in Longest Repeating Character Replacement?
lessons.provenance: Original NextStep lesson on frequency-constrained sliding windows.

lessons.title: Floyd’s Tortoise-and-Hare Cycle & Midpoint Proofs
lessons.measurableObjective: Use `slow` (1 step) and `fast` (2 steps) pointers to locate list midpoints and detect/locate cycle entrances in O(1) space.
lessons.explanation: When `slow` advances by 1 node (`slow = slow.next`) and `fast` advances by 2 nodes (`fast = fast.next.next`) guarded by `while (fast !== null && fast.next !== null)`: (1) On an acyclic list of length `n`, `fast` reaches the end in `floor(n/2)` steps, leaving `slow` at the exact middle node (the second middle on even lengths); (2) On a cyclic list with cycle length `C`, once `slow` enters the cycle, the distance from `fast` to `slow` along the cycle shrinks by `2 - 1 = 1` every step, guaranteeing they collide inside the cycle within `< C` steps without ever jumping over each other!

workedExample.inputDescription: List 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> (back to 2), so pre-cycle length L = 1, cycle length C = 3
stepByStep: Start: slow = 1, fast = 1.
Step 1: slow = 2, fast = 3.
Step 2: slow = 3, fast = 2 (via 4 -> 2).
Step 3: slow = 4, fast = 4 -> collision at node 4!
Phase 2: finder = head (1), slow = 4. Advance both 1 step -> finder = 2, slow = 2 -> return cycle entry node 2.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At collision after k steps, fast has traveled 2k = k + m*C steps, so k is a multiple of C. Walking L more steps from collision reaches L + k ≡ L (the cycle entrance).

pitfalls: Checking `while (fast.next !== null && fast !== null)` in the wrong order, which crashes when `fast` becomes `null` on an even-length list.
Comparing `slow.val === fast.val` instead of node reference identity `slow === fast` when duplicate values exist.

edgeCase.scenario: Single node with no cycle `1 -> null` vs single node pointing to itself `1 -> 1`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If `slow === fast` is checked BEFORE advancing pointers inside the loop, it immediately triggers at `head === head` even on an acyclic list!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Advance `slow` and `fast` first inside the `while` body, then test `if (slow === fast)`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can `fast` (moving 2 steps) never "jump over" `slow` (moving 1 step) inside a cycle without landing on the exact same node?

options.label: Because their relative distance along the cycle decreases by `2 - 1 = 1` node per step, so it must hit `0` before becoming negative.
options.feedback: Exact mathematical reason! Closing the gap by 1 per step cannot skip over 0.

options.label: Because cycle lengths are always odd numbers.
options.feedback: Cycle lengths can be even or odd; a gap reduction of 1 per step hits 0 regardless of parity.

options.label: Because `fast` slows down to 1 step once inside the cycle.
options.feedback: `fast` always moves 2 steps during Phase 1.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A relative speed of `2 - 1 = 1` step per iteration reduces the gap by 1 each time until `gap === 0`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: When splitting a list into two halves for Merge Sort or Reorder List, why do we sometimes want `slow` to stop at the FIRST middle of an even-length list (`fast = head.next`)?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from OpenDSA Floyd cycle detection and runner proofs.

lessons.title: Monotonic Increasing Stack & Histogram Span Boundaries
lessons.measurableObjective: Compute the maximal rectangle for every bar in a histogram in O(n) time by finding each bar’s first smaller left and right neighbors in a single monotonic stack pass.
lessons.explanation: In Largest Rectangle in Histogram, a bar at `mid` of height `H = heights[mid]` can extend horizontally until it hits the first bar strictly shorter than `H` on its left (`leftBound`) and on its right (`rightBound`). If we maintain a **monotonically increasing stack** of indices, then the moment a shorter bar `heights[i] < heights[stack.top]` arrives: (1) `i` is the exact **right boundary** (first smaller on the right) for `mid = stack.pop()`, and (2) the new top of the stack right below `mid` is the exact **left boundary** (first smaller on the left)! Appending a virtual `0`-height sentinel at `i === heights.length` flushes all remaining bars at the end.

lines: if (h * width > maxArea) maxArea = h * width;

stepByStep: i=1 (1 < 2): pop 0 (h=2), stack empty so leftBound=-1, width = 1 - (-1) - 1 = 1 -> area=2. push 1 -> stack=[1(1)].
i=4 (2 < 6): pop 3 (h=6, leftBound=2, width=4-2-1=1 -> area=6); then 2 < 5: pop 2 (h=5, leftBound=1, width=4-1-1=2 -> area=10!). push 4.
i=5 (3), i=6 (sentinel 0): flushes remaining bars; maxArea = 10.
workedExample.outputDescription: 10 (from bars [5, 6] at indices 2..3 of height 5 and width 2)
workedExample.invariantSummary: When mid is popped by index i, i is the first index > mid with heights[i] < heights[mid], and the new stack top is the last index < mid with height <= heights[mid].

pitfalls: Computing `width = i - mid` instead of `width = i - leftBound - 1`, which forgets that the popped bar `mid` can also extend leftward over taller bars that were already popped!
Forgetting to flush bars remaining on the stack after the array ends (solved cleanly by the `i === heights.length` sentinel `curH = 0`).

edgeCase.scenario: Strictly increasing histogram `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: No bar is ever popped during `i = 0..n-1`; without the end-of-loop flush (`curH = 0`), `maxArea` stays `0`!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Run the loop to `i <= heights.length` with `curH = 0` at `i === heights.length` so every positive bar is guaranteed to be popped and scored.

knowledgeCheck.question: When `mid = stack.pop()` is popped at index `i`, why is the rectangle width `i - leftBound - 1` (where `leftBound` is the new stack top) rather than `i - mid`?

options.label: Because any indices between `leftBound` and `mid` that were popped earlier had height `>= heights[mid]`, so bar `mid` can extend leftward across all of them too.
options.feedback: Spot on! Everything between `leftBound + 1` and `i - 1` inclusive is at least as tall as `heights[mid]`.

options.label: Because arrays are 1-indexed in histogram problems.
options.feedback: Indices are 0-based; `i - leftBound - 1` counts the open interval `(leftBound, i)`.

options.label: Because `mid` is always equal to `leftBound + 1`.
options.feedback: Whenever taller bars existed to the left of `mid` and were popped earlier, `mid > leftBound + 1`.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: All bars in `(leftBound, i)` have height `>= heights[mid]`, giving width `(i - 1) - (leftBound + 1) + 1 = i - leftBound - 1`.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How does appending a virtual `0` at `i === heights.length` simplify monotonic stack code?
lessons.provenance: Original NextStep lesson on monotonic span boundaries.

lessons.title: Lowest Common Ancestor & Subtree Witness Propagation
lessons.measurableObjective: Locate the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in both BSTs (`O(h)` split point) and general binary trees (`O(n)` post-order witness return).
lessons.explanation: In a **BST**, the Lowest Common Ancestor of `p` and `q` is simply the first node from the root where `p` and `q` don’t go into the same child: if both `p.val < curr.val` and `q.val < curr.val`, move `curr = curr.left`; if both are `> curr.val`, move `curr = curr.right`; otherwise `curr` is the split point (LCA) in `O(h)` time and `O(1)` space! In a **general binary tree** without BST order, a post-order function `lca(root, p, q)` returns `root` if `root === null || root === p || root === q`. If both `left` and `right` recursive calls return non-null witnesses, then `p` and `q` sit in opposite subtrees of `root`, making `root` the LCA; otherwise we bubble up whichever side is non-null.

workedExample.inputDescription: BST with root 6, left 2 (children 0, 4), right 8 (children 7, 9); find LCA(2, 4)
stepByStep: Start curr = 6: both pVal = 2 < 6 and qVal = 4 < 6 -> move curr = curr.left (2).
At curr = 2: pVal = 2 is not < 2 (and qVal = 4 > 2) -> split condition reached!
Return node 2 (a node can be a descendant of itself).
workedExample.invariantSummary: Throughout the walk, curr is an ancestor of both p and q; the first node that does not place both strictly in the same child subtree is their lowest common ancestor.

pitfalls: Forgetting that a node is considered an ancestor of itself when `p` is the parent/ancestor of `q`.
Using `O(n)` general-tree recursion on a BST when the `O(h)` iterative split-point walk uses `O(1)` space.

edgeCase.scenario: `p` is a direct ancestor of `q` (e.g., `p = 2, q = 4`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Code that only checks `p < curr && q > curr` misses the case where `curr.val === p.val`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: The `else` branch after checking "both `< curr.val`" and "both `> curr.val`" automatically catches both split subtrees AND `curr.val === pVal` or `qVal`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a BST, when walking down from `root` to find the LCA of `p` and `q`, what is true at the very first node `curr` where `p.val` and `q.val` are NOT both `< curr.val` and NOT both `> curr.val`?

options.label: `curr` is guaranteed to be the Lowest Common Ancestor (either `p` and `q` branch into opposite subtrees of `curr`, or `curr` itself equals `p` or `q`).
options.feedback: Correct! Any deeper move into a child would leave at least one of `p` or `q` behind.

options.label: You must still search both subtrees to verify which one is taller.
options.feedback: Subtree height does not affect which node is the split point between `p` and `q`.

options.label: `curr` is the root of the entire tree.
options.feedback: `curr` is only the root if `p` and `q` split immediately at the root; if both were `< root.val`, `curr` already descended left.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Once `p` and `q` diverge (or hit `curr`), no child of `curr` can contain both of them.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How does the general binary tree LCA function handle the case where `p` is an ancestor of `q` without even visiting `q`?
lessons.provenance: Adapted from OpenDSA BST and tree ancestor properties.

lessons.title: K-Way Sorted Stream Merge & Frontier Min-Heap
lessons.measurableObjective: Merge `k` sorted linked lists or matrix rows in `O(N log k)` time by keeping only the current head of each non-empty stream in a Min-Heap of size `<= k`.
lessons.explanation: When merging `k` sorted lists containing `N` total nodes, pushing all `N` nodes into a heap takes `O(N log N)` time and `O(N)` space, ignoring the fact that each individual list is already sorted! Because the global minimum among all remaining nodes MUST be the head of one of the `k` lists, our Min-Heap only needs to hold the **active frontier** of at most `k` head nodes (`O(k)` space). Each step pops the smallest frontier node `u` in `O(log k)`, appends `u` to the merged output tail, and if `u.next !== null`, pushes `u.next` into the heap in `O(log k)`.

stepByStep: Seed non-null heads into minHeap (size <= 3): [1(L0), 1(L1), 2(L2)].
Pop 1(L0), attach to tail, push its next 4(L0) -> minHeap = [1(L1), 2(L2), 4(L0)].
Pop 1(L1), attach to tail, push its next 3(L1) -> minHeap = [2(L2), 3(L1), 4(L0)].
workedExample.invariantSummary: At every step, minHeap contains the first unmerged node of each non-exhausted list (at most k nodes), and every node already in dummy.next is <= minHeap[0].

pitfalls: Pushing `null` heads from empty lists `[null, 1->2]` into `minHeap` without guarding `if (head !== null)`.
Pushing all `N` nodes upfront instead of pushing `smallest.next` lazily (`O(N log N)` vs `O(N log k)`).

edgeCase.scenario: `lists = []` or `lists = [null, null]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Unconditional seeding pushes `null` into the heap and crashes when comparing `a.val < b.val`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Guard seeding with `if (head !== null)` so `minHeap` stays empty and `dummy.next` (`null`) is returned cleanly.

knowledgeCheck.question: When merging `k` sorted lists with `N` total nodes using a frontier Min-Heap of size `<= k`, what are the time and auxiliary heap space complexities?

options.label: O(N log k) time and O(k) heap space, because each of the N nodes is pushed and popped once from a heap containing at most k list heads.
options.feedback: Correct! Keeping only the `k` active stream heads bounds heap size at `k`.

options.label: O(N log N) time and O(N) heap space.
options.feedback: Because we only push `smallest.next` when `smallest` is popped, the heap never exceeds `k` elements.

options.label: O(N * k) time and O(1) space.
options.feedback: `O(N * k)` is the complexity of scanning all `k` heads linearly without a heap.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: `N` pop/push pairs on a heap of size `<= k` take `O(N log k)` time and `O(k)` space.

lessons.title: Directed Cycle Detection & Topological Sort (Kahn Algorithm)
lessons.measurableObjective: Order Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) tasks by dependency and detect directed cycles using Kahn indegree queues.
lessons.explanation: In a dependency graph where directed edge `pre -> course` means `pre` must precede `course`, a topological ordering exists if and only if the directed graph has no cycles (is a DAG). Kahn’s algorithm computes `indegree[v]` for each vertex, seeds a FIFO queue with all vertices where `indegree[v] === 0`, and repeatedly pops `u`, appends `u` to `order`, and decrements `--indegree[v]` for each outgoing neighbor `v`. If `--indegree[v] === 0`, `v` has all prerequisites satisfied and enters the queue. If `order.length < numCourses` when the queue drains, a directed cycle locked the remaining vertices.

lines: for (let u = 0; u < numCourses; u += 1) if (indeg[u] === 0) queue.push(u);

stepByStep: Pop 0 -> order = [0]; decrement indeg[1] to 0 (push 1) and indeg[2] to 0 (push 2).
Pop 1 -> order = [0, 1]; decrement indeg[3] from 2 to 1 (3 waits!).
Pop 2 -> order = [0, 1, 2]; decrement indeg[3] from 1 to 0 (push 3). Pop 3 -> order = [0, 1, 2, 3].
workedExample.invariantSummary: A vertex v is enqueued at the exact moment its final unresolved prerequisite u is popped (--indeg[v] === 0).

pitfalls: Using a single boolean `visited` set in directed DFS to detect cycles—which falsely flags a harmless diamond DAG (`0 -> 1 -> 3` and `0 -> 2 -> 3`) as a cycle!
Returning `order` without checking `order.length === numCourses` when a cycle prevents some vertices from ever reaching `indegree 0`.

edgeCase.scenario: Disconnected 2-cycle (`0 <-> 1`) alongside an independent valid course `2` (`numCourses = 3`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Course `2` has `indegree 0` and gets popped (`order = [2]`), so checking `order.length > 0` instead of `order.length === numCourses` misses the `0 <-> 1` cycle!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always verify `order.length === numCourses`; here `1 !== 3`, so `[]` is returned.

knowledgeCheck.question: After Kahn’s algorithm finishes its `while` loop on a 6-vertex directed graph, `order.length` is `4`. What does this prove?

options.label: The remaining 2 vertices belong to (or depend on) a directed cycle, so no valid topological ordering exists.
options.feedback: Correct! Every vertex in a cycle always has at least one unvisited predecessor in the cycle, keeping its indegree >= 1.

options.label: The graph is disconnected into two separate trees.
options.feedback: Disconnected trees still have roots with indegree 0 and are completely emitted by Kahn’s algorithm.

options.label: Two vertices had no outgoing edges.
options.feedback: Sinks (0 outgoing edges) still reach indegree 0 and are emitted last.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A directed graph has `order.length === V` in Kahn’s algorithm if and only if it is acyclic (a DAG).

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How does 3-state DFS coloring (`0 = unvisited`, `1 = visiting on active stack`, `2 = completely visited`) distinguish a back-edge cycle (`-> 1`) from a cross-edge diamond (`-> 2`)?

lessons.title: Duplicate Pruning & Constraint Ordering
lessons.measurableObjective: Eliminate duplicate branches on multisets by sorting first and skipping equal siblings at the same decision depth (`i > start && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]`).
lessons.explanation: When the input contains duplicate numbers (e.g., `nums = [1, 2, 2]`), picking the first `2` and picking the second `2` at the same decision depth spawn identical subtrees. Sorting `nums` first groups identical values at adjacent indices so the single guard `if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]) continue;` prunes the redundant sibling subtree in `O(1)` time—while still allowing `i === start` in deeper calls so `[1, 2, 2]` is generated!

lines: for (let i = start; i < nums.length; i += 1) {

stepByStep: dfs(0) picks i = 0 (1) -> dfs(1) picks i = 1 (first 2) -> dfs(2) picks i = 2 (second 2, allowed because i === start = 2) -> records [1, 2, 2].
Back in dfs(1) after popping first 2: loop advances to i = 2. Since i > start (2 > 1) and nums[2] === nums[1], i = 2 is skipped!
Back in dfs(0) after i = 1 explores [2] and [2, 2]: i = 2 has i > start (2 > 0) and nums[2] === nums[1], so i = 2 is skipped.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At any fixed recursion call dfs(start), each distinct value v is chosen at most once as the next element.

pitfalls: Writing `if (nums[i] === nums[i - 1]) continue` without `i > start`, which forbids picking duplicate values at deeper positions and misses `[1, 2, 2]` and `[2, 2]`.
Forgetting `nums.sort((a, b) => a - b)` before running the adjacent duplicate check.

edgeCase.scenario: All elements identical `nums = [2, 2, 2]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Without sibling pruning, $2^3 = 8$ subsets are generated and must be deduplicated via string hashing.
edgeCase.howToHandle: `i > start && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]` explores only the `i === start` chain at each depth, generating the 4 subsets `[], [2], [2,2], [2,2,2]` directly.

knowledgeCheck.question: In `if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]) continue`, why is the `i > start` check required?

options.label: Because when `i === start`, `nums[i]` is being chosen for a new deeper position in `path` (after `nums[start - 1]` was already chosen), whereas `i > start` means `nums[i - 1]` was just unchosen for this exact same position.
options.feedback: Correct! `i === start` extends a parent branch with a second copy; `i > start` repeats a sibling branch at the same slot.

options.label: To prevent accessing `nums[-1]` when `start === 0`.
options.feedback: While `i > 0` would prevent `nums[-1]`, `i > 0` alone would still skip `i === start` at depths `start >= 1`!

options.label: Because `start` is always equal to `nums.length`.
options.feedback: `start` ranges from `0` to `nums.length`.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: `i > start` distinguishes a sibling choice at the same depth from a child choice at the next depth.

lessons.title: Sequence Prefix & Subsequence DP (LIS & Word Break)
lessons.measurableObjective: Formulate prefix transitions where `dp[i]` scans all valid prior split points `0 <= j < i`.
lessons.explanation: Many 1D sequence problems cannot transition from `i - 1` alone because the previous valid element or word boundary could sit at any index `0 <= j < i`. In **Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)**, `dp[i]` is defined as the length of the longest increasing subsequence *ending* at index `i`: `dp[i] = 1 + max({ dp[j] : 0 <= j < i and nums[j] < nums[i] })`. In **Word Break**, `dp[i]` is `true` if the prefix `s[0..i-1]` can be segmented: `dp[i] = some(0 <= j < i : dp[j] && wordSet.has(s.slice(j, i)))`.

stepByStep: Init: dp = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Indices 0 (10), 1 (9), 2 (2) have no smaller prior elements -> stay 1.
i = 5 (7): smaller priors are j = 2 (dp=1), j = 3 (dp=2), j = 4 (dp=2) -> dp[5] = 2 + 1 = 3. Return best = 3.
workedExample.invariantSummary: dp[i] equals the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence whose final element is exactly nums[i].

pitfalls: Returning `dp[nums.length - 1]` instead of `Math.max(...dp)` in LIS, when the longest increasing subsequence ends before the last index (e.g., `[1, 2, 3, 0]`).
Forgetting `dp[0] = true` (the empty prefix of length 0 is always valid) in Word Break.

edgeCase.scenario: Strictly decreasing array `nums = [7, 5, 3, 1]` in LIS
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If `dp` is initialized to `0` instead of `1`, no pair satisfies `nums[j] < nums[i]` and the code returns `0` instead of `1`!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Every single element forms an increasing subsequence of length `1` by itself, so initialize `dp.fill(1)` and `best = 1`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Longest Increasing Subsequence, why must `dp[i]` be defined as "the LIS length ENDING AT index `i`" rather than "the LIS length inside prefix `nums[0..i]`"?

options.label: Because to decide whether `nums[i]` can extend a prior subsequence at `j`, we must know the exact ending value `nums[j]` of that subsequence (`nums[j] < nums[i]`).
options.feedback: Correct! Anchoring the state at index `j` exposes `nums[j]` as the terminal element to compare against `nums[i]`.

options.label: Because `dp[nums.length - 1]` is always the global maximum.
options.feedback: `dp[n - 1]` is NOT always the global maximum, which is why we return `Math.max(...dp)`.

options.label: To avoid using a nested loop.
options.feedback: The standard DP still uses a nested `j < i` loop.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Without knowing the last element of a subsequence, you cannot verify whether appending `nums[i]` preserves strict increase.

lessons.title: Subarray Reset Invariants (Kadane) & Cyclic Reversal
lessons.measurableObjective: Decide in O(1) per element whether to extend or reset a contiguous subarray (Kadane) and rotate arrays in-place via three reversals.
lessons.explanation: Many contiguous subarray problems ask for the best slice ending at index `i`. In Kadane’s algorithm, if the best subarray sum ending at `i - 1` is negative, carrying it forward can only hurt `nums[i]`, so we reset the running sum to `nums[i]`. Similarly, when rotating an array right by `k` steps in O(1) space, normalizing `k = k % n` and reversing the full array, then `[0..k-1]`, then `[k..n-1]` restores internal order without extra buffers.

stepByStep: Start currentEnd = -2, best = -2.
i = 1 (val 1): max(1, -2 + 1) = 1 (reset at index 1); best = 1.
i = 2 (val -3): max(-3, 1 - 3) = -2; best stays 1.
i = 3 (val 4): max(4, -2 + 4) = 4 (reset at index 3); best = 4.
i = 4..6 (vals -1, 2, 1): currentEnd moves 3 -> 5 -> 6; best updates to 6.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At iteration i, currentEnd equals the maximum sum among all non-empty contiguous subarrays ending at index i.

pitfalls: Initializing `best = 0`, which returns 0 instead of the least-negative number when all elements are negative.
Forgetting `k %= nums.length` before reversing slices in array rotation, causing out-of-bounds swaps when `k >= n`.

edgeCase.scenario: All-negative array such as [-8, -3, -6, -2, -5]
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Resetting `currentEnd` to 0 whenever it dips below 0 pretends an empty subarray is allowed and returns 0 instead of -2.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Seed both `currentEnd` and `best` with `nums[0]` and compare `nums[i]` vs `currentEnd + nums[i]`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why must you normalize `k = k % nums.length` before performing the three-reversal in-place array rotation?

options.label: Because rotating by a multiple of n is a full cycle, and k >= n would index past the end of the array during slice reversal.
options.feedback: Correct! Normalizing k into 0..n-1 keeps the reversal boundaries [0, k-1] and [k, n-1] valid.

options.label: Because JavaScript arrays automatically resize if you access index k.
options.feedback: While writing to out-of-bounds indices in JS creates sparse holes, the core mathematical reason is that rotations are periodic modulo n.

options.label: Because three reversals only work when k is strictly less than n / 2.
options.feedback: Three reversals work for any k in 0..n-1, even when k >= n / 2.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: A right rotation by n elements returns the array to its starting configuration, so only k mod n steps matter.

lessons.title: Set Sequence Starts & Bijection Validation
lessons.measurableObjective: Achieve true O(n) sequence discovery by starting chains only at Set boundary elements, and enforce 1-to-1 bijections with dual maps.
lessons.explanation: Putting elements in a `Set` gives O(1) membership checks, but a naive loop that walks `x + 1, x + 2, ...` from every element is still O(n^2) on `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. The O(n) insight is a boundary guard: only start walking a streak at `x` if `!set.has(x - 1)`. That guarantees each streak is traversed at most once! Similarly, when checking whether two strings or patterns are isomorphic, a single map `a -> b` only checks a function; you need either two maps (`a -> b` and `b -> a`) or a `usedTargets` Set to guarantee a true one-to-one bijection.

stepByStep: x = 100: 99 not in Set -> start walk: 101 not in Set -> streak = 1.
x = 4: 3 IS in Set -> skip inner while loop completely!
x = 200: 199 not in Set -> streak = 1.
x = 1: 0 not in Set -> start walk: 2, 3, 4 in Set -> streak = 4; x = 3 and x = 2 are skipped.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Every element in numSet is visited by the inner `while` loop at most once because inner walks only launch from elements with no predecessor `x - 1`.

pitfalls: Iterating `for (const x of nums)` instead of `for (const x of numSet)`, which wastes time re-running streak walks on duplicate start values.
Checking only `mapAtoB` in isomorphism problems, which falsely accepts `"ab"` -> `"aa"` because both `"a"` and `"b"` map to `"a"`.

edgeCase.scenario: Input contains many duplicates of the sequence start, e.g., [1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4]
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Looping over `nums` instead of `numSet` triggers the full inner chain walk for every duplicate `1`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always iterate `for (const x of numSet)` so each distinct start value is processed once.

knowledgeCheck.question: In `longestConsecutiveStreak`, why is the overall time complexity O(n) despite having a `while` loop nested inside a `for` loop?

options.label: The guard `!numSet.has(x - 1)` ensures the `while` loop only runs for the minimum element of each contiguous chain, visiting each Set member at most once.
options.feedback: Correct! Across the entire execution, `current += 1` executes at most n times total.

options.label: Because JavaScript Sets automatically sort numeric keys in O(1) time.
options.feedback: JavaScript Sets preserve insertion order; they do not sort elements.

options.label: Because the inner loop terminates after at most log(n) steps.
options.feedback: A single chain can be length n, so the inner loop can run n times—just only once for that chain.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Each element can be part of only one chain walk, making the total inner-loop iterations across all outer steps at most n.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Where else can a "start only at the predecessor boundary" check turn an O(n^2) graph/grid exploration into O(n)?

lessons.title: 2D Matrix Coordinate Mapping & Local Peak Ascent
lessons.measurableObjective: Map 1D binary search indices to 2D row-major matrices in O(1) and find local peaks in O(log n) using neighbour slope comparison.
lessons.explanation: When a 2D `R x C` matrix has each row sorted and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row, it is isomorphic to a flat sorted array of length `R * C`. Any flat index `idx` in `0..(R * C - 1)` maps directly to `row = Math.floor(idx / C)` and `col = idx % C` without allocating a flattened copy. Even more surprisingly, binary search can find a local peak (`nums[i] > nums[i-1]` and `nums[i] > nums[i+1]`) in an unsorted array whenever `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -Infinity`: compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid + 1]`. If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, we are on a rising slope so a peak MUST exist in `[mid + 1..hi]`; otherwise a peak MUST exist in `[lo..mid]`.

stepByStep: lo = 0, hi = 6 -> mid = 3 (nums[3]=3 < nums[4]=5): rising slope to the right -> lo = 4.
lo = 4, hi = 6 -> mid = 5 (nums[5]=6 > nums[6]=4): falling slope to the right -> hi = 5.
lo = 4, hi = 5 -> mid = 4 (nums[4]=5 < nums[5]=6): rising slope -> lo = 5.
lo === hi === 5 -> return index 5 (value 6 is greater than neighbours 5 and 4).
workedExample.invariantSummary: Throughout the loop, the subarray nums[lo..hi] is bounded by lower outer neighbours (nums[lo - 1] < nums[lo] and nums[hi] > nums[hi + 1]), guaranteeing at least one local peak inside [lo..hi].

pitfalls: Dividing and modding by `rows` (`R`) instead of `cols` (`C`) when converting a 1D index into 2D `(row, col)` coordinates.
Accessing `nums[mid + 1]` without ensuring `mid < hi`, which is why `while (lo < hi)` with floor midpoint is essential (so `mid + 1 <= hi` is always in bounds).

edgeCase.scenario: Non-square matrix with 1 row and 5 columns (R = 1, C = 5)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Using `row = Math.floor(idx / R)` and `col = idx % R` computes `row = 3, col = 0` for `idx = 3` and crashes with `matrix[3] is undefined`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always divide and modulo by the number of COLUMNS (`C = matrix[0].length`), because each row contains `C` elements.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a row-major `R x C` matrix (R rows, C columns), how do you convert a 1D flat index `k` (0 <= k < R * C) into `(row, col)`?

options.label: row = Math.floor(k / C), col = k % C
options.feedback: Correct! Every full row advances by C elements, so dividing by C gives the row and the remainder gives the column.

options.label: row = Math.floor(k / R), col = k % R
options.feedback: Dividing by R fails whenever R !== C, because rows have width C, not R.

options.label: row = k % C, col = Math.floor(k / C)
options.feedback: That swaps row and column coordinates.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Row width is C (number of columns), so `Math.floor(k / C)` counts completed rows and `k % C` gives the offset within the row.

lessons.title: Three-Way Partitioning (Dutch National Flag Invariant)
lessons.measurableObjective: Partition an array into three regions (`< pivot`, `=== pivot`, `> pivot`) in a single pass using `low`, `mid`, and `high` boundaries.
lessons.explanation: Edsger Dijkstra’s Dutch National Flag algorithm partitions an array in-place using three pointers (`low = 0, mid = 0, high = n - 1`) that maintain four regions: `nums[0..low-1]` are strictly `< pivot` (`0`), `nums[low..mid-1]` equal `pivot` (`1`), `nums[mid..high]` are unclassified, and `nums[high+1..n-1]` are strictly `> pivot` (`2`). Why do we increment `mid` after swapping with `low`, but NOT increment `mid` after swapping with `high`? Because `nums[low]` comes from the already-inspected `1`s region (or `low === mid`), whereas `nums[high]` comes from the uninspected region and must be examined at `mid` on the next iteration!

stepByStep: low=0, mid=0, high=5: nums[0]=2 -> swap(0, 5) gives [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]; high=4, mid stays 0.
low=0, mid=0, high=4: nums[0]=0 -> swap(0, 0); low=1, mid=1.
low=1, mid=1, high=4: nums[1]=0 -> swap(1, 1); low=2, mid=2.
low=2, mid=2, high=4: nums[2]=2 -> swap(2, 4) gives [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]; high=3, mid stays 2.
mid=2 (1) -> mid=3; mid=3 (1) -> mid=4 > high=3 -> terminate.
workedExample.invariantSummary: At every step: [0..low-1] == 0, [low..mid-1] == 1, [mid..high] is uninspected, and [high+1..n-1] == 2.

pitfalls: Incrementing `mid` after swapping `nums[mid]` with `nums[high]`, which skips inspecting the value swapped in from `high`.
Using `while (mid < high)` instead of `while (mid <= high)`, leaving the last element at `mid === high` uninspected.

edgeCase.scenario: `nums = [2, 0, 1]` where `nums[high]` holds a `0`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If `mid` increments when swapping index 0 (`2`) with index 2 (`1`), or when `nums[high]` is `0`, that `0` gets stranded in the middle.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Only decrement `high -= 1` in the `nums[mid] === 2` branch so the next loop iteration classifies the new `nums[mid]`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the Dutch National Flag partition, why do we NOT increment `mid` after swapping `nums[mid]` (which is `2`) with `nums[high]`?

options.label: Because the value arriving from `nums[high]` belongs to the uninspected region `[mid..high]` and could be `0`, `1`, or `2`.
options.feedback: Correct! `nums[high]` has not been classified yet, so `mid` must stay put to inspect it next.

options.label: Because `high` was not decremented.
options.feedback: `high` IS decremented (`high -= 1`), shrinking the uninspected region from the right.

options.label: To prevent `mid` from exceeding `nums.length`.
options.feedback: The loop condition `mid <= high` already prevents out-of-bounds access.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: The value swapped from `high` is uninspected, whereas the value at `low` is already known to be `1` (or `low === mid`).

lessons.title: Exact-K Subarray Counting via AtMost(K) - AtMost(K - 1)
lessons.measurableObjective: Count subarrays with EXACTLY `k` distinct elements (or odd numbers) by subtracting two monotonic `atMost(k)` sliding window counts.
lessons.explanation: A single sliding window cannot directly count subarrays with **exactly** `k` distinct elements because for a fixed `right`, multiple `left` positions can yield `k` distinct elements. However, "at most `k` distinct elements" IS monotonic! If `[left..right]` has `<= k` distinct elements, then every suffix subarray `[i..right]` for `left <= i <= right` also has `<= k` distinct elements—that is `right - left + 1` valid subarrays ending at `right`! Therefore, `exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1)` solves the exact-count problem in two clean `O(n)` sliding-window passes.

stepByStep: atMost(1): each single-value run has length 1 -> +1+1+1+1+1 = 5.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Once freq.size <= k, all (right - left + 1) subarrays ending at right and starting in [left..right] have at most k distinct values.

pitfalls: Forgetting `if (next === 0) freq.delete(lVal)` when decrementing counts, which leaves `freq.size` inflated by zero-count keys!
Adding `1` instead of `right - left + 1` when counting all valid subarrays ending at `right`.

edgeCase.scenario: `k = 1` where `atMost(k - 1)` calls `atMost(0)`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Without `if (k <= 0) return 0`, the inner `while` loop can push `left` to `right + 1`, require careful bounds handling, or waste a full pass.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Return `0` immediately whenever `k <= 0`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In `atMostKDistinct`, once the `while (freq.size > k)` loop finishes for a given `right`, why do we add `right - left + 1` to `total`?

options.label: Because every subarray `[i..right]` with `left <= i <= right` is a subset of `[left..right]` and therefore also has `<= k` distinct elements.
options.feedback: Correct! There are `right - left + 1` such start indices `i`, and all of them end at `right`.

options.label: Because `right - left + 1` is the maximum window length.
options.feedback: We are summing subarray counts across all `right`, not taking a maximum length.

options.label: Because `freq.size` always equals `right - left + 1`.
options.feedback: `freq.size` is the number of distinct values (`<= k`), whereas `right - left + 1` is the window length.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Any subarray contained inside a valid `<= k`-distinct window also has `<= k` distinct elements.

lessons.title: Doubly-Linked List Splice & Hash-Map LRU Eviction
lessons.measurableObjective: Combine a Hash Map (`key -> node`) with a doubly-linked list bounded by `head` and `tail` sentinels to achieve O(1) `get` and `put` in an LRU Cache.
lessons.explanation: Why can neither a Hash Map alone nor a Linked List alone implement an `O(1)` Least Recently Used (LRU) cache? A Hash Map gives `O(1)` lookup by key, but cannot reorder recency in `O(1)` when a middle item is accessed. A Doubly-Linked List can splice a node out (`node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev`) and insert it at the Most Recently Used (MRU) front in `O(1)`, provided you already have a direct reference to `node`! Storing `key -> DoublyLinkedNode` in a `Map` and sandwiching all real nodes between two permanent sentinels `head <-> ... <-> tail` makes every splice and eviction 4 pointer assignments with zero null checks.

stepByStep: Init: head <-> tail.
put(1, 10): insertAfterHead(1) -> head <-> [1:10] <-> tail.
put(2, 20): insertAfterHead(2) -> head <-> [2:20] <-> [1:10] <-> tail.
get(1): removeNode(1), insertAfterHead(1) -> head <-> [1:10] <-> [2:20] <-> tail (now 2 is LRU at tail.prev).
put(3, 30): insert 3 at front; size > 2 so evict lru = tail.prev ([2:20]): removeNode(2) and map.delete(2).
workedExample.invariantSummary: head.next is always the most recently used node, tail.prev is always the least recently used node, and map.size equals the number of nodes between head and tail.

pitfalls: Forgetting to store `key` on the doubly-linked `node` itself, making it impossible to call `map.delete(lruNode.key)` in O(1) when evicting `tail.prev`!
Updating an existing key via `put(key, newVal)` without moving its node to the MRU position.

edgeCase.scenario: Calling `put(k, v)` on a key `k` that ALREADY exists when the cache is at full capacity
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If you check `map.size === capacity` and evict `tail.prev` BEFORE checking whether `k` is already in `map`, you wrongly evict a valid key on an in-place update!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Check `if (map.has(key))` first (or remove the existing node first) before checking capacity overflow.

knowledgeCheck.question: In an LRU Cache backed by a `Map` and a doubly-linked list, why must each doubly-linked node store both `node.key` and `node.val`?

options.label: Because when capacity overflows we evict `const lru = tail.prev`, and we need `lru.key` to delete its entry from the `Map` in O(1).
options.feedback: Correct! Without `lru.key` on the node, you would have to scan the entire `Map` to find which key pointed to `lru`.

options.label: Because `get(key)` searches the linked list from `head` to `tail` using `node.key`.
options.feedback: `get(key)` looks up the node in O(1) via `map.get(key)`, never by scanning the list.

options.label: Because JavaScript Maps cannot store object references as values.
options.feedback: JavaScript Maps can store any object reference as a value.

lessons.title: Monotonic Deque & O(n) Sliding Window Maximum
lessons.measurableObjective: Maintain the maximum of a sliding window of size `k` in O(1) per step using a double-ended queue (deque) of indices.
lessons.explanation: In Sliding Window Maximum, as window `[i - k + 1 .. i]` slides right, elements enter on the right and expire on the left. Suppose `j < i` and `nums[j] <= nums[i]`. Since `nums[i]` is both **at least as large** as `nums[j]` AND **younger** (will stay in future windows longer than `j`), `j` can NEVER be the maximum of this or any future window! Thus we maintain a **monotonic decreasing deque of indices**: (1) evict front index `deque[0]` if it fell out of the window (`deque[0] <= i - k`), (2) pop back indices while `nums[deque[back]] <= nums[i]`, (3) push `i` to the back, and (4) once `i >= k - 1`, the window maximum sits at `nums[deque[0]]`.

lines: const deque = []; // stores indices, values decreasing
if (head < deque.length && deque[head] <= i - k) head += 1;

stepByStep: i=4 (5): front 1 <= 4-3 (expired, head++), then 5 >= -3, -1 -> pop both, push 4 -> deque=[4(5)]; out=[3, 3, 5].
workedExample.invariantSummary: Active deque indices in [head..deque.length-1] lie within [i - k + 1 .. i], are strictly increasing in index, and are strictly decreasing in nums value.

pitfalls: Calling `Array.prototype.shift()` in JavaScript on a large deque, which is O(k) per shift; using a `head` pointer keeps front eviction strictly O(1)!
Evicting from the front by value instead of by index expiration `deque[head] <= i - k`.

edgeCase.scenario: `k = 1` on any array
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If window answers are only recorded when `i > k - 1` instead of `i >= k - 1`, index 0 is skipped when `k = 1`.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always record `out.push(nums[deque[head]])` whenever `i >= k - 1`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Sliding Window Maximum, why can we permanently discard an older index `j < i` from the back of the deque as soon as `nums[j] <= nums[i]`?

options.label: Because `i` is both >= `nums[j]` in value and expires later than `j`, so `j` can never beat `i` in the current window or any future window.
options.feedback: Correct! Index `i` dominates index `j` in both magnitude and lifetime.

options.label: Because `j` has already fallen outside `[i - k + 1 .. i]`.
options.feedback: `j` is still inside the current window, but it is dominated by the newer, larger element `nums[i]`.

options.label: Because a deque can hold at most 2 elements.
options.feedback: A deque can hold up to `k` elements if the window is strictly decreasing.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Any older element `<= nums[i]` is dominated for the remainder of its lifetime in the window.

lessons.title: BFS Level-Order Traversal & Level-Size Snapshot Invariants
lessons.measurableObjective: Group tree nodes by depth and extract level extrema (such as Right Side View) by snapshotting `const levelSize = queue.length - head` before each level loop.
lessons.explanation: Standard Breadth-First Search (BFS) visits nodes in non-decreasing order of depth, but a single flat `while (queue not empty)` loop blends depth `d` and depth `d + 1` together in the queue. How do we separate levels cleanly? At the start of each outer iteration, the queue contains **all and only** the nodes at the current depth `d`! By snapshotting `const levelSize = queue.length - head` BEFORE the inner `for (let i = 0; i < levelSize; i += 1)` loop, the inner loop dequeues exactly the `levelSize` nodes of depth `d` while pushing their children (depth `d + 1`) to the back for the next outer iteration.

stepByStep: Init: queue = [3], head = 0.
Level 0: levelSize = 1 - 0 = 1. Dequeue 3, push 9 and 20 -> currentLevel = [3].
Level 1: levelSize = 3 - 1 = 2 (nodes 9, 20). Dequeue 9 (no children), dequeue 20 (push 15, 7) -> currentLevel = [9, 20].
Level 2: levelSize = 5 - 3 = 2 (nodes 15, 7). Dequeue 15, 7 -> currentLevel = [15, 7].
head === 5 === queue.length -> return [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]].
workedExample.invariantSummary: At the top of the outer while loop (iteration d), queue[head..queue.length-1] holds all nodes at depth d from left to right.

pitfalls: Writing `for (let i = 0; i < queue.length - head; i += 1)` inline without snapshotting `const levelSize`, which re-evaluates `queue.length` as children are pushed and merges all levels into one!
Forgetting `if (root === null) return []`, which pushes `[null]` into the queue and crashes on `node.val`.

edgeCase.scenario: Right Side View where the deepest node on the right is actually in the LEFT subtree (e.g., `root.right` is a leaf at depth 1, `root.left.right` reaches depth 2)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: Walking only `node = node.right` misses deeper nodes hidden behind a shorter right branch!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Use level-order BFS and pick the last node `i === levelSize - 1` of every level.

knowledgeCheck.question: In level-order BFS, what bug occurs if you write `for (let i = 0; i < queue.length; i++)` (using `queue.shift()`) instead of snapshotting `const levelSize = queue.length` before the `for` loop?

options.label: Because `queue.length` changes dynamically as nodes are shifted and children are pushed, the loop boundary shifts mid-level and mixes nodes from different depths.
options.feedback: Correct! Snapshotting `levelSize` freezes the exact count of nodes belonging to the current depth `d`.

options.label: JavaScript throws a SyntaxError when `.length` is used in a `for` condition.
options.feedback: It is valid syntax, which makes it a subtle logical bug!

options.label: Right children are visited before left children.
options.feedback: Left/right push order is unchanged; the bug is corrupting the level boundary count.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Freezing `const levelSize` before the loop isolates depth `d` from the newly enqueued depth `d + 1` children.

lessons.provenance: Adapted from OpenDSA level-order traversal invariants.

lessons.title: Dual-Heap Running Median Balancing (`maxLow` & `minHigh`)
lessons.measurableObjective: Maintain the exact median of a dynamic data stream in `O(log n)` per insertion and `O(1)` per query by balancing a Max-Heap of the lower half and a Min-Heap of the upper half.
lessons.explanation: The median sits at the boundary between the smaller half and the larger half of the data. If we store the smaller half in a **Max-Heap** (`maxLow`, so its largest element sits at the top) and the larger half in a **Min-Heap** (`minHigh`, so its smallest element sits at the top), then the two heap roots expose the exact middle of the sorted order in `O(1)`! Two invariants must hold after every `addNum(x)`: (1) **Order invariant**: `maxLow.top <= minHigh.top`, and (2) **Size invariant**: `maxLow.size === minHigh.size` (even count) or `maxLow.size === minHigh.size + 1` (odd count). Routing every new `x` through `maxLow` -> `minHigh` and rebalancing size when `minHigh.size > maxLow.size` preserves both invariants in 2–3 heap ops!

lines: export function addNumDualHeap(x, maxLow, minHigh, pushMax, popMax, pushMin, popMin) {

workedExample.inputDescription: Stream: addNum(1), addNum(2), findMedian(), addNum(3), findMedian()
stepByStep: addNum(1): push 1 to maxLow, move max(1) to minHigh, minHigh.len(1) > maxLow.len(0) so move 1 back -> maxLow=[1], minHigh=[].
addNum(2): push 2 to maxLow ([2, 1]), move max(2) to minHigh -> maxLow=[1], minHigh=[2] (equal sizes).
findMedian(): sizes equal -> (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5.
addNum(3): push 3 to maxLow ([3, 1]), move 3 to minHigh ([2, 3]), minHigh.len(2) > maxLow.len(1) so move min(2) to maxLow -> maxLow=[2, 1], minHigh=[3].
findMedian(): maxLow.len (2) > minHigh.len (1) -> return maxLow[0] = 2.
workedExample.invariantSummary: After every addNum: all elements in maxLow <= all elements in minHigh, and 0 <= maxLow.length - minHigh.length <= 1.

pitfalls: Pushing directly into `maxLow` just because `maxLow.length <= minHigh.length` without checking `x > minHigh[0]`, which violates the order invariant `maxLow.top <= minHigh.top`!
Using two Min-Heaps (without negating keys or inverting the comparator for `maxLow`), which exposes the global minimum instead of the top of the lower half.

edgeCase.scenario: Inserting numbers in strictly decreasing order `[10, 8, 6, 4]`
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If new numbers are blindly alternated between `maxLow` and `minHigh` by parity, `10` ends up in `maxLow` while `8` is in `minHigh` (`10 > 8`).
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always pass the new number through one heap into the other (`pushMax` -> `popMax` -> `pushMin`) before equalizing sizes.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does `addNum` push `x` into `maxLow` and immediately move `popMax(maxLow)` into `minHigh` BEFORE checking `if (minHigh.length > maxLow.length)`?

options.label: To guarantee the order invariant (`maxLow.top <= minHigh.top`): even if `x` was huge and belonged in `minHigh`, `popMax(maxLow)` flushes the largest lower-half value over to `minHigh`.
options.feedback: Correct! Routing through `maxLow` -> `minHigh` enforces sorted partitioning before the size check restores balance.

options.label: Because `minHigh` cannot accept elements directly.
options.feedback: `minHigh` is a standard heap; routing through `maxLow` first avoids writing manual value-comparison branches.

options.label: To clear `maxLow` completely on every insertion.
options.feedback: `popMax` only removes the single maximum element of `maxLow`, not the whole heap.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Routing `x` through `maxLow` into `minHigh` guarantees every element in `minHigh` is `>=` every element in `maxLow`.

lessons.title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set) & Weighted Shortest Paths
lessons.measurableObjective: Maintain dynamic connected components with Union-Find and relax non-negative weighted edges with Dijkstra’s min-heap algorithm.
lessons.explanation: When undirected edges arrive dynamically, **Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)** with path compression and union-by-rank tracks connected components in near-constant `O(alpha(V))` time per edge; the first edge `[u, v]` where `find(u) === find(v)` connects two vertices already in the same component and completes a cycle. For shortest paths with non-negative edge weights, **Dijkstra’s algorithm** replaces the FIFO queue of BFS with a Min-Heap ordered by cumulative distance `dist[u]`, relaxing edges `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`.

lines: const parent = Array.from({ length: edges.length + 1 }, (_, i) => i);

stepByStep: Init: parent = [0, 1, 2, 3].
Edge [1, 2]: find(1) = 1 !== find(2) = 2 -> parent[1] = 2.
Edge [1, 3]: find(1) = 2 !== find(3) = 3 -> parent[2] = 3.
Edge [2, 3]: find(2) = 3 === find(3) = 3 -> both share root 3! Return [2, 3].
workedExample.outputDescription: [2, 3] (the exact edge that closes the cycle)
workedExample.invariantSummary: Two vertices u and v belong to the same connected component if and only if find(u) === find(v).

pitfalls: Applying standard Dijkstra without hop-count state when a problem limits paths to at most `K` stops (where a costlier path with fewer hops can beat a cheaper path that exceeds `K` stops).
Using Dijkstra on graphs with negative edge weights.

edgeCase.scenario: Stale heap entries in Dijkstra when a vertex `v` is pushed multiple times with improved distances
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: When the older, larger `[d, v]` entry is later popped from the heap, expanding its edges again wastes `O(E)` work.
edgeCase.howToHandle: Immediately skip stale pops with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;` right after popping `[d, u]`.

knowledgeCheck.question: When processing undirected edges one by one in Union-Find, what condition proves that the current edge `[u, v]` creates a cycle?

options.label: `find(u) === find(v)` BEFORE uniting them, meaning a path between `u` and `v` already exists in the current component.
options.feedback: Correct! Adding an edge between two vertices that already share a component root closes a cycle.

options.label: `parent[u] !== u`
options.feedback: A vertex having a parent just means it has been united with at least one other vertex, not that `u` and `v` are in the same component.

options.label: `u > v`
options.feedback: Vertex numbering does not determine cycle connectivity.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: `find(u) === find(v)` means `u` and `v` are already connected, so `[u, v]` is redundant.

lessons.title: Grid & Constraint Backtracking (Word Search & N-Queens)
lessons.measurableObjective: Enforce spatial and structural constraints using reversible in-place cell marking and O(1) diagonal/column conflict sets.
lessons.explanation: In spatial backtracking (like Word Search on a 2D board or placing `N` non-attacking Queens), each recursive step mutates a board cell or constraint set, explores valid child states, and **restores** the mutation on return. Unlike flood-fill DFS (where any path to a cell suffices), a Word Search path that fails after stepping through `(r, c)` must unmark `(r, c)` so a different path ordering can still use `(r, c)`. In N-Queens, row-by-row placement with sets for `cols` (`c`), `diag1` (`r - c`), and `diag2` (`r + c`) checks attacks in `O(1)` time.

const found = dfs(r + 1, c, idx + 1) || dfs(r - 1, c, idx + 1) ||
dfs(r, c + 1, idx + 1) || dfs(r, c - 1, idx + 1);

Main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) keeps r - c = 1 - 2 = -1 constant (matches (0, 1) and (2, 3)).
Anti-diagonal (top-right to bottom-left) keeps r + c = 1 + 2 = 3 constant (matches (0, 3), (2, 1), and (3, 0)).

Allowing `close > open` in Generate Parentheses, which produces invalid prefixes like `")("`.

options.label: Because Number of Islands uses a 1D array.

lessons.title: 2D Grid & Two-Sequence Alignment DP (LCS & Edit Distance)
lessons.measurableObjective: Tabulate 2D state matrices `dp[i][j]` over grid coordinates or pairs of string prefixes with 1-indexed sentinel borders.
lessons.explanation: When a problem aligns two strings `text1[0..i-1]` and `text2[0..j-1]` (**Longest Common Subsequence**, **Edit Distance**) or counts paths across a 2D grid (**Unique Paths**), the state requires two coordinates `(i, j)`. Allocating an `(m + 1) x (n + 1)` matrix where row `0` and column `0` represent empty prefixes eliminates boundary branches: in LCS, if `text1[i - 1] === text2[j - 1]`, both characters match and consume each other (`1 + dp[i - 1][j - 1]`); otherwise we skip one character (`Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])`).

lines: const dp = Array.from({ length: m + 1 }, () => new Array(n + 1).fill(0));

stepByStep: Row i = 1 ("a"): matches text2[0] = "a" -> dp[1][1] = 1 + dp[0][0] = 1; propagates 1 across dp[1][1..5].
Row i = 2 ("c"): matches text2[2] = "c" -> dp[2][3] = 1 + dp[1][2] = 2; propagates 2 across dp[2][3..5].
Row i = 3 ("e"): matches text2[4] = "e" -> dp[3][5] = 1 + dp[2][4] = 3. Return dp[3][5] = 3.
workedExample.invariantSummary: Cell dp[i][j] holds the exact LCS length of prefix text1.slice(0, i) and prefix text2.slice(0, j).

pitfalls: Writing `1 + Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])` on a character match in LCS instead of `1 + dp[i - 1][j - 1]`, which double-counts a single character against two copies in the other string!
In Edit Distance, initializing row `0` and column `0` to `0` instead of `dp[0][j] = j` (insert `j` chars) and `dp[i][0] = i` (delete `i` chars).

edgeCase.scenario: Edit Distance when one string is empty (`word1 = "", word2 = "ros"`)
edgeCase.whyItBreaksNaiveCode: If base row `dp[0][j]` is left at `0`, `minDistance("", "ros")` returns `0` instead of `3` insertions!
edgeCase.howToHandle: Always initialize `for (let i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;` and `for (let j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;`.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Longest Common Subsequence, when `text1[i - 1] === text2[j - 1]`, why MUST `dp[i][j]` transition from `1 + dp[i - 1][j - 1]` instead of `1 + dp[i][j - 1]`?

options.label: Because pairing `text1[i - 1]` with `text2[j - 1]` consumes BOTH characters; using `dp[i][j - 1]` would allow `text1[i - 1]` to be matched a second time.
options.feedback: Correct! For example, on `text1 = "a", text2 = "aa"`, `1 + dp[i][j - 1]` would falsely return `2` instead of `1`!

options.label: Because `dp[i - 1][j - 1]` is always larger than `dp[i][j - 1]`.
options.feedback: `dp[i - 1][j - 1]` is `<= dp[i][j - 1]`; we use the diagonal specifically to avoid reusing `text1[i - 1]`.

options.label: Because `dp[i][j - 1]` has not been computed yet.
options.feedback: In left-to-right row-major order, `dp[i][j - 1]` was just computed on the previous inner iteration.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Diagonal transition `(i - 1, j - 1)` advances past both matched characters simultaneously.
