exercises.title: Proof Trace: Exclusive Prefix & Suffix Accumulation Around Zeros
exercises.objective: Trace two-pass exclusive prefix/suffix products on an array containing a zero without using division.
exercises.instructions: Follow the left-to-right prefix pass and right-to-left suffix pass on `nums = [2, 0, 3]`. Verify what each cell holds before and after multiplying.

primaryVariant.label: Single Zero in Middle
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Only the index of the single zero (index 1) should survive with a non-zero product (2 * 3 = 6).

steps.prompt: Pass 1 reaches `i = 1` (`nums[1] = 0`). Before line 6 executes, `prefix` is `2`. What happens to `out[1]` and `prefix`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Pass 1 at index 1: out so far is [1, _, _], prefix from index 0 is 2.

choices.label: out[1] receives 2 (the exclusive prefix), then prefix becomes 2 * 0 = 0 for later indices
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Because `out[1] = prefix` runs before `prefix *= nums[1]`, index 1 does NOT get zeroed out by its own zero.

choices.label: out[1] becomes 0 because nums[1] is 0
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `out[1]` excludes `nums[1]`! Line 5 writes `prefix` (2) into `out[1]` before line 6 multiplies by `nums[1]`.

steps.correctExplanation: Assigning before multiplying keeps `out[1] = 2`, while `prefix` becomes 0 for all indices `> 1`.

steps.prompt: After Pass 1 completes, `out` is `[1, 2, 0]`. Pass 2 starts at `i = 2` (`nums[2] = 3`) with `suffix = 1`, then moves to `i = 1` (`nums[1] = 0`) with `suffix = 3`. What happens at `i = 1`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Pass 2 at index 1: out[1] holds prefix 2, suffix from index 2 holds 3.

choices.label: out[1] becomes 2 * 3 = 6, then suffix becomes 3 * 0 = 0 for index 0
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Index 1 combines left prefix 2 and right suffix 3 to get 6, and then zeros `suffix` for index 0.

choices.label: out[1] becomes 6, and suffix stays 3 so we do not lose information
choices.misconceptionFeedback: For index 0, `nums[1] = 0` IS part of its right suffix, so `suffix` must become `3 * 0 = 0`.

steps.correctExplanation: `out[1]` becomes `2 * 3 = 6`, and `suffix` becomes `0`, which then sets `out[0] = 1 * 0 = 0`.

alternateVariant.label: Two Zeros in Array
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: With two zeros, every index has at least one zero in either its left prefix or right suffix.

steps.prompt: In Pass 1 on `nums = [0, 4, 0]`, what is the `out` array after the left-to-right loop finishes?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[0] = 0 immediately turns prefix into 0 after index 0.

choices.label: out is [1, 0, 0] because index 0 has empty prefix 1, and nums[0]=0 zeros prefix for indices 1 and 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Only index 0 escapes the zero at `nums[0]` during Pass 1.

choices.label: out is [0, 0, 0] immediately after Pass 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: At `i = 0`, `prefix` starts at `1`, so `out[0]` is `1` after Pass 1; it only becomes `0` during Pass 2.

steps.correctExplanation: Pass 1 leaves `out = [1, 0, 0]`, and Pass 2 multiplies `out[0]` by `suffix = 0` (from `nums[2] = 0`), yielding `[0, 0, 0]`.

steps.prompt: After Pass 2 sweeps right-to-left over `[0, 4, 0]`, what is the final returned array?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[2] = 0 zeros out suffix before Pass 2 reaches index 0.

choices.label: [0, 0, 0] because index 0 gets multiplied by suffix 0 from nums[2]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exactly! Two zeros mean every single position has at least one other zero elsewhere.

choices.label: [4, 0, 4] by skipping zeros during multiplication
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Zero is a real multiplier in the array, not a missing value.

steps.correctExplanation: Every position excludes itself but still includes the other zero, so the output is `[0, 0, 0]`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: In JavaScript, multiplying `-1 * 0` yields `-0`. How can you normalize `-0` to `0` if a strict test checks `Object.is(val, 0)`?

choices.label: Use `out[i] === 0 ? 0 : out[i]` (or `out[i] + 0`) when storing the product.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! In IEEE-754 floating point, `-0 === 0` is true, so `x === 0 ? 0 : x` (or `x + 0`) converts `-0` to `+0`.

choices.label: Use `Math.abs(out[i])` on every element.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `Math.abs` would destroy legitimate negative products like `-12`!

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Adding `0` (`x + 0`) or checking `x === 0 ? 0 : x` converts IEEE-754 `-0` into `+0` without altering negative numbers.

exercises.referenceInvariant: After Pass 1, out[i] === prod(nums[0..i-1]). At step i of Pass 2, suffix === prod(nums[i+1..n-1]), so out[i] * suffix === prod(nums[0..i-1]) * prod(nums[i+1..n-1]).
exercises.hintText: Write `out[i]` BEFORE updating `prefix` or `suffix` with `nums[i]` so `nums[i]` is never multiplied into its own slot.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: Why does separating exclusive left state and exclusive right state into two passes eliminate all special-case branching for zeros?

exercises.title: Proof Trace: Complement Lookup-Before-Insert on Duplicate Targets
exercises.objective: Trace how checking `indexByVal.has(need)` before `indexByVal.set(nums[i], i)` handles duplicate values and avoids self-matching.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the array pointer and Map entries at each step. Choose the exact state transition for `indexByVal`.

primaryVariant.label: Self-Complement Trap (Half of Target)
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Index 0 has value 3 (`need = 3`), which equals half of `target = 6`. It must NOT match itself at `i = 0`.

steps.prompt: At `i = 0` (`nums[0] = 3`, `target = 6`), `need` is `3`. What is in `indexByVal` when line 5 (`indexByVal.has(3)`) runs?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Checking indexByVal.has(3) before inserting nums[0].

choices.label: indexByVal is empty, so has(3) is false; then line 8 inserts (3 -> 0)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Because we check before inserting, `nums[0] = 3` cannot match itself.

choices.label: indexByVal already contains (3 -> 0) and returns [0, 0]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: That bug only happens if you insert before checking or pre-populate the map without checking `idx !== i`.

steps.correctExplanation: Checking `has(need)` before `set(nums[i], i)` ensures the map only holds indices `< i`.

steps.prompt: At `i = 1` (`nums[1] = 2`, `need = 4`), `4` is not in the map so `(2 -> 1)` is inserted. Now at `i = 2` (`nums[2] = 4`), what happens?

stateSnapshot.annotation: At i = 2 (val 4), need = 6 - 4 = 2. Map holds {3: 0, 2: 1}.

choices.label: indexByVal.has(2) is true and returns [1, 2] immediately
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact match! `indexByVal.get(2)` is `1`, returning `[1, 2]`.

choices.label: It inserts (4 -> 2) and waits until i = 3 to match the two 3s
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Line 6 returns immediately as soon as the first valid pair `[1, 2]` is completed.

steps.correctExplanation: At `i = 2`, partner `2` is already in `indexByVal` at index `1`, so `[1, 2]` is returned.

alternateVariant.label: Duplicate Values Matching Index 0
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Tests both duplicate keys and matching a partner located at index `0`.

steps.prompt: After `i = 0` finishes on `nums = [3, 3]`, what is in `indexByVal` as `i = 1` begins?

stateSnapshot.annotation: i = 1 (val 3) needs 3, which is stored at index 0.

choices.label: Map holds {3 -> 0}; at i = 1, indexByVal.has(3) is true and returns [0, 1] before overwriting key 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Because we check `has(3)` BEFORE calling `set(3, 1)`, we never overwrite index 0 before matching it.

choices.label: The second 3 overwrites (3 -> 0) with (3 -> 1), losing index 0
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Since lookup happens on line 5 before insertion on line 8, `[0, 1]` is returned before `set` is reached.

steps.correctExplanation: Lookup-before-insert matches the second `3` against the first `3` at index 0 without overwriting it.

steps.prompt: Why was `indexByVal.has(need)` critical here instead of `if (indexByVal.get(need))`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: indexByVal.get(3) returns the number 0.

choices.label: Because indexByVal.get(3) returns 0, which is falsy in `if (0)` and would skip the match!
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! `has(3)` returns `true` even when the stored value is `0`.

choices.label: Because `get()` deletes the key from the Map.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `get()` is read-only; the danger is that `0` is falsy in JavaScript.

steps.correctExplanation: `indexByVal.has(need)` returns a boolean and is immune to falsy index `0`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: Suppose `[2, 2, 5]` has `target = 7`. Both index 0 and index 1 hold `2`. If the problem asks for the EARLIEST partner index `[0, 2]`, how should you handle duplicate insertions?

choices.label: Only call `indexByVal.set(nums[i], i)` if `!indexByVal.has(nums[i])`, preserving the first index of each value.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Guarding `set` with `!indexByVal.has(nums[i])` keeps the earliest index (`0`) instead of overwriting it with `1`.

choices.label: Clear the map whenever a duplicate value is encountered.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Clearing the map would erase all previously seen values.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Unconditional `set` keeps the most recent index; guarding with `!map.has(x)` keeps the earliest index.

exercises.referenceInvariant: At line 5 of iteration i, indexByVal contains every value from nums[0..i-1] and no value from nums[i..n-1].
exercises.hintText: Trace the exact moment `has(need)` is called: has `nums[i]` been added to the Map yet?
exercises.reflectionPrompt: When should a hash map keep the FIRST index of a duplicate key versus the MOST RECENT index?

exercises.title: Proof Trace: Prefix-Sum Frequency Map with Negative Numbers
exercises.objective: Trace how `prefixCounts` seeded with `{0: 1}` counts overlapping and negative-sum subarrays summing to `k`.
exercises.instructions: Step through `nums = [1, -1, 1]` with `k = 1`. Watch how revisiting prefix sum `0` increases future match counts.

primaryVariant.label: Revisiting Prefix Zero via Cancelation
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: The prefix sum after `[1, -1]` returns to `0`, meaning there are now TWO earlier prefixes with sum `0`.

steps.prompt: At `i = 0` (`nums[0] = 1`, `k = 1`), `runningSum` becomes `1` and `neededPrefix = 0`. What happens to `totalMatches` and `prefixCounts`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Seed {0: 1} is already in prefixCounts before index 0.

choices.label: totalMatches increases by 1 (matching seed 0), and prefixCounts becomes {0: 1, 1: 1}
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! The seed `{0: 1}` allows the single-element subarray `nums[0..0] = [1]` to be counted.

choices.label: totalMatches stays 0 because index 0 has no elements to its left
choices.misconceptionFeedback: The empty prefix before index 0 has sum 0, which is why `{0: 1}` was seeded!

steps.correctExplanation: Matching `neededPrefix = 0` against `{0: 1}` counts `nums[0..0]` and records `1 -> 1`.

steps.prompt: At `i = 1` (`nums[1] = -1`), `runningSum` returns to `0` (`neededPrefix = -1`, not in map). How does `prefixCounts` update on line 9?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Prefix [1, -1] sums to 0, revisiting key 0.

choices.label: Key 0 increments from 1 to 2 (`{0: 2, 1: 1}`), representing two prefixes with sum 0 (empty prefix and nums[0..1])
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exactly! Both the empty prefix and `nums[0..1]` have sum 0.

choices.label: Key 0 stays 1 because a Set of seen prefix sums is sufficient
choices.misconceptionFeedback: If you only kept `0 -> 1`, you would miss one of the two valid subarrays ending at index 2!

steps.correctExplanation: Incrementing `0 -> 2` records that two distinct split points have prefix sum 0.

steps.prompt: At `i = 2` (`nums[2] = 1`), `runningSum` is `1` and `neededPrefix = 1 - 1 = 0`. How much does `totalMatches` increase on line 8?

stateSnapshot.annotation: At i = 2, prefixCounts.get(0) is 2.

choices.label: It increases by 2 (to 3 total), counting both `nums[0..2] = [1, -1, 1]` and `nums[2..2] = [1]` in O(1)!
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Brilliant! Each of the 2 earlier prefixes with sum 0 defines a distinct valid subarray ending at index 2.

choices.label: It increases by 1 because only one subarray can end at index 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Because `nums[0..1]` sums to 0, both `[1, -1, 1]` and `[1]` end at index 2 with sum 1!

steps.correctExplanation: Looking up `prefixCounts.get(0) = 2` simultaneously counts both subarrays ending at index 2.

alternateVariant.label: Zero Target Sum (k = 0)
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: When `k = 0`, `neededPrefix === runningSum`. Querying BEFORE incrementing prevents matching the current prefix with itself.

steps.prompt: At `i = 0` (`nums[0] = 2`, `k = 0`), `runningSum = 2` and `neededPrefix = 2`. Why does `totalMatches` stay `0`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: k = 0: neededPrefix is 2, which is not yet in prefixCounts.

choices.label: Because line 8 queries prefixCounts.get(2) BEFORE line 9 inserts 2 into the map
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! If line 9 ran first, `runningSum = 2` would match itself and count an empty subarray!

choices.label: Because k = 0 is not allowed in prefix sum maps
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `k = 0` works cleanly as long as you query before inserting.

steps.correctExplanation: Query-before-insert prevents zero-length self-matches when `k = 0`.

steps.prompt: At `i = 1` (`nums[1] = -2`, `k = 0`), `runningSum` becomes `0` and `neededPrefix = 0`. What is returned?

stateSnapshot.annotation: runningSum = 0 matches the seed {0: 1}.

choices.label: totalMatches becomes 1 (from prefixCounts.get(0) === 1), counting [2, -2]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact match! `nums[0..1] = [2, -2]` sums to 0.

choices.label: totalMatches becomes 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: At the moment line 8 runs, `0` has count `1` in the map; it only becomes `2` on line 9 afterward.

steps.correctExplanation: Line 8 reads the pre-existing count `1` for key `0` and returns `1`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: Why does a two-pointer sliding window fail on `nums = [1, -1, 1]` with `k = 1`, whereas the prefix-sum map succeeds?

choices.label: Because negative numbers break window monotonicity: shrinking the left pointer can either increase or decrease the window sum.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Sliding window pointers rely on the guarantee that advancing `left` monotonically changes the window sum.

choices.label: Because sliding windows cannot process arrays of odd length.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Array length has no impact; negative values break the monotonic sum invariant.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Prefix-sum maps depend only on additive inverse (`prefix[R] - prefix[L-1] = k`), which holds for all real/integer values.

exercises.referenceInvariant: At line 8 of step i, prefixCounts.get(p) equals the exact count of indices j in {-1, 0, ..., i-1} whose prefix sum nums[0..j] equals p.
exercises.hintText: Remember that subtracting an earlier prefix sum `nums[0..L-1]` from `nums[0..R]` leaves the contiguous slice `nums[L..R]`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: How does the `{0: 1}` seed unify subarrays that start at index `0` with subarrays that start at `L > 0`?

exercises.title: Proof Trace: Half-Open Lower Bound on Duplicate Targets
exercises.objective: Trace `lo`, `mid`, and `hi` on a sorted array with duplicates to prove `lowerBound` converges to the FIRST index `>= target`.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the `[lo, hi)` interval and `mid` pointer at each iteration. Select the bound update that preserves the lower-bound invariant.

primaryVariant.label: First Occurrence Among Duplicates
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: `nums[3] = 4` matches `target` on the very first probe, but it is NOT the first `4`! Watch how `hi = mid` keeps searching left.

steps.prompt: Start `lo = 0, hi = 6`. `mid = 3` (`nums[3] = 4 >= 4`). Why do we set `hi = 3` instead of returning `3` or setting `hi = 2`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Probing mid = 3 (value 4). Earlier indices 1 and 2 also equal 4!

choices.label: Set hi = 3: index 3 satisfies >= 4 (so it could be the answer), while indices 0..2 might hold an even earlier 4
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! `hi = mid` preserves `mid` as our best-so-far true boundary while continuing to test `0..2`.

choices.label: Return 3 immediately because nums[3] === target
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Returning on the first hit gives index 3, missing the earlier occurrences of 4 at indices 1 and 2!

choices.label: Set hi = mid - 1 (2) to search strictly left of 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: If index 3 had been the ONLY 4 in the array, setting `hi = 2` would discard the answer completely!

steps.correctExplanation: `hi = mid` keeps `mid` as the inclusive right boundary of known-true indices while shrinking the active search space to `[0, 3)`.

steps.prompt: Now `lo = 0, hi = 3`, so `mid = 1` (`nums[1] = 4 >= 4`). What is the next `[lo, hi]` interval?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Probing mid = 1 (value 4 >= 4).

choices.label: lo = 0, hi = 1 (since nums[1] >= 4, hi moves to 1)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Right! Now only index 0 remains to be tested against index 1.

choices.label: lo = 2, hi = 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Advancing `lo` when `nums[mid] >= target` would move right into duplicates instead of finding the leftmost one.

steps.correctExplanation: Since `nums[1] >= 4`, `hi` tightens to `1`.

steps.prompt: Now `lo = 0, hi = 1`, so `mid = 0` (`nums[0] = 2 < 4`). How does the loop finish?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Probing mid = 0 (value 2 < 4).

choices.label: lo becomes mid + 1 = 1; now lo === hi === 1, so the loop exits and returns 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact convergence! All indices `< 1` are `< 4`, and index `1` is the first index `>= 4`.

choices.label: lo becomes mid = 0 and loops one more time
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Setting `lo = mid` when `mid === 0` would leave `lo = 0, hi = 1` forever!

steps.correctExplanation: `lo = mid + 1` brings `lo` to `1 === hi`, terminating cleanly at the first `4`.

alternateVariant.label: Target Larger Than All Elements
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Tests why `hi` starts at `nums.length` (3) rather than `nums.length - 1` (2).

steps.prompt: Start `lo = 0, hi = 3`. `mid = 1` (`nums[1] = 4 < 15`). What is the updated `[lo, hi]`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[1] = 4 < 15 -> false branch.

choices.label: lo = 2, hi = 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Indices 0 and 1 are discarded.

choices.label: lo = 1, hi = 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Index 1 is already proven `< 15`, so `lo` advances to `mid + 1 = 2`.

steps.correctExplanation: `lo` advances to `2` while `hi` stays `3`.

steps.prompt: Now `lo = 2, hi = 3`, so `mid = 2` (`nums[2] = 8 < 15`). What happens next?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[2] = 8 < 15 -> lo advances to 3.

choices.label: lo becomes 3 (=== nums.length), loop exits, and returns 3 as the insertion index past the end
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Returning `nums.length` tells the caller that every element in `nums` is `< target`.

choices.label: It throws an out-of-bounds error by reading nums[3]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Because `lo === hi === 3`, the `while (lo < hi)` guard terminates BEFORE `nums[3]` is ever read!

steps.correctExplanation: Because `mid < hi` whenever `lo < hi`, `nums[nums.length]` is never dereferenced inside the loop.

edgeCaseCheck.question: After `idx = lowerBound(nums, target)` returns, what exact condition checks whether `target` actually exists in `nums`?

choices.label: `idx < nums.length && nums[idx] === target`
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! First verify `idx` did not land at `nums.length`, then verify the element at `idx` equals `target` (rather than being strictly greater).

choices.label: `idx >= 0`
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `lowerBound` ALWAYS returns an index in `0..nums.length`, even when `target` is missing!

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: `lowerBound` finds the first index `>= target`; checking `idx < nums.length && nums[idx] === target` confirms an exact match.

exercises.referenceInvariant: Throughout while (lo < hi), for all i < lo: nums[i] < target; and for all i >= hi: nums[i] >= target.
exercises.hintText: Ask yourself: when `nums[mid] >= target`, is `mid` still a valid candidate for the first index `>= target`? Yes—so set `hi = mid`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: Why does `mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)` guarantee `mid < hi` whenever `lo < hi`, ensuring `nums[nums.length]` is never accessed?

exercises.title: Proof Trace: Rotated Sorted Array Minimum Discrimination
exercises.objective: Trace `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` on rotated and unrotated subarrays to locate the pivot minimum in O(log n).
exercises.instructions: Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]` at each step and choose the interval update that keeps the minimum inside `[lo..hi]`.

steps.prompt: Start `lo = 0, hi = 6`. `mid = 3` (`nums[3] = 7`, `nums[6] = 2`). Since `7 > 2`, where must the minimum lie?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[mid] = 7 > nums[hi] = 2: the rotation drop is to the right of mid.

choices.label: Strictly right of mid (`lo = mid + 1 = 4`), because 7 > 2 proves the cliff is in [4..6]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! And since `7 > 2`, index 3 itself cannot be the minimum, so `lo = 4` safely excludes `mid`.

choices.label: In [0..3] (`hi = 3`), because [0..3] is sorted
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `[0..3]` is the HIGH plateau `[4, 5, 6, 7]` before the wrap-around drop to `0`!

steps.correctExplanation: `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` means the wrap-around drop occurs after `mid`, so `lo = mid + 1`.

steps.prompt: Now `lo = 4, hi = 6` (`subarray [0, 1, 2]`), so `mid = 5` (`nums[5] = 1`, `nums[6] = 2`). Since `1 <= 2`, what updates?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[mid] = 1 <= nums[hi] = 2: right side [5..6] is rising smoothly.

choices.label: hi = mid = 5, keeping mid in play while discarding index 6
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Right! Since `nums[5] <= nums[6]`, index 6 cannot be smaller than index 5, but index 5 (or 4) could be the minimum.

choices.label: hi = mid - 1 = 4
choices.misconceptionFeedback: If `mid` itself had been the minimum (e.g., if `mid` landed on `0`), `hi = mid - 1` would discard the minimum!

steps.correctExplanation: When `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]`, the minimum is at `mid` or to its left, so `hi = mid`.

steps.prompt: Now `lo = 4, hi = 5` (`[0, 1]`), so `mid = 4` (`nums[4] = 0 <= nums[5] = 1`). How does it terminate?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[4] = 0 <= nums[5] = 1 -> hi becomes 4.

choices.label: hi becomes mid = 4; now lo === hi === 4 and nums[4] = 0 is returned
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact convergence to index 4 (`0`).

choices.label: lo becomes mid + 1 = 5 and returns 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `0 <= 1` takes the `else` branch (`hi = mid`), not `lo = mid + 1`.

steps.correctExplanation: `hi = mid` sets `hi = 4 === lo`, returning `nums[4] = 0`.

alternateVariant.label: Unrotated / Full-Cycle Sorted Array
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Proves why comparing against `nums[hi]` works even when the array was rotated 0 (or `n`) times.

steps.prompt: On `nums = [1, 3, 5, 7]`, `lo = 0, hi = 3, mid = 1` (`nums[1] = 3`, `nums[3] = 7`). Which branch executes?

choices.label: 3 <= 7 takes the else branch (`hi = 1`), rightly walking left toward index 0
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Had you compared `nums[mid] > nums[lo]` (`3 > 1`), you might have falsely walked right!

choices.label: lo = 2 because 3 > nums[0]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Walking right on an unrotated array discards the minimum at index 0!

steps.correctExplanation: `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]` shrinks `hi` leftward all the way to `0`.

steps.prompt: Next `lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0` (`nums[0] = 1 <= nums[1] = 3`). What happens?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[0] = 1 <= nums[1] = 3 -> hi becomes 0.

choices.label: hi becomes 0; loop exits and returns nums[0] = 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Zero special cases needed for unrotated inputs.

choices.label: hi becomes -1 and crashes
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `hi` is set to `mid` (`0`), never `mid - 1`.

steps.correctExplanation: `hi = mid` converges to `0` and returns `1`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: What happens if the rotated array contains duplicates such that `nums[lo] === nums[mid] === nums[hi]` (e.g., `[2, 2, 2, 0, 2]` vs `[2, 0, 2, 2, 2]`)?

choices.label: Neither half can be ruled out in O(1); you must conservatively decrement `hi -= 1` (degrading worst-case time to O(n) on all-duplicates).
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! When `nums[mid] === nums[hi]`, the minimum `0` could hide on either side of `mid`, so only `hi -= 1` is safe.

choices.label: Set `lo = mid + 1` anyway because duplicates are always on the left.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: In `[2, 0, 2, 2, 2]`, `mid = 2` has `0` on its LEFT, so `lo = mid + 1` would skip `0`!

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Duplicate plateaus where `nums[lo] === nums[mid] === nums[hi]` destroy O(1) side discrimination, requiring `hi -= 1`.

exercises.hintText: Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]`: if the middle is taller than the right edge, the cliff drop MUST be to the right of `mid`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: Why does `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` allow excluding `mid` (`lo = mid + 1`), whereas `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]` requires keeping `mid` (`hi = mid`)?

exercises.title: Trace: Converging Two-Sum Pointers on Sorted Array
exercises.objective: Step through converging `left` and `right` pointers and verify why each comparison eliminates an entire row or column of candidate pairs.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the sorted array, `left`, `right`, and `sum = nums[left] + nums[right]` at each step, then select the exact pointer transition.

primaryVariant.label: Standard Sorted Target Search
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Watch how `sum > target` eliminates `right` first, then `sum < target` eliminates `left`.

steps.prompt: Start with `left = 0` (`2`) and `right = 4` (`13`). `sum = 2 + 13 = 15 > target (13)`. Which pointer moves and why?

stateSnapshot.annotation: sum = 2 + 13 = 15 > 13. Since 2 is the smallest partner for 13, 13 is too large for every remaining index.

choices.label: Decrement right to 3 (`9`), because 13 + any element >= 2 exceeds 13
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Index 4 (`13`) cannot pair with any index in `[0..3]` without exceeding `13`.

choices.label: Increment left to 1 (`4`), to get closer to the middle
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Incrementing `left` would increase `sum` to `4 + 13 = 17`, moving even further above `target = 13`!

steps.correctExplanation: Since `sum = 15 > 13`, `right` decrements to `3`.

steps.prompt: Now `left = 0` (`2`) and `right = 3` (`9`). `sum = 2 + 9 = 11 < target (13)`. What happens next?

stateSnapshot.annotation: sum = 2 + 9 = 11 < 13. Since 9 is the largest remaining partner, index 0 (2) is too small.

choices.label: Increment left to 1 (`4`), because 2 + any remaining element <= 9 is at most 11 < 13
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Index 0 (`2`) is provably too small for all remaining partners in `[1..3]`.

choices.label: Increment right back to 4 (`13`)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Index 4 (`13`) was already eliminated in Step 0; pointers never move outward.

steps.correctExplanation: `sum = 11 < 13`, so `left` increments to `1`.

steps.prompt: Now `left = 1` (`4`) and `right = 3` (`9`). What does line 5 evaluate?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nums[1] + nums[3] = 4 + 9 = 13 === target.

choices.label: sum === 13 matches target; immediately return [1, 3]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact match! `[1, 3]` is returned in 3 comparisons instead of `O(n^2)`.

choices.label: Continue shrinking until left === right === 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Line 5 returns `[left, right]` as soon as `sum === target`.

alternateVariant.label: Negative Numbers & Target Below Zero
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Verifies that negative numbers obey the exact same sorted monotonicity.

steps.prompt: Start `left = 0` (`-8`), `right = 3` (`4`). `sum = -8 + 4 = -4 < -2`. Which pointer moves?

stateSnapshot.annotation: sum = -4 is strictly less than target = -2 (-4 < -2).

choices.label: left increments to 1 (`-3`), because -4 < -2 requires a larger sum
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Watch negative signs: `-4 < -2`, so we need a larger sum and move `left` rightward.

choices.label: right decrements to 2 (`1`), because |-4| > |-2|
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Compare signed values (`-4 < -2`), never absolute magnitudes!

steps.correctExplanation: `-4 < -2`, so `left` increments to `1`.

steps.prompt: Now `left = 1` (`-3`), `right = 3` (`4`). `sum = -3 + 4 = 1 > -2`. What happens next?

stateSnapshot.annotation: sum = 1 > -2 -> right decrements to 2 (where -3 + 1 = -2).

choices.label: right decrements to 2 (`1`), and on the next check `-3 + 1 = -2` returns [1, 2]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! `right = 2` pairs `-3` and `1` to hit `-2`.

choices.label: left increments to 2 (`1`)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Since `sum = 1 > -2`, we must decrease the sum by moving `right` left.

steps.correctExplanation: `1 > -2` decrements `right` to `2`, where `-3 + 1 === -2`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: Why must the loop condition be `while (left < right)` instead of `while (left <= right)` in Two Sum II?

choices.label: Because `left === right` would sum `nums[left] + nums[left]`, illegally using the same array element twice when `2 * nums[left] === target`.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Two Sum requires two distinct indices `left < right`.

choices.label: Because `left === right` causes an array index out-of-bounds exception.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: The index is in bounds, but it pairs an element with itself.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Strict inequality `left < right` guarantees the two chosen indices are distinct.

exercises.referenceInvariant: For all discarded indices i < left and j > right, no partner in the remaining range can form target with them.
exercises.hintText: Ask whether `nums[left] + nums[right]` is smaller or larger than `target` on the signed number line.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: Why does sorting first (`O(n log n)`) + two pointers (`O(n)`) beat a hash map when you need `O(1)` auxiliary space or 3Sum?

exercises.title: Trace: Bottleneck Wall Elimination (Container With Most Water)
exercises.objective: Trace how moving the shorter wall inward updates `best` area while safely pruning inferior containers.
exercises.instructions: At each step, compute `width * min(height[left], height[right])` and advance the bottleneck pointer.

primaryVariant.label: Outer Low Wall vs Inner Tall Pillars
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Both outer walls (`2` and `3`) are shorter than the inner pillars (`8` and `7`).

steps.prompt: Start `left = 0` (`2`), `right = 4` (`3`). `width = 4`, `min(2, 3) = 2`, so `area = 8`. Which pointer moves?

stateSnapshot.annotation: width = 4, height = min(2, 3) = 2 -> best = 8. Left wall (2) is the bottleneck.

choices.label: best becomes 8, and left increments to 1 (`8`) because height[0] = 2 <= height[4] = 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Keeping index 0 (`2`) with any narrower width could only yield area `< 8`.

choices.label: right decrements to 3 (`7`) because 7 is taller than 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: You cannot peek ahead to decide; even if `right` moved to `7`, `min(2, 7)` would still be capped at `2` with width `3` (`area = 6 < 8`)!

steps.correctExplanation: The shorter wall (`height[0] = 2`) is advanced to `left = 1`.

steps.prompt: Now `left = 1` (`8`), `right = 4` (`3`). `width = 3`, `min(8, 3) = 3 -> area = 9`. What updates?

stateSnapshot.annotation: width = 3, height = min(8, 3) = 3 -> best = 9. Now right wall (3) is the bottleneck.

choices.label: best updates to 9, and right decrements to 3 (`7`) because height[4] = 3 < height[1] = 8
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Now the right wall (`3`) is the bottleneck, so `right` moves inward.

choices.label: left increments to 2 (`5`)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Index 1 (`8`) is taller than index 4 (`3`); moving `left` would discard the tall `8` pillar!

steps.correctExplanation: `best` becomes `9` and `right` decrements to `3`.

steps.prompt: Now `left = 1` (`8`), `right = 3` (`7`). `width = 2`, `min(8, 7) = 7`. What is the new `best`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: width = 2, height = min(8, 7) = 7 -> area = 14 > 9.

choices.label: area = 2 * 7 = 14 updates best to 14, and right decrements to 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! The two inner tall pillars `[8, ..., 7]` hold area `14`.

choices.label: area = 2 * 8 = 16
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Water spills over the shorter wall `min(8, 7) = 7`, so height is `7`, not `8`.

steps.correctExplanation: `2 * min(8, 7) = 14`, updating `best` to `14`.

alternateVariant.label: Wide Low Outer Walls Beat Narrow Tall Inner Walls
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Outer `[4, ..., 4]` at width `5` (`area = 20`) vs inner `[10, 10]` at width `1` (`area = 10`).

steps.prompt: At `left = 0` (`4`), `right = 5` (`4`), `width = 5`. What is `area` and what happens on the tie `4 === 4`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: width = 5, height = min(4, 4) = 4 -> area = 20.

choices.label: best becomes 20, and left increments to 1 because height[0] <= height[5]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Neither wall can achieve `> 20` with any partner at a narrower width, so advancing `left` is completely safe.

choices.label: The algorithm must branch and try both directions recursively on a tie
choices.misconceptionFeedback: No recursion needed! Any future container using ONLY `left=0` or ONLY `right=5` is still capped at height `4` with width `< 5`.

steps.correctExplanation: On a tie, moving either pointer is safe because neither tied wall can form a larger container with any inner wall.

steps.prompt: When the pointers eventually reach `left = 2` (`10`) and `right = 3` (`10`), `area = 1 * 10 = 10`. What is returned at the end?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Inner pillars give area = 1 * 10 = 10 < best (20).

choices.label: best remains 20 from the initial outer walls and 20 is returned
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Right! `best` preserves the global maximum across all steps.

choices.label: 10 is returned because the loop ends on the tallest pillars
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `best` only updates when `area > best` (`10 < 20`).

steps.correctExplanation: The outer container (`20`) beats the narrow inner container (`10`).

edgeCaseCheck.question: When `height[left] === height[right]`, why doesn’t it matter whether you increment `left` or decrement `right`?

choices.label: Because any future container that keeps ONE of those tied walls and pairs it with an inner index has width `< right - left` and height `<= height[left]`, so neither wall can ever beat the current `(left, right)` area on its own.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Only a container where BOTH walls are strictly taller than `height[left]` can beat `(left, right)`.

choices.label: Because input arrays in Container With Most Water never contain duplicate heights.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Duplicate heights are very common (including the canonical example `[1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]`).

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: To beat a tied pair `(left, right)`, a narrower container must use two inner walls that are BOTH strictly taller than `height[left]`.

exercises.referenceInvariant: At each step, moving the shorter wall discards only pairs whose width is smaller and whose height is bounded by that same shorter wall.
exercises.hintText: Always compare `height[left]` and `height[right]`: the smaller one limits the water level and must move inward.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: Why can’t a greedy algorithm that moves toward the larger adjacent neighbor (`height[left + 1]` vs `height[right - 1]`) find the global maximum area?

exercises.title: Trace: Variable Window with Stale-Index Guard ("abba")
exercises.objective: Trace `left`, `right`, and `lastSeen` on `"abba"` to see why `lastSeen.get(ch) >= left` prevents `left` from regressing.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the current window `[left..right]` and the `lastSeen` map at each character, then choose the valid state update.

primaryVariant.label: The Classic "abba" Stale-Map Trap
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: At index 3 (`"a"`), `"a"` is in `lastSeen` at index 0, which is BEFORE `left = 2`.

steps.prompt: After `right = 0` (`"a"`) and `right = 1` (`"b"`), what are `left`, `best`, and `lastSeen`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Window "ab" [0..1] has no duplicates.

choices.label: left = 0, best = 2, lastSeen = { a: 0, b: 1 }
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Both characters are unseen so far, expanding the window to `[0..1]`.

choices.label: left = 1, best = 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `"a"` and `"b"` are distinct, so `left` remains at `0`.

steps.correctExplanation: Window `[0..1]` (`"ab"`) has length 2 and `lastSeen = { a: 0, b: 1 }`.

steps.prompt: Now `right = 2` (`"b"`). `lastSeen.get("b")` is `1 >= left (0)`. How does the window update?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Duplicate "b" at index 1 forces left to jump to 1 + 1 = 2.

choices.label: left jumps to 2 (`1 + 1`), lastSeen.set("b", 2), current window is "b" (len 1), best stays 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Right! Jumping `left` past index 1 excludes the old `"b"`.

choices.label: left increments to 1, leaving window "bb" of length 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: If `left = 1`, the window `[1..2]` still contains both `"b"`s!

steps.correctExplanation: `left` becomes `lastSeen.get("b") + 1 = 2`.

steps.prompt: Now `right = 3` (`"a"`). `lastSeen.get("a") = 0`, while `left = 2`. What does line 6 (`lastSeen.get(ch) >= left`) do?

stateSnapshot.annotation: lastSeen.get("a") = 0 < left (2), so index 0 is outside the active window!

choices.label: Because 0 < 2, line 6 is false: left stays 2, window is "ba" [2..3] (len 2), and best = 2 is returned
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! The stale `"a"` at index 0 is already left of `left = 2` and must not pull `left` backward.

choices.label: left updates to 0 + 1 = 1, making window "bba" of length 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Moving `left` backward to `1` would re-introduce the duplicate `"b"` at index 1!

steps.correctExplanation: `0 < 2` ignores the stale `"a"` outside the window, keeping `left = 2` and returning `2`.

alternateVariant.label: All Identical Characters
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Every step after index 0 triggers `left = right`, keeping window length at `1`.

steps.prompt: At `right = 1` (`"a"`), `lastSeen.get("a") = 0 >= left (0)`. What do `left` and `best` become?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Duplicate "a" immediately advances left to 1.

choices.label: left becomes 1, window is [1..1] of length 1, and best stays 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! A string of identical characters never exceeds window length 1.

choices.label: left becomes 2 (empty window) and best becomes 0
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `left` becomes `0 + 1 = 1 === right`, which is a valid 1-character window `[1..1]`.

steps.correctExplanation: `left` advances to `right` on each duplicate `"a"`, keeping `best = 1`.

steps.prompt: After `right = 2` and `right = 3` finish on `"aaaa"`, what is returned?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Final window is [3..3], best = 1.

choices.label: Returns 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! Every single-character window has length 1.

choices.label: Returns 4
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `"aaaa"` has 4 characters total, but at most 1 unique character in any substring.

steps.correctExplanation: The longest unique-character substring of `"aaaa"` has length `1`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of a variable sliding window that uses `while (set.has(s[right])) { set.delete(s[left]); left++; }` instead of jumping `left` with a `Map`?

choices.label: Still O(n) time! Even with a single-step `while` loop, `left` only increments from `0` to `n - 1` once across the entire run (at most `2n` set operations total).
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Both the `Set` shrink loop and the `Map` jump are `O(n)` time.

choices.label: O(n^2) time because there is a `while` loop nested inside a `for` loop.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Nested loops are only `O(n^2)` if the inner pointer resets on each outer step; here `left` never moves backward!

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Because `left` is monotonically non-decreasing, the inner `while` body executes at most `n` times in total across all `n` outer iterations.

exercises.referenceInvariant: At the end of iteration right, left is the minimum index such that s[left..right] contains all unique characters.
exercises.hintText: Check whether `lastSeen.get(ch)` is inside the current window (`>= left`) before moving `left`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: Why is "amortized pointer monotonicity" (`left` never moves left) the single most important proof technique for sliding windows?

exercises.title: Trace: Frequency-Constrained Window (`windowLen - maxFreq <= k`)
exercises.objective: Trace how `(right - left + 1) - maxFreq` measures the minimum replacements needed to make `[left..right]` uniform.
exercises.instructions: Follow `counts`, `maxFreq`, and `replacementsNeeded = (right - left + 1) - maxFreq` at each step.

primaryVariant.label: Replacing Minority Character (k = 1)
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: When the second `"B"` arrives at index 4, `5 - 3 = 2 > k` forces `left` to advance.

steps.prompt: After scanning indices `0..2` (`"AAB"`), `right = 2`. `counts = { A: 2, B: 1 }`, `maxFreq = 2`. Is `[0..2]` valid for `k = 1`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 3 - 2 = 1 minority character ("B") can be replaced using k = 1.

choices.label: Valid! (3 - 2 = 1 <= 1), so left stays 0 and best becomes 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Replacing the single `"B"` turns `"AAB"` into `"AAA"`.

choices.label: Invalid because "B" !== "A", so left shrinks to 2
choices.misconceptionFeedback: We are allowed `k = 1` replacement, so 1 minority character is permitted.

steps.correctExplanation: `windowLen (3) - maxFreq (2) = 1 <= k (1)`, so `best` becomes `3`.

steps.prompt: At `right = 3` (`"A"`), window is `"AABA"` (`[0..3]`). What are `maxFreq` and `best`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 4 - 3 = 1 <= 1 -> valid 4-character window!

choices.label: maxFreq updates to 3 (for "A"), 4 - 3 = 1 <= 1 is valid, and best updates to 4
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Three `"A"`s and one `"B"` need only 1 replacement.

choices.label: maxFreq stays 2 and left shrinks to 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `counts.get("A")` becomes 3, raising `maxFreq` to 3.

steps.correctExplanation: `maxFreq = 3` and `best = 4`.

steps.prompt: At `right = 4` (`"B"`), window `[0..4]` (`"AABAB"`) has `len = 5`, `counts = { A: 3, B: 2 }`, `maxFreq = 3`. Since `5 - 3 = 2 > k (1)`, what happens?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 5 - 3 = 2 > 1 -> decrement counts[s[0]] ("A") and increment left to 1.

choices.label: counts["A"] decrements to 2, left advances to 1 (window len 4), and best remains 4
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! The window shifts from `[0..3]` to `[1..4]`, maintaining size 4.

choices.label: left resets to 4 and counts is cleared
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Sliding windows shrink incrementally from `left`; they never clear the whole map.

steps.correctExplanation: `left` increments to `1`, keeping window length at `4` and returning `best = 4`.

alternateVariant.label: Zero Replacements Allowed (k = 0)
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: When `k = 0`, any character different from the majority triggers shrinking until the window is pure.

steps.prompt: After `"AAA"` (`right = 0..2`), `maxFreq = 3, best = 3`. Now `right = 3` (`"B"`) enters with `k = 0`. What is `(4 - 3) > 0`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 4 - 3 = 1 > 0 -> left advances to 1, keeping best = 3.

choices.label: 4 - 3 = 1 > 0 triggers the shrink step (left becomes 1), and best stays 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! With `k = 0`, `"AAAB"` cannot expand the valid window size beyond `3`.

choices.label: best becomes 4 because maxFreq is 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: With `k = 0`, `4 - 3 = 1 > 0` is invalid and shrinks `left` before `best` is updated.

steps.correctExplanation: Shrinking `left` to `1` keeps `right - left + 1 = 3`, so `best` stays `3`.

steps.prompt: What value does `characterReplacement("AAAB", 0)` return?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Longest contiguous homogeneous run has length 3.

choices.label: Returns 3 (from "AAA")
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact match! The three consecutive "A"s require 0 replacements.

choices.label: Returns 0 because k = 0
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `k = 0` still allows arbitrarily long runs of identical characters (`"AAA"` -> 3).

steps.correctExplanation: `"AAA"` requires 0 replacements and has length 3.

edgeCaseCheck.question: Why does `characterReplacement` still return the exact maximum valid window length even if `maxFreq` is NOT decremented when `left` shrinks?

choices.label: Because `best` only ever grows when a future window finds a strictly larger `maxFreq` (`newMaxFreq + k`); keeping historical `maxFreq` merely prevents the sliding frame from shrinking smaller than `best`.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! We only care about windows LONGER than `best`, which requires a new character frequency to beat the historical `maxFreq`.

choices.label: Because `s[left]` is never the majority character.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `s[left]` often IS the majority character (as in `"AABAB"` at `left = 0`), yet historical `maxFreq` remains sound for max-length queries.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: A window of length `L > best` is valid if and only if it contains some character with frequency `L - k > historicalMaxFreq`, which will update `maxFreq` anyway.

exercises.referenceInvariant: The maximum valid window length equals max(maxFreq + k) capped at s.length across all windows.
exercises.hintText: Compute `windowLen = right - left + 1`; if `windowLen - maxFreq > k`, you have too many minority characters and must advance `left`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: When would you NEED to maintain the exact current window frequency (or `formed` counter) instead of a historical `maxFreq`?

exercises.title: Trace: Iterative Three-Pointer Linked List Reversal
exercises.objective: Trace `prev`, `curr`, and `nextTemp` across each node flip to verify that the unvisited suffix is never orphaned.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the linked list nodes and pointer references at each step, then select the exact pointer rewiring outcome.

primaryVariant.label: Three-Node Reversal (10 -> 20 -> 30)
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Watch `10.next` flip to `null` first, then `20.next` flip to `10`, then `30.next` flip to `20`.

steps.prompt: Iteration 1 starts with `prev = null`, `curr = 10`. After `nextTemp = curr.next` (`20`) and `curr.next = prev`, what are the links and where do `prev` and `curr` advance?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 10.next now points to null; prev advances to 10; curr advances to 20.

choices.label: 10.next becomes null, prev becomes 10, and curr becomes 20 (via nextTemp)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Saving `nextTemp = 20` before setting `10.next = null` keeps the suffix `20 -> 30` reachable.

choices.label: 10.next becomes 20, prev becomes 20, and curr becomes 30
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `10` is the original head and becomes the new tail, so `10.next` must point to `prev` (`null`).

steps.correctExplanation: After Step 1: reversed prefix is `10 -> null` (`prev = 10`), and remaining suffix is `20 -> 30 -> null` (`curr = 20`).

steps.prompt: Iteration 2 starts with `prev = 10`, `curr = 20`. What holds at the end of Iteration 2?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 20.next flips to 10; prev advances to 20; curr advances to 30.

choices.label: nextTemp saves 30, 20.next flips to 10, prev advances to 20, and curr advances to 30
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! The reversed prefix is now `20 -> 10 -> null`.

choices.label: 20.next flips to null and 10 is lost
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `prev` is `10` (not `null`), so `curr.next = prev` wires `20.next = 10`.

steps.correctExplanation: Node 20 now points backward to 10 (`20 -> 10 -> null`), while `curr` moves to `30`.

steps.prompt: Iteration 3 starts with `prev = 20`, `curr = 30` (`30.next = null`). How does the loop finish?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 30.next flips to 20; prev = 30; curr = null exits loop and returns prev (30).

choices.label: 30.next flips to 20, prev becomes 30, curr becomes null, and line 10 returns prev (30 -> 20 -> 10 -> null)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! When `curr` becomes `null`, `prev` holds the new head `30`.

choices.label: Line 10 returns curr, which is null
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `curr` is `null` when the loop terminates; you must return `prev`!

steps.correctExplanation: Returning `prev` yields the reversed list `30 -> 20 -> 10 -> null`.

alternateVariant.label: Single-Node List (42 -> null)
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Verifies that a 1-node list executes 1 clean iteration and returns `42 -> null` without self-cycles.

steps.prompt: On `head = 42 -> null`, `prev = null, curr = 42`. What happens in the single iteration?

stateSnapshot.annotation: nextTemp = null; 42.next = null; prev = 42; curr = null.

choices.label: nextTemp is null, 42.next stays null, prev becomes 42, curr becomes null
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Zero special-case branches needed for a 1-element list.

choices.label: 42.next becomes 42 (self-loop)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Because `prev` started at `null`, `42.next = prev` sets `42.next = null`.

steps.correctExplanation: `prev` becomes `42` and `curr` becomes `null`.

steps.prompt: Now `curr === null` exits the `while` loop. What is returned?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Returns prev = 42 -> null.

choices.label: Returns prev (node 42 with next === null)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Node 42 is returned as the reversed head.

choices.label: Returns null
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `prev` points to node `42`.

steps.correctExplanation: Node `42` is returned intact.

edgeCaseCheck.question: When reversing a sublist inside a larger list (e.g., second half of `Reorder List` or `Palindrome Linked List`), what happens if you forget to sever `firstHalfTail.next = null` or fail to initialize `prev = null`?

choices.label: The last node of the first half still points into the old head of the second half, creating a bidirectional cycle between the two halves.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Always terminate the tail of each split sublist with `.next = null`.

choices.label: The garbage collector automatically breaks the link.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: GC never mutates live `.next` references; an unsevered link causes an infinite traversal loop.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Splitting a list into two independent chains requires setting `slow.next = null` before reversing the second half.

exercises.referenceInvariant: At the start of each loop iteration, prev is the reversed prefix (terminated by null) and curr is the unreversed suffix.
exercises.hintText: Follow the cyclic assignment chain: `nextTemp` reads `curr.next`, `curr.next` reads `prev`, `prev` reads `curr`, `curr` reads `nextTemp`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: How does drawing the gap between `prev` and `curr` make it impossible to forget `const nextTemp = curr.next`?

exercises.title: Trace: Monotonic Decreasing Stack (Daily Temperatures)
exercises.objective: Trace how a warmer day pops multiple waiting cooler indices off the monotonic stack in a single cascade.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the current index `i`, `temps[i]`, and the waiting `stack` of indices, then select the exact pop/push state transition.

primaryVariant.label: Cool Spell Followed by Multi-Pop Warm Front
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Watch `72` at index 3 pop both `69` (index 2) and `71` (index 1), while `75` (index 0) remains on the stack.

steps.prompt: After scanning `i = 0` (`75`), `i = 1` (`71`), and `i = 2` (`69`), none triggered the `while` loop because temperatures fell. What is on `stack`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Stack holds indices [0, 1, 2] with strictly decreasing temperatures [75, 71, 69].

choices.label: stack = [0, 1, 2] (representing waiting temperatures 75, 71, 69) and ans = [0, 0, 0, 0]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Cooler temperatures cannot resolve warmer predecessors, so their indices accumulate in decreasing order.

choices.label: stack = [2] because 69 overwrites 75 and 71
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Indices are only popped when a WARMER temperature (`temps[i] > temps[top]`) arrives.

steps.correctExplanation: All three indices `[0, 1, 2]` wait on the stack in decreasing temperature order.

steps.prompt: Now `i = 3` (`temps[3] = 72`). How does the `while (temps[3] > temps[stack.top])` loop execute?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 72 > 69 pops idx 2 (ans[2] = 3 - 2 = 1); then 72 > 71 pops idx 1 (ans[1] = 3 - 1 = 2); 72 <= 75 stops.

choices.label: Pops index 2 (ans[2] = 1) and index 1 (ans[1] = 2), stops at index 0 (75 >= 72), and pushes index 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! One warmer day resolves two waiting cooler days in a single cascade.

choices.label: Only pops index 2 (ans[2] = 1) and leaves index 1 (71) on the stack
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Line 5 is a `while` loop, not an `if`—since `72 > 71`, index 1 is also popped!

steps.correctExplanation: Both `69` and `71` are `< 72`, so indices `2` and `1` are popped before `3` is pushed.

steps.prompt: The loop finishes after `i = 3` with `stack = [0, 3]`. What is the final returned `ans` array?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Unpopped indices 0 and 3 keep their initial ans value of 0.

choices.label: Returns [0, 2, 1, 0], where indices 0 and 3 remain 0 because no warmer day ever followed them
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! Pre-filling `ans` with `0` handles all unpopped stack elements automatically.

choices.label: Returns [3, 2, 1, 0]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `72` is cooler than `75`, so index 0 (`75`) was never popped and stays `0`.

steps.correctExplanation: Indices `1` (`ans=2`) and `2` (`ans=1`) were resolved; `0` and `3` remain `0`.

alternateVariant.label: Duplicate Temperatures Plateau
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Tests that `70` at index 1 does NOT pop `70` at index 0 because strict `>` is required.

steps.prompt: At `i = 1` (`temps[1] = 70`), `stack` has `[0]` (`temps[0] = 70`). Does `temps[1] > temps[0]` hold?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 70 > 70 is false -> index 0 stays on stack and index 1 is pushed.

choices.label: No (70 > 70 is false); index 0 stays on the stack and index 1 is pushed, giving stack = [0, 1]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Equal temperatures are not strictly warmer, so both wait for a future day `> 70`.

choices.label: Yes; index 0 is popped with ans[0] = 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Day 1 (`70`) is the same temperature as Day 0 (`70`), not warmer!

steps.correctExplanation: Strict inequality `>` keeps both `0` and `1` waiting on the stack.

steps.prompt: At `i = 2` (`temps[2] = 73`), what happens to `stack = [0, 1]`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 73 > 70 pops idx 1 (ans[1] = 1) and idx 0 (ans[0] = 2).

choices.label: Both index 1 (ans[1] = 2 - 1 = 1) and index 0 (ans[0] = 2 - 0 = 2) are popped, returning [2, 1, 0]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Index 2 (`73`) resolves both `70`s with their respective distances `2` and `1`.

choices.label: Both get ans = 1
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Because each stack frame stored its own index (`0` vs `1`), `i - prev` computes `2 - 0 = 2` for index 0 and `2 - 1 = 1` for index 1.

steps.correctExplanation: `[2, 1, 0]` is returned.

edgeCaseCheck.question: If a problem asks for the Next GREATER OR EQUAL Element (`>=`), how should the `while` condition change?

choices.label: Change `temps[i] > temps[stack.top]` to `temps[i] >= temps[stack.top]` so equal values immediately resolve waiting predecessors (leaving the stack strictly decreasing).
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Strict `>` resolves on strictly greater (stack non-increasing); `>=` resolves on greater-or-equal (stack strictly decreasing).

choices.label: Change the loop direction to right-to-left only.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Direction alone does not change the comparison operator from `>` to `>=`.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: Matching the `while` pop operator (`>` vs `>=`) to the exact relation that resolves a waiting element keeps the stack invariant exact.

exercises.referenceInvariant: Every index currently on the stack is waiting for its first warmer day, and stack temperatures are monotonically non-increasing from bottom to top.
exercises.hintText: Compare `temps[i]` against the temperature at the index on top of the stack (`temps[stack[stack.length - 1]]`).
exercises.reflectionPrompt: How does changing the pop condition from `temps[i] > temps[top]` to `temps[i] < temps[top]` transform Next Greater Element into Next Smaller Element?

exercises.title: Trace: Top-Down Ancestor Range Propagation in Validate BST
exercises.objective: Trace `(low, high)` ancestor intervals down a binary tree to catch a deep grandchild that satisfies its parent locally but violates an ancestor bound.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the active tree node and its inherited `(low, high)` interval at each call.
codeLines: export function isValidBST(node, low = -Infinity, high = Infinity) {

primaryVariant.label: Deep Grandchild Violating Root Bound
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Node `6` is `< 15` (valid relative to parent 15), but `6 <= 10` (invalid inside right subtree of 10!).

steps.prompt: Root `10` is checked with `(-Inf, +Inf)` and left child `5` passes with `(-Inf, 10)`. Now we recurse into right child `15` (line 8). What interval `(low, high)` is passed to `node = 15`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Moving into 10.right tightens low to 10: interval (10, +Inf).

choices.label: low = 10, high = +Infinity (because every node in 10.right must be > 10)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Moving into `node.right` updates the lower bound `low` to `node.val` (`10`).

choices.label: low = -Infinity, high = 10
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `(-Infinity, 10)` was the interval for the LEFT subtree `10.left`.

steps.correctExplanation: Right child `15` inherits `(10, +Infinity)` and satisfies `10 < 15 < +Infinity`.

steps.prompt: From `node = 15` (with `low = 10, high = +Inf`), we recurse into its left child `15.left = 6` (line 7). What interval `(low, high)` is passed to `node = 6`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Moving left from 15 tightens high to 15 while keeping low = 10 -> interval (10, 15).

choices.label: low = 10, high = 15: inherited floor 10 from root and ceiling 15 from parent
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! `15.left` must be both `> 10` (right of 10) and `< 15` (left of 15).

choices.label: low = -Infinity, high = 15
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Never discard the inherited `low = 10` bound when moving left!

steps.correctExplanation: Line 7 passes `(low, node.val)` which is `(10, 15)`.

steps.prompt: Inside `isValidBST(6, 10, 15)`, what does line 3 (`node.val <= low || node.val >= high`) evaluate?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 6 <= low (10) is true -> returns false immediately!

choices.label: 6 <= 10 is true, so line 4 returns false and short-circuits the entire BST check to false
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! The ancestor bound `low = 10` catches the invalid grandchild `6` immediately.

choices.label: Returns true because 6 < 15
choices.misconceptionFeedback: While `6 < 15`, `6 <= low (10)` triggers the first half of `node.val <= low || node.val >= high`.

steps.correctExplanation: `6 <= 10` violates the lower bound inherited from root `10`, returning `false`.

alternateVariant.label: Duplicate Value Rejection ([5, 5])
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Strict BST definition requires `left < node < right`, rejecting duplicate keys.

steps.prompt: Root `5` passes `(-Inf, +Inf)` and calls `isValidBST(node.left, -Inf, 5)` on left child `5`. What happens at line 3?

stateSnapshot.annotation: node.val (5) >= high (5) is true -> returns false.

choices.label: node.val >= high (5 >= 5) is true, so it returns false
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Using `>= high` and `<= low` enforces strict inequality `<` and `>`.

choices.label: Returns true because 5 <= 5
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Standard BST validation requires strictly smaller keys on the left (`< 5`).

steps.correctExplanation: `5 >= 5` triggers line 3 and returns `false`.

steps.prompt: After `isValidBST(node.left, -Inf, 5)` returns `false`, what does the root call return?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Short-circuit && returns false.

choices.label: Short-circuits the && expression and returns false
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Once the left subtree fails, the right subtree is not even visited.

choices.label: Returns true if the right child is valid
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Both subtrees must be valid (`&&`).

steps.correctExplanation: `false && ...` short-circuits to `false`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: Why does an in-order traversal (`left`, `node`, `right`) that verifies `node.val > prevVal` also catch the `[10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20]` bug?

choices.label: Because in-order traversal visits `10` immediately before `15`’s left child `6`, and `6 > 10` is false (`prevVal = 10, node.val = 6`).
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! A binary tree is a valid BST if and only if its in-order traversal sequence is strictly increasing.

choices.label: Because in-order traversal visits nodes from bottom to top.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Post-order visits bottom-to-top; in-order visits `left -> root -> right` in sorted key order.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: In-order traversal visits `10` right before the leftmost node of `10.right` (`6`), directly testing the `10 < 6` lower bound.

exercises.referenceInvariant: Every node u in the tree satisfies low(u) < u.val < high(u), where low(u) is the largest ancestor of u that has u in its right subtree and high(u) is the smallest ancestor of u that has u in its left subtree.
exercises.hintText: When stepping into `node.left`, tighten `high = node.val`; when stepping into `node.right`, tighten `low = node.val`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: When is top-down parameter passing (`low, high`) cleaner than bottom-up return tuples (`min, max, isValid`)?

exercises.title: Trace: BFS Level-Order Queue Snapshot (`levelSize`)
exercises.objective: Trace how snapshotting `levelSize = queue.length - head` separates depth levels cleanly while children are enqueued.
exercises.instructions: Follow `queue`, `head`, `levelSize`, and `currentLevel` across each depth wave.

primaryVariant.label: Three-Level Binary Tree (3 -> 9, 20 -> 15, 7)
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Watch `levelSize` freeze the count of depth `d` nodes before depth `d + 1` children are pushed.

steps.prompt: Wave 0 begins with `queue = [3]`, `head = 0`. `levelSize = 1`. After dequeuing `3` and pushing `9` and `20`, what are `currentLevel`, `head`, and `queue`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Wave 0 finished: levels = [[3]], head = 1, active queue slice = [9, 20].

choices.label: currentLevel = [3], head = 1, and active queue slice is [9, 20] (depth 1)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Because `levelSize` was frozen at `1`, pushing `9` and `20` did not cause the `for` loop to dequeue them during Wave 0.

choices.label: currentLevel = [3, 9, 20] because 9 and 20 were pushed into queue
choices.misconceptionFeedback: The `for` loop ran `i < levelSize` (`1`), stopping after node `3`.

steps.correctExplanation: Wave 0 pushes `[3]` to `levels` and leaves `[9, 20]` in the queue for Wave 1.

steps.prompt: Wave 1 begins with active queue `[9, 20]` (`queue.length = 3, head = 1`). What is `levelSize`, and what happens as `9` and `20` are dequeued?

stateSnapshot.annotation: levelSize = 2: dequeues 9 and 20, enqueues 20’s children 15 and 7.

choices.label: levelSize = 2; dequeues 9 (leaf) and 20 (pushes 15, 7), recording currentLevel = [9, 20]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Depth 1 is cleanly grouped as `[9, 20]`, while depth 2 (`[15, 7]`) waits at the back.

choices.label: levelSize = 3; dequeues 9, 20, and 15 into currentLevel
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `queue.length - head` is `3 - 1 = 2`, not `3`!

steps.correctExplanation: `levelSize = 2` processes `9` and `20` and enqueues `15` and `7`.

steps.prompt: Wave 2 processes `[15, 7]` (`levelSize = 2`), neither of which has children. What is returned at line 16?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Queue exhausted (head === queue.length === 5).

choices.label: Returns [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact match! Each subarray corresponds to one depth level from left to right.

choices.label: Returns [3, 9, 20, 15, 7]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Each wave pushes a 1D `currentLevel` array into `levels`, producing a 2D array.

steps.correctExplanation: Three depth waves produce `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`.

alternateVariant.label: Right Side View with Deeper Left Branch
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: At depth 2, only node `4` (in the left subtree!) exists, so `4` IS visible from the right side.

steps.prompt: After Wave 0 (`[1]`) and Wave 1 (`[2, 3]`), `2` pushed its left child `4`, while `3` had no children. What is in the queue at the start of Wave 2?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Wave 2 has levelSize = 1 containing node 4 from the left subtree.

choices.label: Only node 4 (levelSize = 1), because node 3 was a leaf
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Level-order BFS visits all branches at depth 2, even when `root.right` ended early at depth 1.

choices.label: Queue is empty because node 3 had no right child
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Node 2’s child `4` was enqueued during Wave 1!

steps.correctExplanation: Node `4` is the sole node in Wave 2.

steps.prompt: If we take the last element of each level (`level[level.length - 1]`) for Binary Tree Right Side View, what is returned for this tree?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Levels are [[1], [2, 3], [4]] -> last of each level is [1, 3, 4].

choices.label: Returns [1, 3, 4], proving why walking only root.right ([1, 3]) is wrong
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! At depth 2, node `3` has ended, so node `4` in the left subtree is unobstructed from the right.

choices.label: Returns [1, 3] because 4 is a left child
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Right Side View asks for the rightmost node at EVERY depth level, even if it is a left child.

steps.correctExplanation: Taking the last node of each BFS level (`[[1], [2, 3], [4]]`) yields `[1, 3, 4]`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: What should `levelOrder(null)` return on an empty tree, and why does `const queue = [root]` without `if (!root) return []` fail?

choices.label: It must return `[]`; without the guard, `queue = [null]` has `queue.length === 1`, enters the loop, and throws a TypeError reading `node.val` on `null`.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! `[null]` is a 1-element array, not an empty queue.

choices.label: It returns `[[]]` (an array containing one empty level).
choices.misconceptionFeedback: An empty tree has 0 levels, so it must return `[]`, not `[[]]`.

exercises.referenceInvariant: At the start of outer iteration d, queue[head..queue.length-1] contains all nodes at depth d ordered left-to-right.
exercises.hintText: Freeze `levelSize = queue.length - head` at the top of the `while` loop so newly pushed children wait for the next wave.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: How would you solve Right Side View using DFS (`right` child before `left` child) by comparing `depth === result.length`?

exercises.title: Trace: Size-K Min-Heap Bouncer for K-th Largest Element
exercises.objective: Trace how a Min-Heap of capacity `k = 3` filters a stream so `minHeap[0]` always exposes the 3rd largest element.
exercises.instructions: At each stream arrival `x`, compare `x` against `minHeap[0]` (the bouncer at the root of the size-3 min-heap).

primaryVariant.label: Streaming Additions into Capacity k = 3 Min-Heap
primaryVariant.inputLabel: Initial minHeap = [4, 5, 8] (k = 3); stream: add(3), add(5), add(10)
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: The min-heap root `minHeap[0]` is the smallest of the top 3, which is the 3rd largest overall.

steps.prompt: Start with `minHeap = [4, 5, 8]` (`k = 3`, root `minHeap[0] = 4`). First call: `add(3)`. Since `minHeap.length === 3`, what happens at line 4 (`x > minHeap[0]`)?

stateSnapshot.annotation: x = 3 is not > minHeap[0] (4), so heap is unchanged and returns 4.

choices.label: 3 > 4 is false: 3 is ignored, minHeap stays [4, 5, 8], and 4 is returned in O(1)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Because 3 is smaller than all 3 elements in the heap, it cannot be in the top 3.

choices.label: 3 is pushed into minHeap, making root minHeap[0] = 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Pushing `3` would grow the heap to size 4 and make `minHeap[0]` the 4th largest instead of the 3rd largest!

steps.correctExplanation: `3 <= 4` is rejected at the door; `minHeap[0] = 4` remains the 3rd largest.

steps.prompt: Second call: `add(5)` on `minHeap = [4, 5, 8]`. Since `5 > minHeap[0] (4)`, what updates?

stateSnapshot.annotation: 5 > 4 -> pop 4, push 5 -> minHeap holds [5, 5, 8], root is 5.

choices.label: 4 is popped, 5 is pushed, minHeap becomes [5, 5, 8], and new root 5 is returned
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! The top 3 seen so far are now `8, 5, 5`, so the 3rd largest is `5`.

choices.label: 5 is ignored because 5 is already in the heap
choices.misconceptionFeedback: K-th largest counts duplicate values (sorted order `8, 5, 5, 4, 3` has `5` at index 2).

steps.correctExplanation: Evicting `4` and inserting `5` updates the top-3 multiset to `[5, 5, 8]` with root `5`.

steps.prompt: Third call: `add(10)` on `minHeap = [5, 5, 8]`. Since `10 > 5`, one `5` is popped and `10` is pushed. What is the new heap and returned 3rd largest?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Top 3 are now [5, 8, 10]; smallest of top 3 is still 5!

choices.label: minHeap holds [5, 8, 10] and returns root 5 (since the top 3 are 10, 8, 5)
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Exact! Because there were two `5`s, evicting one `5` leaves the second `5` as the new minimum of `[5, 8, 10]`.

choices.label: Returns 8 because 10 was added
choices.misconceptionFeedback: The top 3 elements are `10, 8, 5`, so the 3rd largest is `5` (`8` is the 2nd largest).

steps.correctExplanation: The top 3 elements are `{5, 8, 10}`, so `minHeap[0]` is `5`.

alternateVariant.label: Underfull Initial Heap (len = k - 1)
alternateVariant.edgeCaseNote: Verifies that when `minHeap.length < k`, even a smaller number is pushed to reach size `k`.

steps.prompt: Start with `minHeap = [7]` and `k = 2` (`minHeap.length = 1 < 2`). Call `add(3)`. Which branch executes?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Heap was underfull (size 1 < 2), so 3 is pushed without eviction -> [3, 7], returns 3.

choices.label: Line 2 (minHeap.length < k) is true: 3 is pushed without popping, giving [3, 7] and returning root 3
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Until the heap holds `k` elements, every element is in the top `k`.

choices.label: 3 is rejected because 3 < 7
choices.misconceptionFeedback: With only `[7]` and `3` seen so far, `3` IS the 2nd largest element!

steps.correctExplanation: Pushing `3` fills the heap to capacity `k = 2` (`[3, 7]`), returning `3`.

steps.prompt: Next call: `add(9)` on `minHeap = [3, 7]` (`k = 2`). What happens?

stateSnapshot.annotation: minHeap becomes [7, 9] and returns 7.

choices.label: 9 > 3 pops 3 and pushes 9, updating minHeap to [7, 9] and returning 7
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Spot on! Among `{3, 7, 9}`, the 2nd largest is `7`.

choices.label: Returns 9
choices.misconceptionFeedback: `9` is the 1st largest; the min-heap root `minHeap[0] = 7` is the 2nd largest.

steps.correctExplanation: `minHeap` holds `[7, 9]` with root `7`.

edgeCaseCheck.question: When `k` is very small compared to `n` (e.g., `k = 5, n = 1,000,000`), how does a size-`k` Min-Heap compare to sorting the array?

choices.label: The size-k Min-Heap takes O(n log k) time and O(k) space (where log_2(5) ≈ 2.3), whereas sorting takes O(n log n) time (log_2(10^6) ≈ 20) and mutates or copies all n elements.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! And if `x <= minHeap[0]` (which happens most of the time), the check is `O(1)` without even touching the heap!

choices.label: Sorting is faster because heaps require O(n^2) pointers.
choices.misconceptionFeedback: A size-`k` array heap uses `k` numbers with zero pointers.

edgeCaseCheck.explanation: A bounded heap of size `k` uses `O(k)` memory and performs `O(log k)` work only when a candidate beats the current `k`-th largest.

exercises.referenceInvariant: After processing m >= k stream items, minHeap has length k, holds the k largest items seen so far, and minHeap[0] is the k-th largest item.
exercises.hintText: First check `minHeap.length < k`; if full, only replace `minHeap[0]` when `x > minHeap[0]`.
exercises.reflectionPrompt: In `Furthest Building You Can Reach`, how does a size-`L` Min-Heap of ladder climbs automatically assign ladders to the `L` largest climbs seen so far?

exercises.title: Trace: Kahn Topological Indegree Frontier
exercises.objective: Trace Kahn’s zero-indegree queue on a 4-course diamond DAG (`0 -> 1, 2 -> 3`) and a cyclic graph (`0 -> 1 <-> 2`) to prove why a node only unlocks when its last prerequisite finishes.
exercises.instructions: Inspect the `indeg` counts and FIFO `queue` at each step and select the exact frontier transition.
codeLines: for (let u = 0; u < n; u += 1) if (indeg[u] === 0) queue.push(u);

primaryVariant.label: Diamond Dependency DAG (0 -> 1, 2 -> 3)
primaryVariant.edgeCaseNote: Course `3` has two prerequisites (`1` and `2`), so it must wait until BOTH `1` and `2` are popped.

steps.prompt: Initially `indeg = [0, 1, 1, 2]` and `queue = [0]`. After popping `u = 0` (`order = [0]`) and relaxing outgoing edges `0 -> 1` and `0 -> 2`, what are `indeg` and the active `queue`?

stateSnapshot.annotation: Popping 0 decrements indeg[1] and indeg[2] from 1 to 0 -> both 1 and 2 enter queue.

choices.label: Both indeg[1] and indeg[2] drop from 1 to 0, so both 1 and 2 are pushed onto queue = [1, 2]
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Correct! Course 0 was the only prerequisite for courses 1 and 2, so both unlock immediately.

choices.label: Nodes 1, 2, and 3 are all pushed onto the queue
choices.misconceptionFeedback: Node 3 is not a direct neighbor of 0 and still has `indeg[3] = 2`.

steps.correctExplanation: Relaxing `0 -> 1` and `0 -> 2` reduces both indegrees to `0`, enqueuing `1` and `2`.

steps.prompt: Next we dequeue `u = 1` (`order = [0, 1]`) and inspect edge `1 -> 3`. Why is course `3` NOT enqueued yet?

stateSnapshot.annotation: --indeg[3] drops from 2 to 1 (!== 0). Course 3 still waits for course 2.
